LABORATORY FINDINGS Absolute lymphocyte count ranges from 5 × 109/L to >500 × 109/L. Leukostasis is uncommon in CLL, probably because of the small size and pliability of the leukemia cells. The lymphocyte count usually gradually increases over time, but fluctuations in absolute lymphocyte count of untreated patients occur, particularly in the setting of infection. The lymphocytes are typically small and mature appearing (Fig. 105.1), but there may be variations in cell morphology, with some lymphocytes being larger or atypical, whereas others may be plasmacytoid or cleaved or there may be prolymphocytes (Fig. 105.2). Ruptured lymphocytes or “smudge” cells are commonly seen in the peripheral smear, reflecting fragility and distortion during preparation of the peripheral smear on the glass slide. Marrow infiltration with CLL is universal, affecting from 30% to 100% of the cellularity, with overall increased marrow cellularity (Fig. 105.3). The patterns of lymphoid infiltration of the marrow seen in biopsy specimens include nodular, interstitial, diffuse, or a combination. Patients with diffuse infiltration typically have advanced disease and worse prognosis. Nodular and interstitial or “nondiffuse” patterns are associated with less advanced disease and better outcomes.

Anemia (hemoglobin <11 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (platelet count <100 × 109/L) are found in a minority of patients at diagnosis but develop with disease progression. A positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is seen in approximately 25% of cases, but overt clinical autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) occurs less frequently. The incidence of a positive Coombs test increases significantly with clinical stage.37 Immune thrombocytopenia is usually diagnosed on the basis of a low platelet count in the presence of adequate numbers of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow. AUTOIMMUNE COMPLICATIONS When autoantibodies occur in CLL, they are usually directed against hematopoietic cells, resulting in AIHA, immune thrombocytopenia, immune-mediated granulocytopenia, or pure red cell aplasia; AIHA is the most common.38 The autoantibodies are typically polyclonal and usually IgG, indicating that they are not produced by the leukemic clone.39 The severity of the autoimmune phenomenon does not necessarily correlate with the severity of CLL, and such events may develop in patients whose disease is responding to therapy. Prednisone is the most commonly used treatment for autoimmune complications, with high initial response rates. It is usually given at a dose of 1 mg/kg orally and tapered once a response is noted. Transient improvement can occur with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) administration. Relapses are not uncommon. The CD20 monoclonal antibody (mAb) rituximab is used alone or in combination with chemotherapy in some patients in whom standard therapy fails.40,41 Cyclosporin A is another effective therapy and can produce good results, even in steroid-refractory patients.42 Splenectomy is also a viable therapeutic option for refractory cases.37,43 STAGING The clinical course for individuals with CLL is variable; survival times range from 2 years to over 20 years from diagnosis. In 1975, Rai et al.44 developed a staging system consisting of five stages (Rai 0 to IV) based on Dameshek’s model of orderly disease progression in CLL (Table 105.2). The Rai staging system was later modified into a three-stage system: low risk (Rai 0), intermediate risk (Rai I, II), and high risk (Rai III, IV). A similar staging system was concurrently developed in Europe by Binet et al.45 Both classifications reflect bulk of disease and extent of marrow compromise (i.e., anemia, thrombocytopenia) and are re

include clinical features and genetic, molecular, and biochemical characteristics; some are associated with one another, others are independent. The utility of prognostic factors in CLL is to inform physicians and patients about clinical expectations; potentially direct management; help identify, characterize, and stratify patients in clinical trials; and identify high-risk patients needing new and novel treatments. Only a portion of the variability in clinical outcomes can be accounted for by known prognostic factors, limiting their utility. Some unfavorable prognostic factors include a short lymphocyte doubling time (<6 months), a diffuse pattern of bone marrow infiltration, advanced age and male gender, abnormal karyotype, high serum levels of β2-microglobulin and soluble CD23, and a CLL-PLL category (11% to 54% prolymphocytes in the blood).46 Newer prognostic factors in CLL include IGHV mutation status, expression of CD38 and ZAP-70, and gene mutations. Multivariable models, prognostic indexes,27,47,48 and nomograms49 are tools to identify and utilize independent prognostic factors in weighted models for outcomes. A prognostic model integrating cytogenetic abnormalities identified by FISH with mutated NOTCH1, SF3B1, BIRC3, and TP53 was proposed as a dynamic prognostic algorithm for overall survival (OS).27 Prognostic models for OS are challenged by the chronicity of the disease and associated serial treatments, each of which can affect the overall outcome; in addition, death may be due to a related but indirect cause, such as infection or second malignancy. With new agents and treatments, factors can lose their prognostic impact, particularly if the agents affect survival such as the new small-molecule inhibitors. Predictive factors correlate with the efficacy of a particular therapy. Few predictive factors have been identified in CLL. With the currently evolving treatment landscape and given the long clinical course of CLL, predictive factors are of greater potential clinical utility. Predictive factors can be used to optimize outcomes for individual patients. PR required 50% reduction in tumor bulk (lymphadenopathy, spleen, etc.) as well as in lymphocytosis and improvement in cytopenias. Historically, computed tomography (CT) scans were not used to assess response in CLL, but with the updated 2008 IWCLL guidelines, CT scans were mandated for lymph node assessment in clinical trial. Because of the distinct pattern of response seen with the BCR inhibitors where there can be marked reduction in tumor bulk but at the same time an increase in lymphocytosis, a new category of response was defined: partial remission with persistent lymphocytosis (PRL). Patients achieving PRL meet all the criteria for PR but their baseline lymphocyte count has not decreased by 50%. In clinical trials, evaluation for minimal residual disease (MRD) is becoming more common as there are regimens with high CR rates. Patients with undetectable MRD following treatment have a longer remission duration and longer survival.51,52 Therefore, in addition to improving CR rates, investigators are focusing on eliminating MRD to improve treatment outcomes. MRD can be measured by flow cytometry or polymerase chain reaction (PCR), but in most clinical trials in CLL, particularly those in Europe, it has been done by flow cytometry. For decades, the mainstay of therapy for CLL was alkylating agents, CLB and CTX. Various doses and schedules of oral CLB were typically administered for several months, and the dose adjusted to avoid its primary toxicity, myelosuppression. The overall response (OR) rate with either CLB or CTX monotherapy as initial therapy is approximately 40% to 60%, with 3% to 5% CR. Alkylating agents were combined with steroids to improve response rates but this increased immunosuppression. Alkylating agent–based combinations have also included an anthracycline. No superior alkylating agent combination has been identified. Bendamustine has a benzimidazole (purine-like) ring structure with an alkylating group and has potent alkylating agent activity, inducing intra- and interstrand DNA crosslinks. Bendamustine was compared to CLB in a randomized phase III trial for previously untreated patients with CLL (Table 105.4).54 Treatment with bendamustine was associated with superior PFS (21.6 versus 8.3 months), and CR (31% versus 2%) and OR (68% versus 31%) rates. Myelosuppression was mild and more frequent with bendamustine but did not result in an increased infection rate. Purine analogs, including fludarabine monophosphate, 2-chlorodeoxyadenosine (2-CdA), and pentostatin (deoxycoformycin), all have activity in treating patients with CLL.55 The major side effects associated with fludarabine are myelosuppression and immunosuppression, with low CD4 counts lasting for many months to years after completion of treatment.55 An oral formulation of fludarabine is available. Several phase III clinical trials of fludarabine versus alkylating agent–based therapy demonstrated improved responses and PFS with fludarabine in both first-line and relapsed settings (see Table 105.4).56–59 There was no improvement in OS seen in these studies. The German CLL Study Group (GCLLSG) CLL5 trial evaluated fludarabine versus CLB monotherapy as initial treatment for patients older than 65 years.59 Surprisingly, whereas treatment with fludarabine was associated with superior CR (7% versus 0%) and OR (72% versus 51%) rates, there was no associated improvement in PFS or OS for these “older” patients. Thus, standard first-line treatment for patients older than 65 years does not require fludarabine. B-Cell Signaling Pathway Inhibitors for Treatment of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia CLL cells receive stimulation, including growth and survival signals, from the microenvironment of bone marrow, lymph nodes, and spleen. The microenvironment provides signals directing CLL cell proliferation and survival through binding and ligation of surface receptors and soluble factors such as cytokines and chemokines. Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) has emerged as a central intracellular signal transduction molecule in CLL cell interactions with the microenvironment and for survival.99 X-linked agammaglobulinemia results from a mutation in BTK, leading to a lack of mature B cells. BTK is essential in the Akt, extracellular signal–regulated protein kinase (Erk), and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling pathways of B cells. BTK is a central molecule in signal transduction for the BCR as well as CD19, CD38, CD40, C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4 (CRCX4), tumor necrosis factor receptors, and Toll-like receptors. BCR signaling and interaction of CLL cells with the microenvironment involve complex biochemical cascades and protein interactions for intracellular signaling. Other key signal transduction molecules include phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) and spleen tyrosine kinase. Cellular Therapy for CLL Immune-based cellular therapy takes advantage of the ability of the immune system to seek out and eliminate malignant cells in the body. It potentially provides a mechanism of surveillance to prevent recurrence of disease. Allogeneic stem cell transplant (allo-SCT) is a form of immune cellular therapy, which is potentially curative for some patients with CLL. Another strategy of immune cellular therapy has been developed, based on T-cell expression of chimeric antigen receptors (CARs). Chimeric Antigen Receptor–Bearing T-cell Therapy CARs are engineered molecules composed of an external antigen-binding domain (single-chain Ig variable genes), a stalk and transmembrane region, an intracellular costimulatory signaling domain and CD3-zeta. Costimulatory signaling domains include CD28 and CD137 (41BB) to provide a “second signal” to fully activate and expand T cells upon antigen binding. Viral vectors are typically used to introduce the CAR gene into T cells ex vivo where they integrate into the genome for stable expression by the transduced T cells. When T cells expressing the CAR are exposed to the respective antigen, binding triggers activation and expansion of the CAR T cells, and elimination of cells with target antigen. The binding domain of the CAR can be directed against any surface antigen. Normal B cells, and malignant counterparts, including CLL, express surface CD19, which was targeted with a CAR in this treatment strategy.125–128 Other molecules are also being targeted, such as ROR1, in CAR T- cell strategies for CLL. PROLYMPHOCYTIC LEUKEMIA PLL is characterized by a high number of circulating prolymphocytes, splenomegaly, minimal lymphadenopathy, and a median survival of <3 years. This leukemia can be present at diagnosis or evolve from CLL.147 Prolymphocytes are larger and less homogeneous than CLL cells and have abundant clear cytoplasm, clumped chromatin, and a prominent nucleolus. Prolymphocytes can be of either B- or T-cell type. B-PLL cells usually do not express CD5 but stain strongly for surface Ig and FMC7 (see Table 105.1). In 20% of cases of PLL, T-cell markers are expressed. Splenectomy and lymphoma-like regimens have been used to treat PLL without much success. Nucleoside analog–based regimens appear to be the most effective, and alemtuzumab has shown promising activity in T-PLL; there is as of yet minimal data describing the use of novel small molecules approved for CLL in the treatment of PLL.148 LARGE GRANULAR LYMPHOCYTE LEUKEMIA Large granular lymphocytes (LGLs) are larger than normal lymphocytes and contain azurophilic granules in their cytoplasm. LGLs comprise 10% to 15% of peripheral blood mononuclear cells and are predominantly of NK cell phenotype, a smaller proportion being of T-cell phenotype. There are generally four lymphoproliferative disorders of LGL: reactive/transient LGL expansion, chronic LGL lymphocytosis, indolent LGL leukemia, and aggressive LGL leukemia.149 Clonal expansion of LGL can be of NK cell or T-cell phenotype; the T-cell phenotype comprises 80% of LGL leukemias. T-LGL cells have a CD3+/CD57+/CD56− immunophenotype, and NK-LGL cells express CD3−/CD561+/CD57−. Clonality in T-LGL leukemia may be established by T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies. T-LGL leukemia is usually indolent. Patients present with cytopenias, including neutropenia with accompanying infections, pure red cell aplasia, thrombocytopenia, and anemia. Serologic abnormalities, such as the presence of rheumatoid factor or antinuclear antibody, or both, hypergammaglobulinemia, and high β2-microglobulin are frequent. A small percentage of LGL leukemias have a more aggressive course, and these cases tend to have an NK cell phenotype. Because lymphocyte counts are usually not elevated, the diagnosis requires a high degree of suspicion and a careful examination of the peripheral blood smear and bone marrow. List INTRODUCTION The myelodysplastic syndromes (MDSs) represent a spectrum of hematopoietic stem cell malignancies that share morphologic features of dysplasia, ineffective hematopoiesis, and a risk for leukemia evolution. The hallmark of early disease is accelerated apoptosis and proliferation of bone marrow precursors that drives increased marrow cellularity and peripheral cytopenias. In advanced disease, increasing maturation impairment is accompanied by the acquisition of survival signals that leads to increasing proportions of myeloblasts. MDSs are clonal stem cell neoplasms that arise from interplay of genetic and epigenetics events with altered microenvironmental pressures that are senescence and inflammation dependent. Although the risk of progression to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) varies, the majority of patients succumb to complications related to cytopenias.1 HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE The description of MDS dates back to early 1900s when reference was first made to a group of patients with a form of anemia refractory to available treatments. The term anemia pseudoaplastica was one of the earliest descriptions of MDS.2 In the late 1940s, it was thought that the disease progresses to leukemia, and, hence, the term preleukemia was applied.3 The definition was expanded to include peripheral blood descriptors such as neutropenia and thrombocytopenia in the early 1950s.4 The French-American-British (FAB) group coined the term myelodysplastic syndromes in a series of proposals on acute leukemias in 1976 and later expanded the FAB classification in 1980s.5,6 The original FAB classification included only two categories: refractory anemia with excess blasts (RAEB) and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML), to which others were added in 1982. In 1997, the International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS) was introduced.7 Under the auspices of the World Health Organization (WHO), the pathologic classification of MDS was refined and later revised in 2008 and 2016.1,8–10 New prognostic models were later introduced, such as the WHO Prognostic Scoring System, the Global MD Anderson Risk Model, the Lower Risk MD Anderson Model, and, more recently, the revised-IPSS (IPSS-R).11–14 Recent years witnessed acceleration in understanding the disease biology and associated molecular geneti

Familial/genetic predisposition contributes to a small proportion of MDS cases.21 There is an increased risk of MDS among inherited bone marrow failure syndromes, such as Fanconi anemia, dyskeratosis congenita, severe congenital neutropenia, and Shwachman–Diamond syndrome.21 Familial cases of MDS beyond bone marrow failure syndromes are well recognized and molecularly distinct. Two important familial syndromes are the familial platelet disorder with a propensity to myeloid malignancy, arising from an autosomal-dominant RUNX-1 germline gene mutation that results in thrombocytopenia with a corresponding frequency of MDS/AML in carriers that approaches 50%22 and familial MDS/AML with GATA2 mutation, which is also autosomal dominant but with variable penetrance.23 A recent study using exome sequencing of tumor and matched normal samples from 26 familial MDS/AML cases and asymptomatic carriers identified recurrent mutations in the cohesin-associated factor PDS5B, co- occurrence of somatic ASXL1 mutations with germline GATA2 mutations, and recurrent mutations in other known MDS/AML drivers. In 67% of asymptomatic RUNX1 carriers, clonal skewing of hematopoiesis was observed, stipulating a potential biomarker for surveillance in high-risk families.24 Acquisition of somatic gene mutations with aging is demonstrable in 10% to 20% of older individuals older than the age of 70 years termed clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP). Those with CHIP progress at a rate of 0.5% to 1% per year to MDS and other hematologic malignancies.25,26 Benzene exposure is a well-recognized environmental exposure linked to AML/MDS.27 The risk of MDS but not AML was increased among petroleum distribution workers at relatively lower levels of exposure in a dose- dependent manner.28 Cigarette smoking had also been associated with an increased risk of developing MDS. PATHOGENESIS MDS is a clonal disease driven by acquisition and expansion of genetic alterations that interplay with inflammation and immune deregulation in the bone marrow (Fig. 106.2). The clonal nature of many MDS cases was first apparent by the conventional metaphase karyotype analysis. Studies leveraging restriction fragment length polymorphisms of X-chromosome genes in females, single nucleotide polymorphism arrays, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase analyses confirmed that hematopoiesis is clonal across all subtypes of MDS.54–57 The two most comprehensive studies demonstrating the frequency and nature of chromosome abnormalities in MDS confirmed that approximately 50% of patients with MDS harbor a chromosome abnormality.58,59 The most common recurrent abnormalities were del(5q) (30%), −7 or 7q− (21%), and +8 (16%). Deletion of genes encoded within the commonly deleted region (CDR) of humandel(5q) MDS is sufficient to induce an MDS phenotype, indicating that these recurrent genetic lesions are critical to the development of the disease.60 In addition to large chromosomal deletions or duplications, DNA sequencing technology has uncovered gene mutations that aggregate within

Lastly, the specific type and number of gene mutations directly impacts clinical behavior and risk of progression to AML. Elegant work using whole genome sequencing to reconstruct the clonal architecture of MDS cases that transform to AML at sequential time points demonstrates that this transformation is associated with the acquisition and expansion of distinct genetic events.79 Emerging data, however, suggest that these events do not display complete fidelity. That is, the same genetic events can be responsible for disease initiation, and therefore, disease founding in one case while representing a secondary event in another case with the same diagnosis. Collectively, these and other gene mutations described in Table 106.2 demonstrate that distinct genetic events can result in MDS and are likely the major drivers of the disease and its behavior. Dysregulation of Immunity as a Driver in Myelodysplastic Syndromes The environmental cues that are conducive to emergence of the genetic events that lead to MDS are unknown. Bone marrow stromal alterations have been implicated, but an intriguing emerging hypothesis that immune dysregulation and associated chronic inflammatory changes may be a critical environmental pressure in MDS pathogenesis. Clinical and laboratory evidence suggests that both adaptive and innate immunity is altered and potentially contributory to MDS pathogenesis. For patients with a higher risk, the goal of therapy is to alter the natural history of the disease and to extend survival. The goal of therapy in lower risk MDS is to alleviate symptomatic cytopenias using treatments that may restore effective hematopoiesis and lessen associated complications. The prognosis will depend on the inherent disease’s specific features and host-related features. Risk models in MDS are constructed by incorporating several validated prognostic variables in a weighted scoring system, permitting patients to be divided into defined risk groups. The International Prognostic Scoring System The IPSS remains the most widely used staging system in MDS.7 It has been embraced by community oncologists, adopted in clinical trials, and forms the basis of determining the time table for allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT) in decision models. However, IPSS has several shortcomings. It was not developed as a dynamic system, it does not account for severity of cytopenias, and it overlooks two-thirds of the cytogenetic abnormalities encountered. Moreover, the IPSS is not applicable to patients with MDS/MPN or t-MDS. The Revised International Prognostic Scoring System The IPSS-R was proposed as a refinement to adjust for those deficiencies of the original IPSS.13 The major changes include the incorporation of less common karyotype abnormalities, the prognostic relevance of which was discerned from the larger patient cohort, and the weighing of the severity of each lineage of cytopenia. Several groups have validated the new prognostic system.110,111 IPSS-R was developed for untreated MDS patients based on clinical data. A recently validated new model attempts to incorporate mutational data in IPSS-R to make it dynamic and enhance its predictive ability in treated MDS patients regardless of their initial or subsequent therapies.112 The Global MD Anderson Scoring System The Global MD Anderson Scoring System (MDAS) incorporates host factors such as age and performance status12 as well as anemia, transfusion burden, karyotype, and, most importantly, the severity of thrombocytopenia. Vincent Rajkumar and Shaji Kumar INTRODUCTION Plasma cell neoplasms encompass a spectrum of disorders that include monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), smoldering multiple myeloma (SMM), multiple myeloma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. MGUS represents one end of the spectrum, an asymptomatic premalignancy, whereas multiple myeloma and Waldenström macroglobulinemia are serious malignancies representing the other end of the spectrum. SMM is an intermediate entity comprising a mixture of patients who share a similar clinical phenotype but are biologically heterogeneous, with some having premalignancy (MGUS) and some having occult malignancy (multiple myeloma). In addition to these disorders, because plasma cells normally secrete antibodies (immunoglobulins), a clonal premalignant or malignant proliferation of these cells can lead to multiple other well- established diseases depending on the idiosyncratic physical or functional properties of the secreted antibody. Important disorders in this category include cryoglobulinemia, immunoglobulin light chain (AL) amyloidosis, and light chain deposition disease (Table 107.1).1 Because they arise from a single clone, secreted antibodies in plasma cell neoplasms are electrophoretically and immunologically homogeneous (monoclonal proteins). They share the same heavy and light chain immunoglobulin types and can be readily identified on protein electrophoresis or immunofixation. Monoclonal proteins are commonly referred to as M proteins, myeloma proteins, or paraproteins. In the majority of clonal plasma cell disorders, intact immunoglobulin molecules are secreted as M proteins. However, in most patients with multiple myeloma and approximately one-third of patients with MGUS, there is additional secretion of excess monoclonal free light chains (FLCs) that circulate unbound to immunoglobulin heavy chains (IgH). In some patients, heavy chain expression is completely lost, and only monoclonal FLCs (commonly referred to as Bence Jones proteins) are secreted. Rarely, only heavy chains are secreted, resulting in heavy chain diseases. Approximately 2% of patients with multiple myeloma secrete no identifiable immunoglobulin (nonsecretory myeloma). Thus, in 2014, the International Myeloma Working Group revised the diagnostic criteria for multiple myeloma, allowing the use of specific biomarkers in addition to traditional end-organ damage to define the disease, which represents a major paradigm shift. The diagnosis of multiple myeloma now requires 10% or more clonal bone marrow plasma cells (BMPCs) in the bone marrow and/or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma plus one or more of the following multiple myeloma-defining events (MDE): evidence of end-organ damage (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, or bone lesions) attributable to the underlying plasma cell disorder, 60% or more clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow, serum involved/uninvolved FLC ratio #x2265;100 (provided involved FLC level is #x2265;100 mg/L), or more than one focal lesion (#x2265;5 mm in size) on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (see Table 107.1).2–8 In addition, the new diagnostic criteria also allow the use of computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography (PET)-CT to diagnose myeloma bone disease. These changes enable early diagnosis and allow the initiation of effective therapy in order to prevent the development of end-organ damage in patients who are at the highest risk.9–13 Incidence and Prevalence Multiple myeloma accounts for approximately 10% of hematologic malignancies. In a study conducted in Olmsted County, Minnesota, the annual incidence, age-adjusted to the 2000 U.S. population, was 4.3 per 100,000 (95% confidence interval [CI], 3.0 to 5.5 per 100,000).14 In this study, Poisson regression analysis showed no statistically significant differences in incidence rates over six decades. Approximately 30,000 new cases are expected to occur in the United States in 2017.15 Although these numbers appear to have risen over the past decade, such differences likely reflect increased awareness and disease detection and changes in diagnostic criteria. PATHOGENESIS Establishment of Premalignant Clone Almost all patients with multiple myeloma evolve from the asymptomatic premalignant stage termed MGUS. MGUS is present in over 3% of the population older than age 50 years and progresses to multiple myeloma or related malignancy at a rate of 1% per year.18,19 The sequence of events by which normal plasma cells transform to a premalignant clone is unclear but likely starts when plasma cells are dividing in response to antigenic stimulation (Fig. 107.1). During this period of antigenic stimulation, dividing plasma cells are felt to acquire the key first hit (primary cytogenetic abnormality) resulting in the establishment of the premalignant MGUS clone. The rate of progression of MGUS to multiple myeloma or related malignancy is remarkably stable at 1% per year regardless of the known duration of antecedent MGUS, indicating that this second hit is a random event and not caused by a cumulative damage model.18 Recent studies using gene sequencing indicate that there are two main paths by which the progression event occurs, MYC translocations and mutations in the MAP kinase pathway. In one study, MYC structural variants (translocations, inversions, and duplications) were not detected in MGUS or in patients with SMM who did not progress over the 5 years but were detected in 49% of patients with SMM who progressed within 2 years. Patients with MYC structural variants had a significantly shorter median time to progression (TTP) compared to patients without such abnormalities (median TTP, 11.5 versus 61 months, respectively; P #x003C; .0001).32 In another study, mutations in MAPK pathway genes, namely KRAS, NRAS, and BRAF, were detected in 21.7% of patients with high-risk SMM versus 0% of patients with low-risk SMM (P = .004).33 Other abnormalities associated with progression include chromosome 1q21 (gain 1q), p16 methylation, and p53 mutations. In a series of patients with a spectrum of plasma cell neoplasms, gain 1q was seen in over 40% of patients with SMM and multiple myeloma compared to 0% of patients with MGUS.34 In addition to these changes, there are also additional genetic abnormalities that occur in subpopulations, resulting in significant clonal heterogeneity, which eventually leads to altered drug sensitivity patterns as a different dominant clone emerges through the course of various treatments.35 Besides the key second-hit events occurring in the tumor cell described earlier, progression is also accompanied by dramatic changes in the bone marrow microen

Osteoblast inhibition is mediated by increased dickkopf 1 (DKK-1) expression by myeloma cells.44 DKK-1 inhibits the Wnt signaling pathway by binding to Wnt receptors and thereby preventing the normal binding of Wnt glycoproteins to Wnt receptors.41 The inhibition of Wnt signaling prevents the intracellular stabilization of β- catenin, leading to the phosphorylation and degradation of β-catenin through the proteasome pathway. Normally, β-catenin plays an important role in osteoblast activation, and its absence reduces the activity of osteoblasts. Increased levels of DKK-1 may also play a role in osteoclast activation. Further, cytokines such as IL-3 and IL-7 may also contribute to osteoblast inhibition. The combination of osteoclast activation and inhibition of osteoblast differentiation is felt to be the mechanism behind the development of osteolytic lesions in multiple myeloma. CYTOGENETIC CLASSIFICATION Myeloma can be classified into subtypes based on the primary cytogenetic abnormalities in clonal plasma cells that occur with the onset of MGUS (see Table 107.2).45,46 Although each cytogenetic type probably represents a unique disease, due to similarities in clinical phenotype and the relative rarity of the disease, each is still considered a subtype of multiple myeloma.45 Accordingly, the six main cytogenetic subtypes of multiple myeloma are trisomies t(11;14), t(4;14), t(6;14), t(14;16), and t(14;20).22–24 Approximately 10% of patients have both trisomies and one of the IgH translocations.45 A small subset of patients have other cytogenetic abnormalities in the absence of one of the primary six cytogenetic abnormalities, including monosomy 14, and rarer translocations involving the IgH locus on chromosome 14q32 and an uncommon partner chromosome. No abnormalities can be detected on clinical fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) studies in some patients, but this is most likely due to insufficient plasma cells or inadequate probes to identify the underlying cytogenetic type. Most if not all of these patients will have an identifiable primary cytogenetic abnormality on sequencing studies. It is likely that these translocations play an important pathogenetic role in the resultant limited clonal proliferation that is clinically

manifested as MGUS. CLINICAL FEATURES Most patients with myeloma present with bone pain from osteolytic lesions or fatigue and weakness from anemia.17 Osteolytic bone lesions may cause pathologic fractures of the long bones and vertebral compression fractures. Bone pain may be persistent or migratory, often in the lower back and pelvis. Pain may be sudden in onset when associated with a pathologic fracture. Extramedullary expansion of vertebral bone lesions may cause nerve root or spinal cord compression. Bone lesions in myeloma can be readily detected on routine radiographs, MRI, CT scans, or fluorodeoxyglucose PET-CT scans. Anemia occurs in 70% of patients at diagnosis and is the primary cause of fatigue and weakness. In most patients, anemia is commensurate to the extent of bone marrow involvement. However, in some patients, there is a disproportionate level of anemia relative to bone marrow infiltration, possible due to cytokine-mediate suppression of normal hematopoiesis. Leukopenia and thrombocytopenia can occur in the newly diagnosed setting but are more common in relapsed disease. Approximately 15% of patients present with acute renal failure. In most patients, renal failure is related to high amounts of serum FLC levels causing light chain cast nephropathy (Fig. 107.3). Other causes include prerenal failure, drug-induced nephrotoxicity, hyperuricemia, and hypercalcemia. Hypercalcemia is found in one-fourth of patients and is usually found in the context of myeloma bone disease. Most myeloma patients have suppression of uninvolved normal immunoglobulins and are immunosuppressed. Thus, throughout the clinical course of the disease, patients are at increased risk of infections. In some patients, bony plasmacytomas can protrude out through the cortical bone and become visible and/or palpable. Soft tissue and extramedullary plasmacytomas can also occur, usually in patients with aggressive disease at diagnosis or in patients with advanced relapsed disease. In occasional patients, multiple myeloma can present with multiple plasmacytomas with no significant bone marrow involvement. These patients are also considered to have multiple myeloma and are managed as such. Serum Free Light Chain Assay. The serum FLC assay provides an important tool to quantify monoclonal light chains secreted by myeloma cells, especially in patients who secrete small amounts of intact monoclonal immunoglobulin. This automated nephelometric assay allows quantitation of free #x03BA; and #x03BB; chains (i.e., light chains that are not bound to intact immunoglobulin) secreted by plasma cells. It is more sensitive that electrophoresis or IFE in detecting monoclonal FLCs. Patients with a #x03BA;/#x03BB; FLC ratio below the normal range are defined as having monoclonal #x03BB; FLC, and those with ratios above the normal range are defined as having a monoclonal #x03BA; FLC. Assessment of Bone Disease The preferred method to detect bone disease in multiple myeloma is whole-body low-dose CT. By this method, more than 80% to 90% of patients with multiple myeloma will show evidence of bone disease. The osteolytic bone lesions in multiple myeloma have a characteristic punched-out appearance. Osteoporosis and/or fractures can also be present. Occasionally, osteosclerotic lesions can occur. If whole-body low-dose CT is not available, conventional radiography can be used to detect bone disease but is less sensitive and often more cumbersome to the patient. Fluorodeoxyglucose PET-CT is an equally sensitive alternative to whole-body low-dose CT49 and is of particular value in monitoring response to therapy in patients with oligosecretory multiple myeloma, in assessing extramedullary disease, and whenever there is a concern that the adequacy of disease assessment may be inadequate with other imaging modalities (Fig. 107.5A). MRI is of particular value in assessing spinal involvement and in the assessment of possible spine cord compression (Fig. 107.5B). MRI and/or PET-CT or whole-body low-dose CT are also required to differentiate SMM and solitary plasmacytoma from multiple myeloma. Bone Marrow Examination A unilateral bone marrow aspiration and biopsy is indicated in all patients with multiple myeloma. Almost all patients with multiple myeloma will have 10% or more clonal BMPCs. If a lower extent of involvement is detected, one is either dealing with an erroneous diagnosis or there is a sampling error due to patchy marrow involvement, in which case a repeat marrow biopsy is indicated. The monoclonal (or more accurately monotypic) nature of BMPCs is established by the demonstration of an abnormal #x03BA;/#x03BB; ratio on multiparametric flow cytometry. On flow cytometry, plasma cells in multiple myeloma typically stain positive for CD38 and CD138, are usually negative for CD45 and CD19, and are positive only for one of the two light chain isotypes, indicating they are monoclonal (either #x03BA; or #x03BB;). Up to 20% of myeloma cells may stain positive for CD20. Morphologically, the presence of immature “blast”-like plasma cells (plasmablastic morphology) carries an adverse prognosis. Given their impact on prognosis (see “Prognosis” section later in this chapter), bone marrow sample FISH studies or other molecular methods must be performed to detect trisomies, the five most common IgH translocations, MYC translocations, and abnormalities of chromosomes 1, 13, and 17.50 The BMPC proliferative rate (S phase) should be estimated by multiparametric flow cytometry, if available. Gene expression profiling studies, if done, can provide additional prognostic information.51,52 DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS Multiple myeloma is usually suspected in patients who present with unexplained lytic bone lesions, anemia, hypercalcemia, or acute renal failure. There are multiple staging systems that have been used to estimate tumor burden, provide prognostic information, and aid comparison of results across clinical trials in multiple myeloma (Table 107.3).53,54 The Durie-Salmon staging system provides the best estimate of true tumor burden but is cumbersome to use and has subjective elements that make it less reproducible.55 The International Staging System uses serum albumin and β2- microglobulin levels only and discriminates three prognostic groups (see Table 107.3).53 The International Staging System has been recently replaced by the Revised International Staging System (RISS) (see Table 107.3).54 The RISS incorporates important markers of disease biology including cytogenetics to provide a more accurate estimation of prognosis than prior staging systems. However, the RISS is not a true staging system; it does not measure tumor burden but is rather a prognostic index that incorporates elements of host characteristics, tumor burden, renal function, and disease aggressiveness. TREATMENT The treatment of multiple myeloma depends on risk stratification and eligibility for stem cell transplantation. Eligibility for stem cell transplantation is determined by age, performance status, and coexisting comorbidities. Multiple myeloma is a disease of remissions and relapses. Few patients achieve a permanent disease-free state in the absence of ongoing therapy (true cure). With modern therapy, myeloma patients achieve an initial remission that lasts approximately 3 to 4 years. Subsequent remissions are of shorter duration. Given the multitude of available treatment options, patients with multiple myeloma are not uncommonly treated with five or more lines of therapy in a sequential manner over many years. At present, it is not clear whether treatment should be modified to try and achieve an MRD-negative state; trials in this regard are ongoing. The toxicity of additional therapy to achieve and maintain an MRD-negative state needs to be balanced against the possible benefits of improved long-term survival.63,64 In the absence of data from well-designed trials in which MRD status is used as an integral biomarker, modifying therapy based on MRD results is not recommended for clinical p

Table 107.6 lists the most common regimens used in the treatment of multiple myeloma.61,68– 78 This section provides an overview of the active drugs used in the treatment of myeloma, including mechanism of action, side effects, and dosage. Alkylating Agents. Alkylating agents, especially melphalan and cyclophosphamide, have been used in the treatment of multiple myeloma for decades, typically in combination with corticosteroids. They are directly cytotoxic to myeloma cells. Melphalan and prednisone (MP) was the standard frontline treatment of multiple myeloma from the 1960s to the 2000s. Melphalan acts slowly, and the appropriate dosage may be difficult to establish in some patients. It has fallen out of favor because of the long-term risk of leukemia and marrow toxicity. Melphalan is still used in combination with other agents in the treatment of multiple myeloma in resource-constrained settings. Randomized studies have shown that the combination of melphalan, prednisone, and thalidomide (MPT) improves response rates compared with MP.79–84 OS was improved in three trials.79,80,83 However, MPT is inferior to lenalidomide plus low-dose dexamethasone (Rd)85 and hence is not recommended any longer as initial therapy if lenalidomide is available. The combination of bortezomib plus MP (VMP) is associated with significantly improved OS compared with MP.86,87 It is still commonly used in countries that lack access to lenalidomide in the frontline setting. At present, the main role for melphalan is in the setting of ASCT, where it is used in high doses as the conditioning regimen. Melphalan is available in both oral and intravenous formulations. A newer version of intravenous melphalan, Captisol-enabled melphalan, was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2016 for use in myeloma as a conditioning agent prior to ASCT and for palliative use in patients who are not candidates for oral therapy. Captisol-enabled melphalan contains a specially modified cyclodextrin that improves the solubility and stability of melphalan, eliminating the need for propylene glycol, an additive that can cause renal and cardiac side effects. However, given higher cost and limited incremental benefits, conventional melphalan remains the preferred option for most patients and clinical settings. Cyclophosphamide has a more predictable dose response and fewer side effects than melphalan. It is currently used in several treatment regimens for the treatment of newly diagnosed and relapsed myeloma, typically in a once-weekly dosing schedule. Cyclophosphamide is used intravenously in patients who are unable to tolerate oral therapy and when used as a stem cell–mobilizing agent prior to ASCT. Corticosteroids. Corticosteroids have been an essential component of myeloma therapy for decades. They are present in most active myeloma regimens. They are directly cytotoxic to myeloma cells. High doses of dexamethasone administered in a pulsed manner (40 mg on days 1 to 4, 9 to 12, and 17 to 20 every 28 days) can be used for a short duration of time (1 to 2 months) in patients with aggressive relapse or in the setting of acute renal failure. However, in most patients, and for long-term therapy, the once-weekly dosing is preferred. In a randomized trial conducted by the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG), lenalidomide in combination with high-dose dexamethasone was associated with significantly inferior OS and higher grade 3 or 4 toxicity compared with Rd.68 As a result, the low-dose dexamethasone schedule (20 to 40 mg once weekly) is now the preferred schedule for corticosteroids used in myeloma and is the established backbone of most regimens. Even older regimens that were developed using the high-dose pulsed dexamethasone schedule are now modified to use the low-dose dexamethasone schedule. The lowercase “d” is used to indicate the preferred use of the low-dose once-weekly schedule in dexamethasone-containing regimens. The usual dosage of lenalidomide is 25 mg on days 1 to 21 orally every 28 days, adjusted lower depending on tolerance. In elderly patients, it is reasonable to start at lower doses (10 to 15 mg). Pomalidomide is a newer analog of lenalidomide and thalidomide first approved by the FDA in 2013 for the treatment of relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma.93 Schey et al.94 showed remarkable single-agent activity of pomalidomide in a small phase I trial in relapsed refractory multiple myeloma. It has significant activity in relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, even in patients failing lenalidomide93,95 or lenalidomide and bortezomib.69,96 As with lenalidomide and thalidomide, strict precautions to prevent pregnancy are needed for patients taking pomalidomide. All patients also need DVT prophylaxis. Side effects are similar to lenalidomide. The usual dosage is 2 to 4 mg daily orally on days 1 to 21 every 28 days. Although, thalidomide, lenalidomide, and pomalidomide are termed immunomodulatory agents, their exact mechanism of action is still unclear. Immunomodulatory agents bind to cereblon and activate cereblon E3 ligase activity, resulting in the rapid ubiquitination and degradation of two specific B-cell transcription factors, Ikaros family zinc finger proteins Ikaros (IKZF1) and Aiolos (IKZF3).97–99 They may cause direct cytotoxicity by inducing free radical–mediated DNA damage.100 They also have antiangiogenic, immunomodulatory, and tumor necrosis factor-α inhibitory properties. Radiation therapy is effective but must be avoided except in select circumstances for most patients because it affects bone marrow reserves and may compromise the administration of other effective treatments including ASCT. Currently, radiation therapy is used primarily for palliation in settings where systemic therapy is not effective. It is also used for the treatment of urgent complications such as spinal cord compression. Radiation therapy is the mainstay of therapy for solitary plasmacytoma, where it is administered with curative intent. In the past, total-body radiation was combined with high-dose melphalan in the conditioning regimen prior to ASCT, but this has added toxicity and is inferior to high-dose melphalan alone and is no longer recommended. Infections Patients should receive pneumococcal and influenza vaccinations. A small randomized placebo-controlled trial of trimethoprim- sulfamethoxazole in 57 patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma demonstrated benefit with routine prophylaxis administered with the first two cycles of chemotherapy.200 In another small randomized trial, no significant benefit was noted with prophylactic antibiotics administered during initial therapy.201 More recently, however, prophylactic levofloxacin administered daily for 12 weeks in patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma was associated with significant decrease in infections as well as lower early mortality rate.202 Based on this trial and the high risk of serious infections, routine prophylactic antibiotics for approximately 3 months are recommended in patients starting treatment for multiple myeloma. MONOCLONAL GAMMOPATHY OF UNDETERMINED SIGNIFICANCE INTRODUCTION MGUS is an asymptomatic, premalignant clonal plasma cell proliferative disorder (see Table 107.1).204,205 It is the most common plasma cell neoplasm. MGUS is of considerable clinical importance given its relatively high prevalence in the general population, lifelong predisposition to multiple myeloma or related disorder, and the various associated clinical syndromes. There are three main types of MGUS based on the predominant mode of clinical progression: IgM MGUS, non-IgM MGUS, and light chain MGUS.2,206 IgM MGUS carries a risk of progression to Waldenström macroglobulinemia, but in rare cases, it can lead to multiple myeloma (IgM multiple myeloma). Non-IgM MGUS and light chain MGUS carry a risk of progression to multiple myeloma or solitary plasmacytoma. All three forms can lead to AL amyloidosis. The pathogenesis of MGUS has been discussed earlier under “Multiple Myeloma.” The cytogenetic classification of MGUS is the same as multiple myeloma. The cytogenetic subtypes of multiple myeloma listed in Table 107.2 are thought to originate at the MGUS stage. INCIDENCE AND PREVALENCE The annual incidence of MGUS in men is estimated to be 120 per 100,000 at age 50 years and rises to 530 per 100,000 at age 90 years.207 The rates for women are 60 per 100,000 at age 50 years and 370 per 100,000 at age 90 years. MGUS is prevalent in approximately 4% of the general population aged 50 years or older. Studies conducted in Olmsted County, Minnesota, show that approximately 3% of the population #x2265;50 years old have IgM or non-IgM MGUS, whereas an additional 1% have light chain MGUS.19,206 Several other studies have reported similar prevalence estimates.208 The prevalence of MGUS increases with age and is approximately 2% in those aged 50 to 59 years and over 5% to 6% in those older than age 70 years. WALDENSTRÖM MACROGLOBULINEMIA Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a rare clonal IgM monoclonal protein–secreting lymphoid/plasma cell disorder. In the past, some patients were classified as having lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma; the two entities are now considered the same disease.267,268 The median age at diagnosis is approximately 65 years, with a slight male predisposition. The typical symptoms at presentation are weakness and fatigue due to anemia. Other clinical manifestations may include constitutional symptoms (fever, night sweats, and weight loss), hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, hyperviscosity, cryoglobulinemia, and sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy.269 Unlike multiple myeloma, primary IgH translocations are not seen in Waldenström macroglobulinemia.270 A majority of patients with Waldenström macroglobulinemia have a recurrent mutation of the MYD88 gene (MYD88 L265P).271,272 Presenting symptoms include anemia, pancytopenia, organomegaly, neuropathy, amyloidosis, cryoglobulinemia, night sweats, and symptomatic hyperviscosity. DIAGNOSIS The diagnostic criteria for Waldenström macroglobulinemia are listed in Table 107.1, and diagnosis requires 10% or greater lymphoplasmacytic infiltration of the bone marrow.3–5,18 Presence of less than 10% lymphoplasmacytic infiltration in the absence of end-organ damage is considered IgM MGUS, and such patients have

Dr. AVR @ TMH general population and are best not considered to have malignant disease.4,273 Historically, patients with an IgM M protein less than 3 g/dL meeting criteria for Waldenström macroglobulinemia have been classified as having lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with an IgM M protein. However, except for hyperviscosity, the clinical picture, therapy, and prognosis in these patients are no different than in patients classified as having Waldenström macroglobulinemia who have an IgM M protein level #x2265;3 g/dL.274 By the current definition, patients are considered to have Waldenström macroglobulinemia regardless of the size of the serum M protein. PROGNOSIS Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a fairly indolent, chronic disease in most patients. The median survival has varied in studies, from 5 years to nearly 11 years.275 Adverse prognostic factors include age #x003E;70 years, hemoglobin #x003C;9 g/dL, weight loss, and cryoglobulinemia.276 Several staging systems have been proposed to risk stratify patients with Waldenström macroglobulinemia and to aid in prognosis (Table 107.16).275,277,278 Of these, the most recent is a standardized scoring system known as the International Prognostic Scoring System for Waldenström macroglobulinemia, which is designed to help guide treatment based on prognosis in symptomatic patients.275 TREATMENT Patients meeting the diagnostic criteria for smoldering Waldenström macroglobulinemia who are asymptomatic do not need immediate therapy.273 The indications for therapy include anemia (hemoglobin #x003C;11 g/dL) or thrombocytopenia (platelet count #x003C;100,000/#x03BC;L) felt to be related to Waldenström macroglobulinemia; constitutional symptoms such as weakness, fatigue, night sweats, or weight loss; hyperviscosity; symptomatic cryoglobulinemia; and significant hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. There are no good data from randomized trials to guide the choice of initial therapy in Waldenström macroglobulinemia among modern regimens. Initial therapy is usually given for approximately 6 months, and then patients are observed. The three commonly preferred treatments for initial therapy are bendamustine plus rituximab (BR); dexamethasone, rituximab, and cyclophosphamide (DRC); and ibrutinib.268,279 The choice of initial therapy varies according to cost and drug availability in various countries. Patients should preferably be treated on clinical trials as much as possible. Figure 107.10 provides an approach to the treatment of newly diagnosed Waldenström macroglobulinemia. BR is usually the preferred regimen for initial therapy. In a randomized trial, BR was compared to rituximab plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) in patients with low-grade lymphoma.280 Among patients with Waldenström macroglobulinemia, a marked improvement in PFS was seen with BR compared with R-CHOP. Among the 41 patients with Waldenström macroglobulinemia included in the study, both arms showed 95% response rates, with longer PFS in the BR arm versus R-CHOP (70 versus 28 months, respectively). There were also lower rates of adverse events observed in the BR arm versus R-CHOP. The DRC regimen is well tolerated and is a reasonable alternative for initial therapy. In a phase II trial of symptomatic, treatment-naive patients, DRC was associated with an 83% overall response rate and 7% complete response rate.281 The 2-year OS rate was 81%, with a PFS rate of 67%. The usual regimen of DRC consists of dexamethasone 20 mg intravenously followed by rituximab 375 mg/m2 intravenously on day 1 and cyclophosphamide 100 mg/m2 twice daily on days 1 to 5. This regimen is repeated every 21 days for 6 months.281 Ibrutinib is a third option for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma. It is an irreversible and selective inhibitor of Bruton tyrosine kinase and is approved for initial therapy by the FDA. Efficacy of ibrutinib appears to be higher in patients with MYD88 mutations.282 A major advantage of ibrutinib is that it can be administered orally and has a high single-agent activity. Relapsed Disease and Supportive Care At relapse, regimens used in initial therapy can be considered again.267 In fact, the same initial therapy can be tried again at relapse, if there is an adequate interval between cessation of therapy and relapse. In addition, there are additional options for therapy including purine nucleoside analogs (fludarabine and cladribine), proteasome inhibitors (bortezomib and carfilzomib), immunomodulatory agents (thalidomide, lenalidomide, and pomalidomide), ASCT, and alkylators (chlorambucil). Ibrutinib is of particular value in the treatment of relapsed disease. In one study, among 50 evaluable patients, 60% responded to therapy, with a median PFS of 14 months.286 In another phase II study, among 63 patients with symptomatic relapsed or refractory disease treated with ibrutinib, the overall response rate was 62%.287 The most common side effects with ibrutinib are low blood counts, gastrointestinal symptoms, rash, muscle spasms, and fatigue. Purine nucleoside analogs have considerable activity, with response rates of 40% to 90%.277,288–292 Alkylators such as chlorambucil remain an option especially for elderly patients. Combination regimens such as R-CHOP can also be considered in refractory patients.279 ASCT is a reasonable salvage option in selected patients who have good performance status and whose disease is chemotherapy sensitive at the time of transplant.293 A small subset of chemotherapy-resistant patients may respond to splenectomy.294 Patients with refractory anemia or anemia during chemotherapy will benefit from erythropoietin and/or and red cell transfusions. Dr. AVR @ TMH The diagnosis of systemic AL amyloidosis requires documentation of positive amyloid staining on a tissue biopsy as well as supporting evidence that the amyloid is derived from immunoglobulin light chains (see Table 107.1). It should be suspected when patients with the appropriate clinical syndrome (e.g., nephrotic syndrome, axonal neuropathy, restrictive cardiomyopathy) display evidence of a plasma cell proliferative disorder such as a serum or urine monoclonal protein. Systemic AL amyloidosis should be differentiated from localized amyloidosis, which can be derived from immunoglobulin light chains in many patients (localized AL amyloidosis).296 The clinical manifestations vary greatly and depend on the dominant organ involved. Nephrotic syndrome, restrictive cardiomyopathy, and peripheral/autonomic neuropathy are common presenting syndromes. Patients may also have associated macroglossia, carpal tunnel syndrome, and purpura involving the neck, face, and eyes. IFE reveals an M protein in the serum or urine in almost 90% of patients at diagnosis. The FLC ratio is abnormal in most of the patients with a negative IFE. Systemic AL amyloidosis and symptomatic multiple myeloma can coexist in the same patient, but usually one of the two disorders dominates the clinical picture. SOLITARY PLASMACYTOMA Solitary plasmacytomas are early-stage plasma cell tumors that are in an intervening stage between SMM and multiple myeloma. They may be confined to bone (solitary bone plasmacytoma) or occur in extramedullary sites (extramedullary plasmacytoma). Extramedullary plasmacytoma is localized to the upper respiratory tract (nasal cavity and sinuses, nasopharynx, and larynx) in over 80% of cases but can also occur in the gastrointestinal tract, central nervous system, urinary bladder, thyroid, breast, testes, parotid gland, or lymph nodes. Patients with solitary plasmacytoma are at risk for progression to multiple myeloma. DIAGNOSIS AND PROGNOSIS Diagnostic criteria are listed on Table 107.1. An MRI of the spine and pelvis and/or PET-CT should be performed in addition to a skeletal survey because approximately one-third of patients may have additional occult lesions that will be missed in the absence of these studies.318 Recent studies show that accurate diagnosis plays a major role in ascertaining prognosis.319 The diagnosis of solitary plasmacytoma requires evidence of a normal bone marrow with no clonal plasma cells on multiparametric flow cytometry. Patients with an apparent solitary plasmacytoma who have limited (#x003C;10%) clonal marrow involvement are considered to have solitary plasmacytoma with minimal marrow involvement (see Table 107.1). The risk of recurrence or progression to multiple myeloma within 3 years is approximately 10% in patients with solitary plasmacytoma versus 20% to 60% in patients with solitary plasmacytoma and minimal marrow involvement. Prognosis is generally better in patients with solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma, compared with solitary bony plasmacytoma. Persistence of an M protein 1 year or more after radiation therapy has been associated with an increased probability of progression to multiple myeloma in patients with solitary bone plasmacytoma.320 An abnormal FLC ratio at baseline or persistent abnormal FLC ratio after radiation is predictive fo

progression.321 TREATMENT Treatment consists of radiation in the range of 40 to 50 Gy to the involved site. Patients with solitary plasmacytoma plus minimal marrow involvement are also treated with radiation therapy to the involved site and then observed until disease. There is no proven benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy. Progression to multiple myeloma, when it occurs, usually appears within 3 years, but patients must be followed indefinitely. POEMS SYNDROME POEMS syndrome (polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal plasma cell disorder, skin changes) is defined by the criteria listed in Table 107.1.322 It is a rare, atypical, plasma cell proliferative disorder. Almost all patients have either osteosclerotic lesions or Castleman disease. The major clinical features are a predominantly motor chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, sclerotic bone lesions, and a varying number of associated abnormalities such as hepatomegaly, hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy, clubbing, polycythemia, thrombocytosis, and Castleman disease. The pathogenesis of the syndrome is not clear but appears to be at least in part cytokine mediated, and elevated vascular endothelial growth factor levels are commonly found. POEMS syndrome may have an indolent or a fulminant course. In one study of 99 patients, median survival was 14 years.7 If the lesions are in a limited area, radiation therapy (40 to 50 Gy) produces substantial improvement of clinical symptoms and signs in more than 50% of patients.322 For patients with widespread osteosclerotic lesions, treatment is similar to multiple myeloma and depends on eligibility for stem cell transplantation. In eligible patients, ASCT has provided significant responses.323 Supportive care, including aggressive physical and occupational therapy, is an important component of care.

108 Cancer of Unknown Primary Sarah Yentz, Manali Bhave, Erin Cobain, and Laurence Baker INTRODUCTION Cancer of unknown primary (CUP) is defined as a biopsy-proven malignancy without an identified primary site of origin despite a comprehensive evaluation. CUP represents a heterogeneous group of malignancies with diverse biology often leading to significant clinical symptoms, early metastatic disease, and mortality. Although the exact incidence is unknown due in part to varying definitions of CUP, CUP tumors account for approximately 2% of all cancers. The American Cancer Society estimates 33,770 cases of unknown primary were diagnosed in 2017. This number is expected to decrease as our diagnostic capabilities improve and primary sites of malignancy are identified, although CUP continues to provide clinical challenges in making a diagnosis and selecting therapies. Patients with CUP often present with metastatic carcinoma with a variety of histologic tumor types and clinical presentations. Although these patients often carry a poor prognosis with an overall survival (OS) historically of <1 year, there have been major advances in the identification of a primary site of disease allowing for site-specific therapy and/or targeting of oncogenic drivers that have changed the diagnostic and treatment paradigms in CUP. This chapter reviews the pathologic evaluation, clinical features, and treatment of patients with CUP as well as the evolving use of genomic/molecular profiling and targeted agents in CUP. PATHOLOGY EVALUATION The initial pathology evaluation of a patient with unknown primary relies on standard histologic examination combined with immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining. Standard hematoxylin and eosin stains in conjunction with IHC are used to subtype the cancer into one of the major histologic diagnostic categories: carcinoma, lymphoma, melanoma, or sarcoma. The majority of CUPs fall into the category of carcinoma of unknown primary. Carcinoma of unknown primary can be further subdivided into (1) adenocarcinoma of unknown primary (70%), (2) poorly differentiated carcinoma (20% to 25%), (3) squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary (5%), and (4) neuroendocrine tumor of unknown primary (1% to 3%). Initial classification into one of these large groups is important for guiding clinical workup, as described in the following text. Histopathologic subtyping typi

Dr. AVR @ TMH primary sites.4 Although suggestive, IHC staining should not be used as an isolated diagnosis tool and the entire clinical picture should be taken into consideration. Accuracy of Immunohistochemical Staining Although IHC is a helpful tool, unfortunately its diagnostic accuracy is not perfect. For example, some anaplastic carcinomas can be keratin negative, whereas some sarcomas express cytokeratins. In addition, dedifferentiated melanomas can be negative for melanoma-specific markers, including S100. Many different carcinomas may have the same basic IHC staining; hence, IHC does not always allow for identification of one tissue of origin. USE OF NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING Although the management of patients with CUP has historically relied on identifying a likely primary histology, advances in molecular and genomic profiling have allowed for a more personalized treatment approach with the use of potentially targeted therapeutics. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is now a part of the standard management for patients of many different cancer types where clinically actionable mutations are identified and targeted; however, the role of NGS in CUPs is less defined. There have been several studies published recently that have provided some insight on the utility of genomic profiling in patients with advanced carcinomas of unknown primary. A large cohort of patients with CUP were evaluated at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center between January 2014 and June 2016, including demographic and clinical information, along with pathology and molecular/genomic profiling with NGS.11 Of the 333 CUP patients evaluated, 150 patients (45%) underwent NGS using MSK-IMPACT, a deep-coverage hybridization capture-based assay encompassing 34 (later expanded to 410) cancer-associated genes. The most frequent histology was adenocarcinoma, followed by carcinoma not otherwise specified and squamous cell carcinoma. A total of 137 patients (91%) were found to have at least 1 alteration with a known or likely oncogenic function with an average of 3.1 oncogenic alterations. Potentially clinically actionable mutations were found in the tumors of 45 patients (34%) with a total of 54 potentially actionable mutations. Of these patients, only 15 patients received targeted therapy with time-to-treatment failure ranging from 1 to 14 months. Although historical data suggests an OS range of 3 to 8 months, patients in this analysis were found to have an OS of 13 months. It is unclear whether the prolonged OS in this cohort is reflective of improved treatment approaches with the use of targeted agents as only a minority of patients with actionable alterations received targeted therapy or whether the improved OS was more reflective of improvements in diagnostic testing and cancer-related therapy

Rosenzweig INTRODUCTION Malignant mesotheliomas (MMs) are highly aggressive neoplasms that arise primarily from the surface serosal cells of the pleural, peritoneal, and pericardial cavities. The disease is characterized by a long latency from the time of exposure to asbestos to the onset of disease, suggesting that multiple somatic genetic events are required for tumorigenic conversion of a normal mesothelial cell. EPIDEMIOLOGY The death rates for mesothelioma parallel the consumption of asbestos by individual countries. When one considers mesothelioma death rates from 2000 to 2004 as a function of asbestos usage in the 1960s, Australia has the highest death rate for the disease in the world.1 It is predicted that between 2000 and 2049, over 400,000 lives will be lost in those countries from the disease.2 In the United States, there have been about 3,200 deaths per year from the disease since 2000, with workers with industrial exposures in construction and shipbuilding being at highest risk, followed by plumbers, pipe fitters, and steamers.3 Most mesotheliomas affects men in their late 50s, 60s, and 70s due to the aforementioned 25- to 40-year latency period between occupational asbestos exposure and the development of the tumor.4 The male-to-female ratio is approximately 4.5:1; there is a similar ratio between pleural and peritoneal mesothelioma as asbestos reaches first the lung, from there the pleura via lymphatics, and eventually, especially in cases with significant exposure, such as insulators, the peritoneum.5 MECHANISM OF ASBESTOS CARCINOGENESIS For regulatory purposes, six different types of mineral fibers that were used commercially were collectively named asbestos in the 1970s: amosite, crocidolite, anthophyllite, actinolite, tremolite, and chrysotile.6 The five types other than chrysotile are termed amphibole asbestos. Millions of workers were professionally exposed to asbestos during the past century, and exposure continues in developing countries. Several other mineral fibers (e.g., erionite, antigorite) share structural and chemical characteristics with “asbestos” and can cause mesothelioma in humans. However, because these fibers have “rarely” been used commercially, human exposure is limited. Importantly, all carcinogenic fibers

Animal Models of Asbestos Carcinogenicity Mesotheliomas and sarcomas are induced in a dose-dependent fashion after intrapleural and intraperitoneal injection of asbestos into animals.12–14 Chronic inhalational studies are thought to be the best representation of asbestos carcinogenicity. Because of the high cost of these experiments, however, very few have been performed. Asbestos Carcinogenicity in Humans Although injection and inhalation studies in animals suggest that all forms of asbestos are equally carcinogenic and that there is a clear dose–response relationship between asbestos exposure and mesothelioma risk, epidemiologic studies in humans do not match these observations. The proportion of pleural mesotheliomas that are thought to be associated with asbestos varies in the literature from 16% to 90%.6 This wide range may reflect the distinct populations studied, and it is also influenced by the method used to determine exposure rates.6 Peritoneal mesotheliomas are less frequently associated to asbestos exposure. In the past, when most mesotheliomas occurred in asbestos workers, about 50% of peritoneal mesotheliomas had been linked to asbestos exposure. Recently, about 8% of U.S. patients with peritoneal mesothelioma had a demonstrable asbestos exposure.15 Indeed, there is an increase of peritoneal mesothelioma among young patients that have not worked in asbestos trades and that do not have markers of exposure, such as lung fibrosis, pleural plaques, asbestos, or asbestos bodies. A subset of these mesotheliomas has been linked to ALK rearrangements.16 Moreover, recent data suggest that germline mutations of several genes involved in DNA repair increase susceptibility to asbestos and to mesothelioma, underscoring the role of genetics in this malignancy.17 Epidemiologic studies demonstrated that erionite, crocidolite, and amosite are the most potent mineral fibers in causing mesothelioma.18,19 The ability of chrysotile to cause human mesothelioma continues to be debated as epidemiologic studies have not provided definitive results.18,19 Chrysotile has a limited biopersistence in tissues; therefore, continuous and prolonged exposure is required to sustain the chronic inflammation and genetic alterations that over time can lead to mesothelioma.20 Exposure to multiple types of fibers is common. BAP1 regulates DNA repair via homologous recombination, an error-free repair mechanism; accordingly, reduced levels of BAP1 increased DNA damage.84 Cells with extensive DNA damage should die and not grow into malignancies. However, it was found that in the cytoplasm, BAP1 deubiquitylates and thus stabilizes the type 3 inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R3), which regulates the transfer of Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum to the mitochondria and therefore influences numerous cellular activities responsible for malignant transformation and tumor growth including cell death following DNA damage. Because DNA-damaged BAP1 mutant cells do not die due to the reduced apoptosis, they continue to divide and over time may become malignant. Accordingly, decreased levels of BAP1 lead to enhanced DNA damage following exposure to asbestos, ultraviolet (UV) light, and ionizing radiation (due to decreased nuclear BAP1 activity), reduced apoptosis (due to decreased cytoplasmic BAP1 activity), and increased cell transformation (due to both decreased nuclear and cytoplasmic following DNA damage).85 In parallel studies, it was found that heterozygous germline BAP1 mutations induce alterations of metabolic pathways consistent with a “Warburg effect” (i.e., aerobic glycolysis) that are detectable in human plasma and in primary cells.86 Thus, cells from BAP1 mutation carriers do not need to go through a selection process that favors the emergence of clones with a Warburg effect required for tumor growth: BAP1 mutant cells constitutionally derive a large part of their metabolism through aerobic glycolysis. Thus, when these cells develop mutations, they are already primed for cancer growth. At the same time, these metabolic alterations compromise the ability of BAP1 mutant cells to adapt to metabolic stress,87 such as glucose starvation, providing a possible novel therapeutic avenue that should be explored. Mesothelioma developing in carriers of germline BAP1 mutations are characteristically of the epithelioid type, show well- differentiated tubular and papillary structures, and although they are invasive, they are much less aggressive—average survival rates of 5+ years—compared to sporadic mesotheliomas carrying acquired BAP1 mutations or without BAP1 mutations.88 Although acquired BAP1 mutations do not appear to be related with survival, they influence susceptibility to t

Biphasic mesotheliomas can be distinguished from carcinosarcomas metastasizing from various organs using immunohistochemistry94 and from biphasic synovial sarcomas by using either electron microscopy or molecular testing for the X;18 translocation that is diagnostic of synovial sarcoma.95 CLINICAL PRESENTATION Symptoms As many as 25% of patients with the disease have symptoms for ≥6 months before seeking medical attention. The right side is affected more than the left side (60% versus 40%), most likely because of the right side’s greater volume. Approximately 60% of the patients present with nonpleuritic chest pain that classically is located posterolaterally and low in the thorax. Dyspnea is present in 50% to 70% of the cases, and, indeed, 80% of the patients present with dyspnea and effusion. The presence of a pleural effusion is documented at some time in the course of the disease in 95% of patients with malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM). With the increasing use of positron emission tomography (PET) for pretreatment planning, between 5% and 25% of patients are found to have metastatic disease at presentation.96

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH FOR PRESUMED MESOTHELIOMA Thoracentesis and Closed Pleural Biopsy Patients who present with a large, unexplained pleural effusion and minimal or moderate evidence of pleural thickening should have initial thoracentesis and pleural biopsy, especially if a history of asbestos exposure or mesothelioma in a family member is elicited. By preserving a cell block from the pleural fluid and using both histochemical and immunohistochemical staining techniques along with electron microscopic analysis, the diagnosis of mesothelioma can be obtained from the pleural effusion in as high as 84% of suspected cases.126,127 Thoracoscopy A video-assisted thoracoscopy is indicated for patients at risk for mesothelioma who (1) develop a large effusion and who have negative studies on thoracentesis and pleural biopsy or (2) recur with effusion after initial thoracentesis. Thoracoscopy can be invaluable for estimating extent of disease with regard to the lung, diaphragm, pericardium, chest wall, and nodes.128–130 If there is no free pleural space because of previous treatment of pleural effusion and the bulk of the disease in the hemithorax is solid, open biopsy should be performed such that the scar can be incorporated into the incision at the time of cytoreduction surgery. NATURAL HISTORY The majority of patients with treated or untreated pleural mesothelioma die of complications of local disease because of (1) increasing tumor bulk that eventually replaces the pleural effusion and causes progressive respiratory compromise, pneumonia, or myocardial dysfunction with arrhythmias; (2) unrelenting chest wall pain requiring narcotics, which leads to cachexia; and/or (3) dysphagia from tumor compression of the esophagus. Patients generally die of respiratory failure or pneumonia. Extrathoracic metastases occur late in the course of disease and are not

TREATMENT Overview For unresectable patients who are candidates for chemotherapy, the well-powered phase III trial that showed a 3- to 4-month survival advantage for the two-drug regimen of pemetrexed and cisplatin compared with the one-drug regimen of cisplatin has defined the standard of care.152 Recommendations for the management of pleural mesothelioma have been made by the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO)153 and the National Comprehensive Cancer Center Network (NCCN).154 Supportive Care The median survival of patients with MPM who select supportive care ranges only from 4 months136 to 13 months.155 This variation is likely due to variations in tumor biology, host response to tumor, detection bias, lead- time bias, and the use of ad hoc or unreported treatments by some patients and physicians. There are a number of options for the control of pleural effusion, including repeated thoracenteses, talc pleurodesis, or placement of a PleurX (Denver Biomedical, Denver, CO) catheter.156 Talc pleurodesis is performed by instilling 2 to 5 g of asbestos-free, sterile talc over the lung and the parietal surfaces. Success rates in effusion control with talc, used either via thoracoscopy or via slurry, approach 90%. The MesoVATS trial was a randomization between 2003 and 2012 of 87 video-assisted thoracoscopic pleurectomy or 88 talc pleurodesis. Although there was no difference in survival between the two groups, pleural

Moreover, there was a significant benefit in quality of life at 6 months and 12 months in favor of the pleurectomy group.157 The chest pain of MM requires narcotics, and these patients should be seen in consultation by a dedicated pain management team to assist in the optimization of the patient’s quality of life. Subcutaneous tunneling of epidural catheters for long-term out-of-hospital use has also been used in selective cases. When only local RT has been delivered solely for chest wall pain or chest wall nodules, the median survival has been reported to be 4 to 5 months.158,159 Surgery for Pleural Mesothelioma The Controversy Surgery for pleural mesothelioma remains a controversial subject not only among medical oncologists but also among thoracic surgeons. Much of the controversy remains as the result of the early trials of EPP with reported mortality rates of 31%,160 as well as the lack of systemic therapies besides pemetrexed and cisplatinum with response rates >30%, which can complement present surgical therapy with mortality rates of 4%. As discussed in the following, the type of operation to be performed (EPP or some sort of lung-sparing P/D) is one of the more debatable subjects for the management of the disease, and at present, suffers from the lack of randomized data that defines the present cadre of surgical interventions in a uniform manner.
