As detailed in one of the early systematic reviews of the use of EPP for MPM,164 which included survival and perioperative outcomes, the median OS varied from 9.4 to 27.5 months, and 1-, 2-, and 5-year survival rates ranged from 36% to 83%, 5% to 59%, and 0% to 24%, respectively. IMRT offers the potential for administering higher doses of RT with better target coverage to the hemithorax while minimizing normal tissue toxicities. IMRT is a highly conformal radiation technique that allows more effective sparing of normal tissues, providing an opportunity for safer, less toxic treatments and increased efficacy by enabling higher radiation doses to the tumor. It comes with a much higher level of dosimetric control and leads to better target coverage than conventional techniques.249 Areas of dose inhomogeneity are readily recognizable and can be corrected. Rice et al.250 and Forster et al.251 at the MD Anderson Cancer Center (MDACC) treated patients with MPM with IMRT after EPP. Recurrences in the irradiated field occurred in only 3 patients, and distant disease observed in 54% of patients was the major pattern of failure. 110 Peritoneal Metastases and Peritoneal Mesothelioma Alvaro Arjona-Sanchez, Marcello Deraco, Olivier Glehen, David Morris, and Paul H. Sugarbaker INTRODUCTION Peritoneal carcinomatosis, mesothelioma, and sarcomatosis are included in the group of diseases collectively referred to, in this chapter, as peritoneal metastases. Over the past three decades, there has emerged an increasing optimism concerning an individualized management plan for cancer dissemination within the abdomen and pelvis. The clinical problem was originally defined by several important clinical studies that established the natural history of peritoneal surface malignancy.1–3 Concomitant with these manuscripts that identified the dismal prognosis of patients with peritoneal metastases, isolated reports appeared concerning an emerging technology that described a new approach to management. This alternative treatment plan had two essential components. First, cytoreductive surgery (CRS) was used in an attempt to resect all visible implants within the abdomen and pelvis. Peritonectomy along with visceral resections was developed to surgically eradicate cancer on peritoneal surfaces.4 The second component was local-regional chemotherapy (intraperitoneal chemotherapy) used in the operating room or within the early postoperative period before adhesions develop. Chemotherapy used in the operating room with moderate heat has been referred to as hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC)5; chemotherapy used within the early postoperative period has been referred to as early postoperative intraperitoneal chemotherapy (EPIC).6 The chemotherapy is used in an attempt to eradicate free cancer cells and minute attached nodules that remain following surgery.7 The unique aspect of this new combination of treatments was the perioperative timing of the chemotherapy. Currently, the perioperative chemotherapy may be both intravenous and intraperitoneal and may be administered in the operating room or in the early postoperative period. It is not adjuvant chemotherapy, and it is not neoadjuvant chemotherapy; it is chemotherapy used simultaneously with a major cytoreductive surgical procedure. Of course, all efforts to maintain benefits from systemic chemotherapy in patients with peritoneal metastases or mesothelioma must continue. Patients with peritoneal surface malignancy are required to be a focus of the

PATIENT SELECTION USING QUANTITATIVE PROGNOSTIC INDICATORS With some variations between diseases, the same group of quantitative prognostic indicators is used to select patients with peritoneal surface malignancy from many different primary sites for treatment. Prognostic indicators refine the selection of patients to those most likely to benefit and to exclude those who are unlikely to benefit.11,12 Histopathology, the peritoneal cancer index (PCI), the completeness of cytoreduction score (CC), radiologic imaging by computed tomography (CT), and tumor, node, metastasis (TNM) stage with peritoneal cytology play a central role in patient selection. Figure 110.1 Intraoperative dissemination of gastric cancer cells. If cancer cells gain access to the peritoneal space either prior to or at the time of gastrectomy, two patterns of dissemination are observed. A low density of cancer cells into the free peritoneal space results in nodules as peritoneal implants. A high density of cancer cells dropped into the cancer resection site results in a layering of cancer. Biologic Aggressiveness as Measured by Histopathology for Epithelial Appendiceal Neoplasms and Peritoneal Mesothelioma Mucinous appendiceal neoplasms have a broad spectrum of aggressiveness, and the histologic type of the

appendiceal neoplasm has a profound effect on survival following treatment by CRS and perioperative chemotherapy.13 Patients with adenomucinosis obtain maximal survival benefit, whereas those with mucinous carcinoma show survivals similar to that for peritoneal metastases of colorectal origin.14 Seven different histologic patterns of peritoneal mesothelioma contribute to three distinct histologic groups that have a very different prognosis following treatment with CRS and perioperative chemotherapy: poor prognosis for sarcomatoid, deciduoid, or biphasic types; intermediate prognosis for papillary and epithelial types; and excellent prognosis for low-grade or multicystic types.15 Extent of Disease as Measured by the Peritoneal Cancer Index at the Time of Abdominal-Pelvic Exploration The PCI is an assessment combining lesion size (0 to 3) with tumor distribution (abdominopelvic regions 0 to 12) to estimate the extent of disease within the abdomen and pelvis as a numerical score (Fig. 110.2).16 It is calculated from observations obtained at the time of surgical exploration of the abdomen and pelvis and should be recorded by the surgeon before leaving the operating room. The higher the PCI, the less likely CRS and perioperative chemotherapy will result in long-term survival for all the peritoneal surface malignancies discussed in this chapter. The Completeness of Cytoreduction Score Performed after the Resection The size of residual tumor nodules visually determined after CRS has been determined to have a profound effect on outcome. The definition of complete cytoreduction is no visible evidence of cancer or only minute nodules reliably penetrated by perioperative chemotherapy, a CC-0 or CC-1, respectively. With few exceptions, a CC-0 or CC-1 score is necessary for long-term benefit with CRS and perioperative chemotherapy.17 Figure 110.2 The peritoneal cancer index (PCI). This index combines a size and a distribution parameter to achieve a numerical score. The lesion size (LS) is used to quantitate the size of peritoneal nodules. The distribution of tumor is determined within the 13 abdominopelvic regions. Preoperative Radiologic Imaging by Computed Tomography

Dr. AVR @ TMH CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is an essential tool in the selection of patients for treatment. Systemic metastases and spread to pleural surfaces must be identified before these local-regional treatments proceed. The location and quantity of mucinous carcinoma within the peritoneal cavity can be accurately determined.18 Unfortunately, nonmucinous peritoneal metastases may be greatly underestimated by CT.19,20 If the small bowel and its mesentery are layered by tumor or a large mass of cancer occupies the epigastric region, the likelihood of achieving complete cytoreduction is small. The CT with maximal intravenous and oral contrast can identify 15 concerning features that are associated with suboptimal cytoreduction or technically more complex procedures that carry increased morbidity and mortality.21 Tumor, Node, Metastasis Stage; Peritoneal Cytology; and Clinical Features of the Primary Cancer A meticulous visual survey of the peritoneal surfaces at the time of primary gastrointestinal cancer resection combined with a knowledgeable and timely gross and histopathologic assessment of the resected specimen can accurately predict the incidence of peritoneal metastases that will occur in follow-up. Also, in advanced gastrointestinal cancers, peritoneal cytology provides important prognostic information. This information should be used by the MDT to consider proactive treatment with CRS and HIPEC. APPENDICEAL MALIGNANCY Natural History Although similarities exist, there are unique features of appendiceal malignancies as compared to colorectal adenocarcinoma. The first and probably the most obvious difference between the colon and the appendix malignancies is the diameter of the bowel lumen at the primary site. A colon tumor grows as an intraluminal mass in the bowel and will invade through the wall. The intraluminal growth pattern causes the primary cancer to breech the serosa in a late stage. In contrast, the appendix is a small organ, up to 1 cm in diameter, with a thin wall. A tumor may obliterate the appendix lumen in an early stage. This can cause an early rupture of the wall of the appendix, allowing a spreading of tumor cells into the abdominal and pelvic cavity. Early in the natural history of the disease, these neoplastic cells implant with a high efficiency throughout the peritoneal cavity and progress as peritoneal metastases.

Unfortunately, the majority of patients at the time of diagnosis of colorectal peritoneal metastases will only be suitable for palliative treatment options.35 When peritoneal metastases are of limited extent, potentially curative options should be explored. Patients are usually diagnosed with presenting signs and symptoms of advanced disease. In a recently published series of 81 patients with diffuse MPM reported by an Italian group, ascites, abdominal pain, and asthenia were the most frequent symptoms present on 77%, 69%, and 43% of patients, respectively. Pavlick INTRODUCTION Metastatic choroidal melanoma (CM) patients rarely present with the classic “distended abdomen and a glass eye.” Although metastases occur in up to 50% of cases, most do not cause symptoms and are discovered by periodic hepatic screening.1,2 The rationale for early detection is that it allows for palliative treatment, enrollment in clinical trials, and end-of-life planning.3 Prosthetic eyes are less commonly required after uveal melanoma (UM) treatment. This is because fewer patients with UM are being treated with removal of the eye (enucleation). For example, at the New York Eye Cancer Center, about 7% of patients with UM require enucleation as primary treatment. The trend toward eye preservation can be related to early detection; referral of smaller, more treatable UMs; and the widespread belief that radiation is equivalent to enucleation for the prevention of metastases.4 Confronted with the choice between enucleation and eye-sparing radiation therapy, patients prefer to keep their eye. Eye- and vision-sparing radiation therapy techniques are widely used around the world. For example, 47 eye cancer specialists from 10 countries participated in a committee to create the American Brachytherapy Society Ophthalmic Oncology Task Force (ABS-OOTF) guidelines for plaque radiation therapy.5 In these guidelines, enucleation was recommended only in cases of American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) stage T4e UMs, tumors with basal dimensions that exceed the limits of irradiation, blind painful eyes, and those with no light perception vision. Thus, multicenter, international ABS-OOTF consensus allows for eye- and vision-sparing plaque brachytherapy for almost all patients.5 This shift toward eye preservation has been augmented by the advent of postradiation eye- and vision-preserving laser photocoagulation as well as anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) treatment. In 2005, physicians at the New York Eye Cancer Center first suppressed radiation maculopathy and radiation optic neuropathy using periodic intraocular injections of bevacizumab (Avastin; Roche-Genentech, South San Francisco, CA).6,7 Since that time, centers around the world have used anti-VEGF treatment to preserve useful vision and quality of life for most patients. Dr. AVR @ TMH The uvea is the primary vascular matrix of the eye. It is continuous within the iris, ciliary body, and choroid. Melanocytes within any of these structures can transform. However, intraocular melanoma location affects tumor size at diagnosis, prognosis for vision, and risk for metastasis. Iris melanomas are the most easily visible. They tend to be the smallest at diagnosis, spindle cell type, and least likely to metastasize. In contrast, ciliary body melanomas are the least visible because they are hidden behind the iris, are typically discovered when they are larger, and are more likely to have metastasized.13 CMs are located posterior to the ciliary body. CMs are often asymptomatic and found during routine periodic ophthalmic examination. In developed countries, CMs are typically AJCC T1 to T3. When symptomatic, CMs can induce early changes in vision and/or cause symptoms of “flashing lights” due to tumor-induced exudative retinal detachment. A subset termed subfoveal choroidal melanomas are located beneath the center of vision and are recognized earlier due to visual symptoms and, thus, are typically smaller and less likely to have metastasized.14 Therefore, unless melanomas are large enough to be visible, extend into the visual axis, tilt the lens, induce a symptomatic exudative retinal detachment, or displace the fovea, they are discovered during routine eye examination. Histology UMs arise from a preexisting choroidal nevus or de novo. Biopsy reveals distinct types of melanocytes within UMs.15 In 1931, the Callender classification divided UMs into spindle cell melanomas (spindle A, spindle B), mixed cell melanomas, and epithelioid cell melanomas (each associated with a progressively worse prognosis for survival).16 Iris Melanoma Iris melanomas typically originate in the iris stroma. While growing, they can displace, erode, or consume the underlying iris pigment epithelium.17 Along its posterior margin, it may invade the trabecular meshwork, gaining egress to the episcleral aqueous veins, and/or grow into the adjacent ciliary body. When discohesive, tumor-cell dispersion can affect the trabecular ocular outflow channels and thus induce secondary glaucoma.18 Other signs that suggest malignancy include iris dysfunction such as corectopia (irregular pupil) or dysmorphisms such as ectropion uveae and tumor neovascularization (Fig. 111.1, left)

OPHTHALMIC DIAGNOSIS The Finger MOST Mnemonic There is consensus that, when seen together, the most common characteristics of CM are diagnostic. As a CM invades and destroys the overlying retinal pigment epithelium, accumulations of orange pigment (lipofuscin and melanolipofuscin) can be visualized on the surface of a CM (Fig. 111.2, top left). CM-associated incontinent tumor blood vessels leak serum beneath the retina, seen as overlying retinal pigment epithelial detachments or subretinal fluid. Finally, CMs are typically ≥2.0 mm thick. Therefore, Dr. Finger created the mnemonic MOST, where Melanoma = Orange pigment + Subretinal fluid + Thickness of ≥2.0 mm. That said, not all CMs will exhibit all three findings. However, MOST is diagnostic when all three are present (Figure 111.2). Select cases may require orbital radiographic imaging (magnetic resonance imaging [MRI], computed tomography [CT], or positron emission tomography [PET]/CT). Ophthalmic Photography and Angiography Photographic techniques include slit-lamp and gonioscopy for iris and ciliary body tumors as well as fundus photography for CM. Photography documents the current state of the affected eye, facilitates observations of tumor characteristics, and plays an important role in the diagnosis of tumor growth, evaluation of posttreatment tumor response, and identification of normal tissue side effects. Fundus Autofluorescent Imaging Light (500 to 750 nm; peak 630 nm) is used to induce hyperautofluoresence from orange pigment lipofuscin.20 Although CM can exhibit obvious or grossly visible orange pigment lipofuscin, fundus autofluorescent imaging may be needed to highlight occult orange pigment lipofuscin deposits. Thus, fundus autofluorescent imaging can be used to detect and/or document one of the most important diagnostic characteristics of CM (Fig. 111.2, top right). Intraocular Angiography Angiographic photography is used to evaluate tumor microcirculation. Although some CMs may demonstrate a pathognomonic choroidal “double circulation” pattern and late diffuse microaneurysms, many merely show diffuse or focal hyperfluorescence. However, these findings can be used to distinguish between the hypofluorescence of choroidal hemorrhage, the coarse vascular pattern of choroidal hemangioma, and the plethora

of subretinal hyperfluorescent microaneurysms typically seen with angiography of choroidal metastasis. Optical Coherence Tomography Optical coherence tomography is a laser light–based computerized imaging system used to create tomographic slices and three-dimensional volumes of the retina, choroid, and sclera. Interacting with the three-dimensional image, tumor-associated intraretinal fluid and the subretinal fluid used for the MOST mnemonic are best seen with optical coherence tomography (Fig. 111.2, bottom left). Ophthalmic Ultrasound Imaging Ultrasound imaging offers 0.1-mm resolution of intraocular tissues. Ultrasound imaging of CM typically reveals low to moderate internal tumor reflectivity, a dome shape, and/or secondary exudative retinal detachment (Fig. 111.2, bottom right).19 Less common ultrasound-imaged tumor characteristics include a mushroom shape, choroidal excavation, extrascleral extension, and internal vascularity on dynamic examination. Alternative tumor- specific diagnostic findings of choroidal hemangioma, osteoma, hemorrhage, or metastasis may be evident on ultrasound. High-frequency (20 to 50 MHz) ultrasonography, also called ultrasound biomicroscopy, has allowed almost histopathology-quality imaging of iris melanoma capable of viewing extension into the underlying pigment epithelium or adjacent ciliary body.21 Thus, even smaller ciliary body melanomas have been detected, potentially saving both vision and lives. Ultrasound imaging is the standard way to measure the height and basal dimensions of all UMs.19,21 Tumor measurements have been used to detect tumor growth, facilitate radiation therapy (plaque brachytherapy and proton beam), and monitor posttreatment tumor regression. Intraocular Tumor Biopsy Unlike cutaneous melanoma, biopsy of UM is controversial. Unlike in transcorneal biopsy of iris melanomas, transvitreal and transscleral biopsy requires a conjunctival and scleral incision. Discohesive tumor cells are liberated within the eye and exit through the sclerostomy into the orbit. No statistically significant evidence exists regarding whether there is a metastatic risk associated with CM biopsy. Known risks include vitreous hemorrhage, retinal tear, retinal detachment, infection, traumatic optic neuropathy, epiretinal membrane formation, and cataract. The CM study enrolled 1,317 patients from 43 centers in the United States and Canada who were randomly assigned to enucleation or iodine- 125 (125I) plaque brachytherapy. At 12 years, 471 of 1,317 patients died. The 12-year all-cause mortality rate was statistically equivalent (43% in the 125I brachytherapy arm and 41% among those enucleated). This result prompted a shift toward eye- and vision-sparing treatment within subspecialty eye cancer centers.4,5 The second COMS study was limited to large CMs primarily to determine whether enucleation induced metastasis. Patients with large CMs were randomized to receive either 20 Gy (4 Gy in five daily fractions) of radiation or no radiation prior to enucleation. At 12-year follow-up, no survival advantage attributable to pre- enucleation radiation was found, effectively ending this practice.9 OVERVIEW: TREATMENT OF UVEAL MELANOMA Small T1 Uveal Melanomas Eye cancer specialists and their patients may elect to observe small CMs for evidence of tumor growth prior to treatment. This is due to current belief that small CMs carry a tumor size–dependent low risk (approximately 11%) for metastases and that current treatments risk severe vision loss. In addition, observation of small CMs has been justified by the concept that tumor growth demonstrates malignancy because multiple studies have demonstrated that increased tumor size (specifically largest tumor diameter) is associated with an increased risk of metastatic death. It is reasonable to assume that documenting growth increases (albeit marginally) a patient’s risk for metastatic disease.24 If they so choose, all patients with small CMs can be offered prompt radiation therapy.26 Patients typically require small treatment volumes, which are associated with less vision loss. If radiation retinopathy and optic neuropathy occurs, it can be suppressed with intravitreal anti-VEGF medications.6,7,26,27 The clinical decision to treat or not to treat a small CM is both complex and controversial (https://eyecancer.com/eye-cancer/research- articles/small-choroidal-melanoma-to-treat-or-not-to-treat-that-is-the-question). For example,106Ru plaques emit electrons with limited intraocular penetration, thus resulting in a higher sclera-chorio- retinal base dose and less side scatter penumbra (compared to 103Pd or 125I). Conversely, 103Pd and 125I offer greater intraocular penetration and more side scatter. All these characteristics must be taken in to account when choosing a radionuclide source and plaque size.28,32 Lastly, it is important to consider dose to normal ocular structures, because side-effects may be predicted based on these measurements.14,33–35 Proton Beam Radiation Proton beam radiation for UM is available at select institutions around the world. Pioneered at Harvard University, typical treatment involves surgical placement of metallic markers on the episclera around the tumor’s base.29 Then, protons are administered over 4 consecutive days, thus providing four high-dose treatment fractions to a prescription dose of 60 Gy. Proton therapy has been effective for local tumor control, preservation of the globe, and vision. However, in contrast to low-energy plaque therapy, proton beam therapy typically requires an anterior entrance dose, resulting in more commonly reported lash loss, dry eye, neovascular glaucoma, and cataract.36,37 Also unlike plaque therapy, proton treatment can be confounded by eye movement, leading to a mobile target volume.37 TREATMENT FOR SPECIAL CASES Iris and Iridociliary Melanoma The overall 5-year risk for iris melanoma metastasis is 10.7%. However, small iris melanomas are often observed for growth prior to treatment. Surgical iridectomy or iridocyclectomy used to be the most common treatment. However, there has been a transition to relatively safe, tissue-sparing radiation therapy techniques.5,38,39 For example, plaque brachytherapy not only avoids the uncommon risks of intraocular surgery (e.g., infection, hemorrhage, acute cataract, and retinal detachment) but also offers iris retention, retained iris function, and relatively large treatment margins. With long-term follow-up, epicorneal 103Pd plaque brachytherapy has been associated with excellent local control, a high risk of radiation cataract formation, and almost no risk for radiation- related keratopathy, retinopathy, or optic neuropathy.35 Choroidal Melanomas t

Although postresection radiation typically involves 6-MV photons from a linear accelerator, this treatment is typically associated with significant loss of hair (eyelashes and eye brow), dry sunken sockets, and a poor cosmetic result. Alternatively, high-dose interstitial brachytherapy has improved cosmesis without sacrificing local control.42 Radiation Retinopathy and Optic Neuropathy Radiation retinopathy and optic neuropathy are secondary complications of radiation therapy of CM. These diseases are characterized by a progressive obliterative arteritis that stimulates VEGF production with resultant vascular transudation, edema, dependent tissue necrosis, optic nerve damage, and neovascularization. Left untreated, the retina and/or optic nerve becomes atrophic, and neovascularization can induce secondary glaucoma, retinal detachment, and vitreous hemorrhage. Radiation retinopathy and optic neuropathy are amenable to suppression by intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy (e.g., ranibizumab, bevacizumab, aflibercept); however, treatment is not curative.6,7,27 DIAGNOSIS OF METASTASIS The Incidence of Metastasis The majority of UM metastases occur within the liver.3 Other much less common sites of disease are the lungs and bone.3 Metastatic tumors are often discovered on surveillance imaging, and patients are usually completely asymptomatic. It is for this reason that early referral of high-risk UM patients to a medical oncologist who has experience with UM is prudent. This allows for a trusting relationship to develop, so the relating of bad news is easier for both parties. History and Physical Not all eye cancer specialists are located in subspecialty centers. Therefore, each eye cancer specialist (often without medical oncology guidance) typically determines how patients will be initially staged and subsequently screened for metastatic disease. Worldwide patterns are largely dependent on social and economic conditions as well as the availability of radiographic imaging. That said, when medical oncologists are referred patients with a history of UM, the initial TNM staging (eighth edition AJCC) should be used to help determine their metastatic risk (see Table 111.1).24 A history of weight loss, early satiety, abdominal pain, or subcutaneous nodularity should raise suspicion. After Treatment In consideration of the incidence of metastasis after local treatment in patients with high-risk tumors, follow-up staging should include abdominal imaging every 6 months for 5 years and then annually for at least 5 additional years (Fig. 111.3). However, in consideration of the risks of repeated ionizing radiation exposure and the greater efficacy of contrast-enhanced MRI, MRI is preferred over CT. PET/CT can evaluate postirradiation CM viability, clarify the nature of suspicious CT or MRI findings and detect multi-organ disease. A complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel with a serum lactate dehydrogenase can also be ordered. Abnormal serum chemistries can indicate possible bone metastasis (elevated alkaline phosphatase), more aggressive disease (elevated lactate dehydrogenase), or underlying liver disease or other conditions that could influence the ability to give future therapies. Adjuvant Therapy for High-Risk Uveal Melanoma Patients with large UMs (T3 or T4), those with extrascleral extension, and those with known monosomy 3 have been offered adjuvant therapy on clinical trials in an attempt to reduce their risk of metastatic disease. There have been many trials using chemotherapy, interferon, and bacillus Calmette-Guérin that have all provided patients with no measurable improvement in survival or risk reduction.49 Current clinical trials are exploring antiangiogenesis agents, checkpoint inhibitors, and targeted therapies. A retrospective study of high-risk UM patients (monosomy 3 and 8q amplification or monosomy 3 and T3 or T4 tumors) treated at a single institution with sunitinib for 6 months compared to institutional controls suggested a benefit. Although these data are interesting, these results must be confirmed in a controlled clinical trial setting to be validated and not reflective of selection bias.50 Biopsy at the time of diagnosis (for genetic or molecular biomarkers) may be performed for patients considering enrollment onto in to adjuvant therapy studies. Liver-Directed Therapy UM patients with metastatic disease located only in their liver should be considered for liver-directed therapy if they cannot participate in clinical trial or there are no available trials. There are several modalities used for the management of liver metastases, and these include surgery, microwave radiofrequency ablation, chemo- or immune-ablation, and yttrium-90 (90Y) spheres.40,51 The extent of hepatic disease, the location of the tumors, the patient’s performance status, and the institution’s interventional capability dictate the potential for these options. Relatively rare cases of solitary, slow-growing hepatic or extrahepatic metastases, typically found 5 or more years after treatment of the primary UM, have been treated by local metastasectomy.52 Figure 111.4 Metastatic uveal melanoma treatment pathway. Surgical Resection Selection of patients for surgical resection requires limited disease, an excellent performance status, and disease- free interval. Most patients develop recurrent disease within the liver, so aggressive surgical management is usually not recommended. Resections occur infrequently due to the rarity of isolated, small liver metastases, so randomized trials have not been performed. The literature suggests there may be an improvement in overall survival in this small subset of patients.53 Radiofrequency Ablation, Chemoembolization, and Immunoembolization Radiofrequency ablation or microwave ablation uses percutaneous heat or microwave to ablate tumors. Chemoembolization combines hepatic artery embolization with the local infusion of concentrated doses of chemotherapeutic agents to isolated tumors. Immunoembolization combines hepatic artery embolization with the local infusion of concentrated doses of immunotherapy agents. These therapies can be considered for patients with low disease burden (usually three or fewer tumors) who also have small (<5 cm) accessible tumors. Tumors located near vessels, tumors adjacent to the heart, and subdiaphragmatic tumors may not be accessible for this type of therapy. This percutaneous modality may provide local control of small and few tumors and prolong time to progression or delay the need for systemic therapy. None of these methods has resulted in an improvement in overall survival.54,55 Radioembolization using 90

Retrospective trials have reported high local response rates (60%), with no impact on overall survival.56 In summary, liver-directed therapy has not been shown to be curative but may delay progression of disease and thus provide excellent palliation. There is significant interest in combining liver-directed therapy with checkpoint inhibition in clinical trials in an attempt to maximize the effect of both therapies. Systemic Therapy Metastatic UM is not curable. Although there are several interventions used to control a patient’s disease for months to years, none have demonstrated durable disease-free survival. For this reason, participation in clinical trials offers patients cutting edge, otherwise unavailable treatment. This also increases their options and provides them with their best chance for extended survival. It is important to note that standard treatment options are available (including other clinical trials) if their metastatic disease does not respond to a clinical trial therapy (see Fig. 111.4). Single-agent or multiagent chemotherapy and chemotherapy in combination with biologics or interferon-α have not demonstrated any meaningful impact on this disease. Several clinical trials of single-agent or combination chemotherapy demonstrated response rates of ≤1%.57–59 Immunotherapy With the dramatic impact of immunotherapy on cutaneous melanoma, there has been significant interest in using these agents for metastatic UM. In 2011, ipilimumab was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of metastatic cutaneous melanoma. Ipilimumab is a human monoclonal antibody that blocks the immune checkpoint interaction between cytotoxic T-cell lymphocyte-4 on activated T cells and B7 on antigen- presenting cells.60 A randomized phase III trial in previously treated metastatic cutaneous melanoma patients demonstrated an overall improvement in survival with a 20% response rate.61 Unfortunately, clinical trials exploring ipilimumab as a single agent in metastatic UM demonstrated only a 5% response rate and no impact on survival.62,63 The anti–programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) agents, namely, pembrolizumab and nivolumab, received U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval for metastatic cutaneous melanoma in 2015. Genetic tumor typing offers the potential to identify high-risk patients for treatment of presumed subclinical metastatic disease. BIOMARKERS: PROGNOSTIC AND PREDICTIVE FACTORS Clinical Prognostic Factors Tumor Size and Location UM size or largest tumor dimension has been the most reproducible biomarker for CM metastasis. The eighth edition of AJCC includes a prognostic staging table now supported by three separate studies and thus a retrospective analysis of almost 19,000 patients.13,70,71 It is useful because noninvasive tumor measurements are available at the time of diagnosis. Additional evidence that tumor size can be correlated to metastatic risk comes from the study by Diener-West et al.,46 which was a COMS meta-analysis of 5-year mortality among enucleated patients; weighted estimates of 5-year mortality after enucleation were 16% for small tumors, 32% for medium-sized tumors, and 53% for large tumors. Iris melanomas are typically smaller and thus carry a four- to five-fold lower (5-year Kaplan-Meier estimate of 10.7%) mortality rate. Among biopsy-proven iris melanomas, other risk factors include tumors >5 mm in largest diameter and tumors confluent with the ciliary body. Because ciliary body melanomas are typically hidden behind the iris, they can develop “ring melanoma” and thus large basal dimensions with a 5-year mortality of 53%. Other metastatic risk factors include advancing age, local recurrence, and extrascleral extension.42,72

Diffuse melanomas are low-lying tumors often with indistinct or irregular margins that are more difficult to treat. Iris melanomas can also occur as the diffuse variant, starting as a solitary tumor and then evolving to multifocal lesions after treatment.73 Histopathologic, Physiologic, Genetic, and Molecular Prognostic Factors Genetics and Molecular Biology Of the cytogenetic and molecular genetic changes within UM, it is the partial or complete loss of one chromosome 3 that is most widely described.74,75 This has not only been associated with aggressive features such as greater tumor size, ciliary body involvement, the presence of epithelioid cells, and closed loop vasculogenic mimicry but is also considered a biomarker of metastasis. Gene expression profiling involves the simultaneous measurement of mRNA expression of multiple genes to obtain a real-time view of tumor biology. Three gene expression profiling subgroups have been identified and related to risk for metastatic disease. Cytogenetic Abnormalities Monosomy 3 is present in approximately 50% to 60% of UM cases. The loss of heterozygosity indicates deletions around 3p25–26 and on 3q and a region at 3p11–14.76,77 Loss of the long arm and gain of the short arm of chromosome 6 are other frequently observed chromosomal aberrations in UM.78 Monosomy 3 and additional copies of 8q correlated with reduced survival.76 A deletion in chromosome 1 concurrent with monosomy 3 is an independent predictor of disease-free survival. The combination of monosomy 3 with cell type analysis or tumor diameter has been shown to have a greater prognostic impact than monosomy 3 alone. Earlier studies of molecular deregulation provided interesting insights into the molecular pathogenesis of UM. For example, Rb protein is expressed in virtually all melanomas, indicating a lack of Rb gene mutation.79 A combination of microarray gene expression profiling and comparative genomic hybridization showed that gain of chromosome 8q correlates strongly with expression of DDEF1, a gene located at 8q24.80 Therefore, DDEF1 overexpression might be a pathogenetically relevant consequence of chromosome 8q amplification associated with aggressive UMs.80 Genetic Mutations Individual gene mutations have improved our understanding of the etiology of UM.

Dr. AVR @ TMH 112 Superior Vena Cava Syndrome Andreas Rimner and Joachim Yahalom INTRODUCTION Superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS) is the clinical expression of obstruction of blood flow through the superior vena cava (SVC). Characteristic symptoms and signs may develop quickly or gradually when this thin-walled vessel is compressed, invaded, or thrombosed by processes in the superior mediastinum. Most cases reported in the past were due to syphilitic aneurysms or tuberculosis mediastinitis.1 Nowadays, malignancy is the most common underlying process in patients with SVCS.2 With the increased use of intravascular devices such as catheters and pacemakers, thrombosis of the SVC caused by these foreign bodies has been more frequently observed.3 It is estimated that SVCS develops in 15,000 people in the United States each year.2 ANATOMY AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY The SVC is the major low-pressure vessel for drainage of venous blood from the head, neck, upper extremities, and upper thorax. It is located in the right superior mediastinum and is surrounded by the sternum, trachea, right mainstem bronchus, aorta, pulmonary artery, and perihilar and paratracheal lymph nodes. The SVC extends from the junction of the right and left innominate veins to the right atrium, over a distance of 6 to 8 cm. The distal 2 cm of the SVC are within the pericardial sac, with a point of relative fixation of the vena cava at the pericardial reflection. The left and right brachiocephalic veins merge at the level of the aortic arch to form the SVC. The brachiocephalic veins themselves receive contributions from the internal and external jugular veins, subclavian veins, internal mammary veins, pericardiophrenic veins, superior intercostal veins, and inferior thyroid vein.4 The azygos vein, the main auxiliary vessel, enters the SVC posteriorly, just above the pericardial reflection. The physiologic width of the SVC is 1.5 to 2 cm. The SVC is thin walled, compliant, and easily compressible and therefore vulnerable to any space-occupying process in its vicinity. The SVC is completely encircled by chains of lymph nodes that drain the right thoracic cavity. Other critical structures in the mediastinum, such as the auxiliary azygos vein, main bronchi, esophagus, and spinal cord, may be involved by the same process that leads to obstruction of the SVC. When the SVC is fully or partially obstructed, veno

chylous. Rarely do patients present with life-threatening symptoms such as confusion, obtundation, stridor or syncope without precipitating factors, hypotension, or renal insufficiency. Malignant disease is currently the most common cause of SVCS. The percentage of patients in different series with a confirmed diagnosis of malignancy varies from 60% to 86% (Table 112.2).8,10–13 In a large series of lung cancer patients, SVCS was identified in 4% to 8.6% of the patients.14,15 Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) and squamous cell carcinoma are the most common histologic subtypes because they frequently present with bulky involvement of the mediastinum or paramediastinal, central location.8,16,17 Lymphoma involving the mediastinum is the cause of SVCS in 2% to 21% of patients (see Table 112.2). In a large series of lymphoma patients, most patients with SVCS had either diffuse large-cell lymphoma or lymphoblastic lymphoma.18 The presence of dysphagia, hoarseness, or stridor was a major adverse prognostic factor for patients with lymphoma who presented with SVCS. In a series of patients with primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma with sclerosis, SVCS was present in 57% of patients.19 Other primary mediastinal malignancies that may cause SVCS are thymomas and germ cell tumors. SCLC, non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL), and germ cell tumors constitute almost half of the malignant causes of SVCS. Hodgkin lymphoma commonly involves the mediastinum, but it rarely causes SVCS. Rare tumors such as thymic malignancies, pleural mesothelioma, sarcomas, and primary mediastinal germ cell tumors may cause SVCS as well. Breast cancer is the most common metastatic disease that causes SVCS in up to 11% of the cases.10,11 The prognosis of patients with SVCS strongly correlates with the prognosis of the underlying disease. In recent years, nonmalignant conditions causing SVCS have been more often observed. In data collected from general hospitals, as many as 40% of patients had noncancerous causes of SVCS, most commonly due to thrombosis due to the presence of central vein catheters for the delivery of chemotherapy agents or hyperalimentation or pacemakers.8,11,13,20 The increasing use of such catheters in conjunction with a common thromboembolic disposition in many patients with cancer contributes to the development of SVCS.20

Obstruction of SVC in the pediatric age group is rare and has a different etiologic spectrum, mainly iatrogenic, secondary to cardiovascular surgery for congenital heart disease, orthotopic heart transplantation, ventriculoatrial shunt for hydrocephalus, SVC catheterization for parenteral nutrition, and mediastinal fibrosis secondary to histoplasmosis.21–23 Rarely, congenital vascular malformations may present with SVCS. DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP The modern treatment of SVCS has become disease-specific from the outset. Therefore, a clear diagnosis prior to initiation of emergency treatment such as mediastinal irradiation should be made. Mediastinal irradiation before a biopsy may preclude proper interpretation of the specimen in almost half of the patients and should be avoided.24 The safety of modern, minimally invasive diagnostic procedures such as bronchoscopy, mediastinoscopy, computed tomography (CT)-guided biopsy, or supraclavicular lymph node biopsy has markedly improved, and concerns about risks from these procedures should not preclude proper diagnostic workup. In contrast to past opinions, there is little evidence to suggest that diagnostic procedures such as venographies, thoracotomies, bronchoscopies

Percutaneous transthoracic CT-guided fine-needle biopsy is an effective and safe alternative to an open biopsy or mediastinoscopy.29 In the presence of a pleural effusion, thoracentesis can establish the diagnosis of malignancy in 71% of patients with malignancy.9 A thoracoscopic biopsy or thoracotomy is diagnostic if all other procedures have failed. DISEASE-SPECIFIC MANAGEMENT AND OUTCOMES The goal of treatment of SVCS depends on the cause and—in malignancies—the stage of the disease. Malignant tumors are potentially curable if they present at a nonmetastatic stage, even in the presence of SVCS. The treatment of SVCS should be selected according to the histologic disorder and stage of the primary process. During the diagnostic process, the patient can benefit from bed rest and oxygen administration. Some clinicians advocate the use of diuretics and/or corticosteroids if the patient is uncomfortably symptomatic. This should only be considered after pathologic confirmation of the cause of SVCS in symptomatic patients who require urgent palliation, as steroid initiation prior to pathologic confirmation can significantly hamper efforts for an accurate diagnosis, especially with lymphomas. Prophylactic anticoagulation in the absence of thrombosis is of no proven benefit and may interfere with diagnostic procedures. When the therapeutic goal is only palliation of SVCS or when urgent treatment of the venous obstruction is required, direct opening of the occlusion should be considered. Endovascular stenting and angioplasty with possible thrombolysis may provide prompt relief of symptoms before more cancer-specific therapy.3,30 SMALL-CELL LUNG CANCER Platinum-based chemotherapy alone or in combination with thoracic radiation therapy is the standard treatment for SCLC and is effective in rapidly improving the symptoms of SVCS.15–17,31 SCLC is highly sensitive to both platinum and etoposide chemotherapy and radiation therapy. No significant difference in response rates to chemotherapy or radiation therapy has been detected in most studies. Response rates to chemotherapy range from 73% to 93% and to radiation from 43% to 94%.15,31 Relief of SVCS typically occurs within 7 to 10 days after initiation of therapy. In patients with SCLC with recurrent or persistent SVCS, additional chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy is still likely to relieve sy

Patients with nonmalignant SVCS often have longstanding symptoms before they seek medical advice, and the time to establish the diagnosis and survival are typically markedly longer.11 The average survival rate has been reported as 9 years for benign causes, compared with 5 months for lung cancer as the cause of SVCS. A total of 12 of 16 (75%) patients with benign SVCS had a mediastinal granuloma that was attributed to histoplasmosis.32 Ten patients who were available for 1 to 11 years were all doing well at the time of the report. Given the good prognosis of patients with benign SVCS, a need for SVC bypass surgery may not be justified, except for patients in whom SVCS develops, progresses, or persists after 6 to 12 months of observation for possible collateral development.32 Ketoconazole may prevent recurrent SVCS from active histoplasmosis. CATHETER-INDUCED OBSTRUCTION In catheter-induced SVCS, the mechanism of obstruction is usually thrombosis. Streptokinase, urokinase, or recombinant tissue-type plasminogen activator may achieve lysis of the thrombus early in its formation.33 Heparin and oral anticoagulants may reduce the extent of the thrombus and prevent its progression. Removal of the catheter should be considered, if possible, in combination with anticoagulation to avoid embolization. In patients for whom electrodes of a pacemaker must be changed, the wires should be removed to prevent the risk of developing SVCS.34 Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty, with or without thrombolytic therapy, and stent insertion have been successfully used to open catheter-induced SVC obstructions.35 TREATMENT Radiation Therapy Radiation therapy is a treatment option for most patients with malignant SVCS. It does not only provide immediate relief of the obstruction but also treat the underlying cause of the obstruction, thus improving symptoms in the long-term and effectively preventing SVCS recurrence. The primary effect of palliative radiation therapy for SVCS is exerted by decreasing the extrinsic pressure on the SVC by the surrounding or invading malignant masses. However, serial venograms and autopsies suggest that the symptomatic improvement may be enhanced by the development of collaterals after the pressure in the mediastinum is eased. In general, when radiation is given as initial treatment, CT-based simulation and fractions of 1.8 to 2 Gy are recommended for

Dr. AVR @ TMH Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty using balloon dilatation, insertion of expandable metal stents, or both have been successfully used to open and maintain the patency of SVC obstruction resulting from malignant and benign causes.3,30,35,38,39 It is an effective initial treatment for obtaining immediate relief of the obstruction if the clinical status of the patient is deteriorating. Median symptom-free survival of 6 months has been reported in a large series of 149 patients with malignant SVCS.38 However, long-term experience in maintaining patency after stent therapy in patients with SVCS from benign causes who are expected to have long survival is still limited.35 Complication rates for endovascular therapy range from 0% to 50% and include bleeding, stent migration, stent occlusion, and pulmonary embolus.3 A prospective study examining the outcomes of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene-covered stents found a higher patency and median survival compared to uncovered stents from a historic patient population.40 Thrombolysis is often an integral part of the endovascular management of SVCS because thrombosis is frequently a critical component of the obstruction and lysis is necessary to allow the passage of the wire. Most reports have emphasized the use of combination endovascular therapy: thrombolysis, angioplasty, and stent insertion.3,30 Successful experience with thrombolytic agents was also obtained in the treatment of catheter- induced SVCS.3,33 The higher yield of thrombolytic therapy in patients with catheters is probably related to the mechanism of obstruction, the ability to deliver the agent directly to the thrombus, and earlier recognition of SVCS in patients with malfunctioning catheters. Early intervention and use of urokinase and recombinant tissue- type plasminogen activator were associated with favorable results.33 Surgery In malignancy-induced SVCS, the tumor involvement causing SVCS is typically so extensive that it is not considered technically resectable. There may be exceptions in which definitive surgical resection may be considered if feasible (e.g., in a young, fit patient with a nonlymphomatous, nonmetastatic diagnosis of malignancy). SVC reconstruction using grafts such as expanded polytetrafluoroethylene have become possible with modern surgical techniques.41 In most cases, however, palliative surgical intervention sh

(>85%) with SVCS, the symptoms are not severe (grades 0, 1, and 2) and cancer-specific treatment could follow appropriate diagnosis and staging. Grade 3 (severe) patients who present with mild or moderate cerebral edema, mild or moderate laryngeal edema, or diminished cardiac reserve may be considered for immediate stent intervention or early radiation therapy; otherwise, they should receive disease-specific treatment. Only the rare (<5%) grade 4 (life-threatening) patients, who develop significant cerebral edema or laryngeal edema with stridor or have significant hemodynamic compromise, should undergo stent insertion immediately. The benefit of either short- or long-term anticoagulation therapy for SVCS is unclear, although thrombolytic agents have been used effectively in patients with vena caval thrombosis.2 Most experts recommend anticoagulation after thrombolysis (to prevent disease progression and recurrence) and aspirin after stent placement in the absence of thrombosis, but data are limited. The optimal management of recurrent obstruction of the SVC is also controversial. Placement of a stent is often considered because of the limited benefit or the risk of excessive toxic effects from repeat chemotherapy or radiation, but data to guide decision making are limited. RECOMMENDATIONS The clinical course of SVCS rarely represents an absolute emergency. In patients without a clear cause of SVCS who do not have life-threatening symptoms, an efficient diagnostic effort should be attempted before any oncologic treatment is given. If all the proposed testing has failed to establish the diagnosis, the location of the suspicious lesion in the chest and the experience of the surgical team should determine whether mediastinoscopy or thoracotomy is performed. After the cause of SVCS has been established, treatment of the primary process should promptly follow. Combination chemotherapy with an appropriate regimen is the treatment of choice for SCLC and NHL. Radiation therapy of the lesion and adjacent nodal areas may enhance control after initial response to chemotherapy. NSCLC causing SVCS is best treated with radiation therapy. Baehring INTRODUCTION An increase in intracranial pressure (ICP) is a common neurologic complication of patients with cancer involving the nervous system. Various pathomechanisms have to be considered in this patient population. Large cerebral metastases are the most common cause and can give rise to intracranial hemorrhage. Subependymal or leptomeningeal masses located at “bottlenecks” of spinal fluid pathways such as the foramen of Monro or the aqueduct of Sylvius raise pressure by obstructing spinal fluid flow. A cancer-related hypercoagulable state can lead to dural sinus thrombosis or extracranial venous outflow obstruction, and coagulopathies predispose to subdural bleeding. The cancer patient as an immunocompromised host is at risk for infections of the nervous system such as fungal or bacterial meningitis or a bacterial abscess, which can all result in increased ICP. Similarly, aseptic meningitis can be seen as a consequence of intrathecal chemotherapy administration. Communicating hydrocephalus reflects decreased reabsorption of spinal fluid, which can be seen in leptomeningeal carcinomatosis or after an infection. Dural venous sinus stenosis from dural metastases causes a syndrome resembling idiopathic intracranial hypertension. This chapter provides an overview of the various mechanisms of increased ICP and the clinical manifestations, diagnosis, and treatment options. PATHOPHYSIOLOGIC CONSIDERATIONS Intracranial volume is not expandable in an adult because of its containment by the skull and the dura. The brain itself has an average volume of 1,400 mL, spinal fluid of 52 to 160 mL, and blood of 150 mL.1 An increase in the volume of one compartment occurs at the expense of the other two (Monro-Kellie hypothesis).2–4 If brain volume increases as a result of a brain tumor, the spinal fluid volume decreases as a compensatory mechanism. Up to an ICP of 200 to 250 mm Hg, an increase in cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) volume results in only minor increases in ICP as long as CSF flow is not obstructed, the rate between CSF production and reabsorption remains constant, and the dural venous sinuses remain open. However, intracranial compliance decreases with rising ICP (i.e., with rising pressure, increase in volume leads to a disproportionate increase in pressure). This is reflec

fluid is produced at an average rate of 21 to 22 mL per hour or approximately 500 mL per day. CSF represents a plasma filtrate passively diffusing through the choroid plexus of the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles. It is reabsorbed within the arachnoid granulations overlying the cerebral hemispheres. Mass lesions in proximity to bottlenecks of CSF flow (foramen of Monro, cerebral aqueduct, medullary foramina, basilar subarachnoid cisterns) cause obstructive or noncommunicating hydrocephalus. Carcinomatosis or meningitis directly interferes with CSF reabsorption at the arachnoid granulations. Under chronic conditions, the spinal fluid pressure reaches a new equilibrium within the high normal range and gives rise to a condition called normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) characterized by ventricular enlargement out of proportion to age-related cortical atrophy. Increased production of CSF is a rare cause of raised ICP. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) or pseudotumor cerebri denotes a syndrome characterized by signs of increased ICP in the absence of mass lesions or hydrocephalus. Although poorly defined from a pathophysiologic standpoint, an increasing number of patients with IIH have been found to have partial obstruction of dural venous sinuses. Iatrogenic causes of IIH include all-trans retinoic acid, tetracycline antibiotics, and sulfonamides. Acute increases in arterial and venous pressure result in an increase in ICP. Cerebral perfusion is kept constant over a wide arterial pressure range (50 to 160 mm Hg). Once this autoregulatory mechanism fails, further increase in arterial blood pressure passively increases ICP. Venous obstruction can be reproduced with the Queckenstedt maneuver (manual compression of both internal jugular veins). Dural venous sinus pressure fluctuates with intrathoracic pressure changes. Thus, coughing, sneezing, and straining (Valsalva maneuver) are accompanied by an increase in ICP. In a patient with increased ICP and decreased intracranial compliance, gagging or coughing can lead to transient decompensation and the acute onset of symptoms (syncope in patients with colloid cyst of the third ventricle, plateau waves). Depending on the etiology and location of an increase in cerebral parenchymal or extra-axial volume, patients may have relatively few symptoms until herniation ensues. Brain abscess complicates neurosurgical interventions for resection of metastases, drainage of cerebral hemorrhage, or placement of ventricular catheters. Autoimmune inflammatory encephalomyelitis has been described as a rare entity in patients after stem cell transplantation. Immunologic therapies, such as bispecific antibodies (e.g., blinatumomab) and chimeric antigen receptor T cells, have been associated with diffuse cerebral edema. The mechanism is unclear but felt to be possibly related to cytokine release syndrome with inflammatory cytokines leading to increased endothelial permeability.12 Disorders Affecting Cerebrospinal Fluid Production or Reabsorption A syndrome resembling NPH has been observed in long-term survivors of whole-brain or, less commonly, partial- brain irradiation. Fibrosis of arachnoid granulations has been suspected to play a role in the pathogenesis of this entity, which is also characterized by extensive white matter demyelination and frank necrosis. Selected patients seem to respond favorably to ventriculoperitoneal shunting.13–15 An acute imbalance between CSF production and reabsorption occurs in neoplastic meningitis and opportunistic meningeal infections in the immunocompromised cancer patient. Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis is almost invariably associated with elevation of ICP. Patients after splenectomy are susceptible to meningitis with encapsulated bacteria. The pathogenesis of communicating hydrocephalus in patients with spinal cord tumors or nonobstructive masses of the cerebellopontine angle is not well understood. Most commonly, ependymomas, but also schwannoma, meningioma, neurofibroma, and glioma, might release protein degradation products or cells into CSF that obstruct the arachnoid granulations.16,17 However, the protein level is rarely elevated in these patients. Others have suspected blockage of the lumbar CSF reservoir,18–20 arachnoiditis, or increased fibrinogen levels21 as the cause of this syndrome. All-trans retinoic acid, a differentiating agent used for the treatment of promyelocytic leukemia, has been associated with episodes of communicating hydrocephalus, likely as a consequence of decreased CSF reabsorption.22,23 Increased IC

Temporal and occipital lobe disease causes visual field deficits. An upward gaze paresis occurs in patients with tumors of the tectal region such as pineal neoplasms or metastases. Hyponatremia as a result of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone is observed as a metabolic complication of increased ICP. Sphincter incontinence occurs in chronically elevated ICP. Dr. AVR @ TMH rising ICP is known as the Kocher-Cushing reflex.35 In uncal herniation from temporal lobe masses or herpes encephalitis, ipsilateral compression of the third nerve and associated parasympathetic nerve fibers leads to pupillary dilatation before extraocular dysmotility. With progressive shift of brain substance, complete third nerve palsy ensues and signs of midbrain dysfunction appear. Patients develop contralateral hemiparesis from pressure on the cerebral peduncle and ultimately become stuporous. Increasing pressure from hemispheric or diencephalic mass lesions results in central (transtentorial) herniation. This leads to a progressive syndrome reflecting sequential damage to brain stem structures in a rostrocaudal fashion.33 At the early diencephalic stage, mild changes in the patient’s alertness are accompanied by periodic breathing, yawning, or hiccupping. Pupils are small but remain reactive to light. With further progression of central herniation, the patient becomes obtunded or stuporous. Roving eye movements reflect diffuse cortical dysfunction and preservation of lower brain stem gaze centers. Noxious stimuli elicit flexion of upper extremities and extension of lower extremities (decorticate posturing). Midsize pupils unresponsive to light indicate midbrain dysfunction. Damage to the mesencephalic reticular activating system produces coma. A fast and regular breathing pattern evolves (central neurogenic hyperventilation). Transition to the pontine stage of central herniation is accompanied by extensor posturing of all limbs to noxious stimulation (decerebrate posturing). Absence of the oculocephalic reflex (doll’s head maneuver) and horizontal eye movements to caloric stimulation of the vestibular system indicate damage to pontine structures. Breathing becomes apneustic with pontine compression. When the cerebellar tonsils herniate through the foramen magnum, ataxic breathing is observed and the blood pressure drops.33 The syndrome of raised ICP and cerebral herniation can evolve slowly over days to weeks or acutely over hours. Rapid progression usually indicates hemorrhage. Subdural hematomas in patients with coagulopathies can evolve so rapidly that signs of cerebral herniation are present before an imaging study can be obtained. Hemorrhage into a metastatic focus is typically characterized by the sudden onset of focal neurologic s

ischemia or high cellularity suggestive of malignant tumor growth. CSF flow studies (cine MRI) are helpful to evaluate the functional significance of minute structural lesions within or surrounding the cerebral aqueduct. Slit- like ventricles in the correct clinical setting are indicative of IIH. Coronal images through the orbit may reveal dilatation of the optic nerve sheaths in this condition. Ex vacuo ventricular dilatation out of proportion to cortical atrophy is characteristic for NPH. MRI of the spine should be considered in patients with unexplained communicating hydrocephalus. Transcranial Doppler sonography is helpful in the intensive care unit for monitoring cerebral perfusion and alteration in cerebrovascular resistance (e.g., in vasospasm or intra-arterial disease) in patients with increased ICP.45 Continuous electroencephalogram (EEG) is often applied to monitoring patient’s with neurologic disorders; however, the role of EEG in monitoring ICP changes has not yet been conclusively established.46 TREATMENT In the majority of cases, the onset of increased ICP in cancer patients is protracted over days to weeks. After increased ICP is recognized and symptomatic measures have been initiated to lower pressure, a diagnostic procedure can be performed before definitive treatment is provided. Fewer patients present as an emergency but are the ones who do require immediate neurosurgical intervention. The normovolemic patient with increased ICP and suspected decreased intracranial compliance is best positioned with head and upper trunk slightly elevated (approximately 30 degrees). Because fever above 100.5°F contributes to elevated ICP, it is common practice to use antipyretics such as acetaminophen above this threshold. Serum osmolality is kept in the high normal range. Isotonic saline solutions are recommended for intravenous hydration, whereas hypotonic fluids are avoided because free water shifts along an osmolar gradient further exacerbate increased ICP. Corticosteroids are effective agents for the initial management of increased ICP caused by vasogenic edema. No benefit has been convincingly shown for cytotoxic edema of an acute ischemic stroke or intracranial hemorrhage secondary to remote effec

to ICP elevation. Careful blood pressure adjustment is needed to avoid blood pressure peaks without decreasing cerebral perfusion. The most rapid method to decrease ICP is intubation with mechanical hyperventilation. The partial pressure of carbon dioxide should be decreased to 25 to 30 mm Hg. Lower partial pressure of carbon dioxide levels are avoided because cerebral perfusion is reduced. The effect of hyperventilation is transient, and thus, other measures such as corticosteroid use and osmotic diuresis need to be initiated simultaneously. Obstructive hydrocephalus constitutes a neurosurgical emergency. Rapid neurologic deterioration with signs of cerebral herniation mandates the immediate placement of an external ventriculostomy. Permanent drainage of CSF through a ventriculoperitoneal shunt or endoscopic placement of a third ventriculostomy may be necessary when the cause of spinal fluid flow obstruction cannot be definitively treated. Although filter systems are available, ventriculoperitoneal shunting is avoided in patients with leptomeningeal tumor in order to prevent peritoneal seeding. NPH responds favorably to ventriculoperitoneal shunting. It is the task of the clinician to carefully select patients who may benefit from this procedure. Patients with a short history of the classic clinical triad of gait apraxia, precipitate micturition, and cognitive decline are most likely to respond. Extended lumbar drainage, large-volume spinal fluid releases, and scintigraphic cisternography have been used as objective means to predict outcome of a shunting procedure.48 Ventriculoperitoneal shunting can be considered for palliation in patients with increased ICP related to leptomeningeal carcinomatosis that does not respond to medical therapy.49 Disease-specific treatment of increased ICP in addition to symptomatic management with corticosteroids or osmotic diuresis is indicated in the majority of cases. Infectious complications are treated with antimicrobial therapy. Patients with a brain abscess undergo surgical drainage and a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics. A hematoma within a metastatic focus is resected if located in a noneloquent area of the brain and in the absence of widely metastatic disease. Spratt INCIDENCE AND ETIOLOGY In the United States, approximately 300,000 adults have metastatic disease involving the bone. The spine is the most common location of bone metastases, with an estimated 60% of bone metastases arising in the spine. Approximately 10% of patients with spine metastases will develop malignant spinal cord compression (MSCC), with an estimated 18,000 patients diagnosed each year in the United States with MSCC.1,2 Autopsy series have demonstrated up to 70% of patients with advanced metastatic disease have spine metastases, and thus, the true incidence of MSCC is likely underreported.3 The majority of patients with MSCC are older than age 50 years, and the cumulative incidence of MSCC decreases with age.4 Of patients who develop MSCC, the most common cancer types include lung cancer (25%), prostate cancer (16%), multiple myeloma (11%), and breast cancer (7%). Cancers with the highest cancer-specific incidence include multiple myeloma (15%), lymphoma (14%), and prostate cancer (6%).5 The tumor spectrum causing MSCC in the pediatric population differs from adults, largely due to differences in the prevalence of various tumor histologies. In the pediatric population, Ewing sarcoma, neuroblastoma, primary vertebral osteosarcoma, germ cell tumors, and lymphoma are all potential causes of MSCC.6 Approximately 20% of MSCC cases lack a history of cancer.7 MSCC as the primary manifestation of malignancy is most common in non-Hodgkin lymphoma, myeloma, and lung cancer, especially small-cell lung cancer.8,9 ANATOMY AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY The spinal cord is composed of the central gray matter and the peripheral white matter. Contained with the white matter are ascending and descending tracts, whereas gray matter contains various somatic, visceral, sensory, and motor nuclei. The spinal cord is surrounded in order by pia mater, subarachnoid space, arachnoid dura, subdural space, dura mater, epidural space (contains fat), and the vertebral bones. In addition, there are important ligamentous structures that strengthen the spinal column, notably the posterior longitudinal ligament. The thoracic spine is the most common location of MSCC (approximately 60% of cases), thought to be secondary to its greater number of vertebrae. The most common mechanism of spinal cord

CLINICAL PRESENTATION MSCC is the presenting sign of cancer in only 1 in 500 cancer patients.15 Most patients have an underlying diagnosis of metastatic cancer or recent history of primary cancer treatment. The most common clinical presentations of MSCC are pain (70% to 96%), sensory deficit (46% to 90%), weakness (61% to 91%), and autonomic dysfunction (40% to 57%).4 In cancer patients, new-onset back pain with or without a neurologic deficits must be considered spine metastases and potential MSCC until proven otherwise. Pain is the most common presenting symptom of MSCC and is often multifactorial (Table 114.1). The four predominant pain types include biologic, mechanical, radicular, and funicular pain. Back pain usually exists for a median of 8 weeks or more prior to the diagnosis of MSCC. It typically begins with involvement of the osseous vertebral column and then rapidly progresses once the epidural venous plexus is obstructed. If the pain disappears without treatment, it may be a manifestation of chronic MSCC that has caused permanent neurologic damage of sensory pathways. However, acute MSCC with associated neurologic compromise over hours to days is possible and is more common in rapidly proliferating tumors (e.g., multiple myeloma). Motor dysfunction manifesting as weakness and spasticity is the earliest sign and usually occurs before sensory disturbance. Typical early complaints are leg “heaviness” and difficulty climbing stairs or getting up from a chair. As the majority of malignancy-related cord compressions occur at the level of the thoracic spinal cord, most patients present with a paraparesis. Dr. AVR @ TMH Standard x-rays, computed tomography (CT) scans, bone scans, and positron emission tomography (PET) scans are unable to reliably document the presence or degree of spinal cord compression. For most patients, MRI is the preferred imaging modality given its excellent soft tissue resolution, clear delineation of the spinal cord on T2- weighted sequences, and noninvasive nature of image acquisition. However, MRI has limitations and disadvantages for select patients. For these patients, a CT myelogram is preferred. It is a relatively quick procedure where approximately 1 mL of radiopaque dye is injected into the subarachnoid space. As with any subcutaneous injection, however, there is a risk of pain, infection, or bleeding with this procedure. Thus, patients on full anticoagulation must be bridged in order to safely undergo the myelography. Imaging of the entire spine is recommended as up to one-third of patients with MSCC will have multilevel involvement and it is critical to rule this out prior to surgical intervention.17,18 If a patient presents with MSCC but no history of cancer, a biopsy is mandatory prior to initiation of therapy. This can be done by excisional biopsy of the mass or by CT-guided needle biopsy. If these cannot be safely or successfully performed, tissue should be obtained by surgical resection because knowledge of the tumor histology is critical in the treatment paradigm of managing spine metastases. GRADING Bilsky et al.19 have developed 4- and 6-point grading systems for spinal cord compression. The 6-point scale has shown good reliability between spine specialists but has not been validated across specialties.19 We favor the simpler, 4-point grading system in order to facilitate communication between multidisciplinary providers (Fig. 114.1). This grading system is based on a scale of 0 to 3, where 0 is bone-only disease; 1 is epidural extension and impingement on the thecal sac without spinal cord compression; 2 is epidural extension without spinal cord compression or obliteration of cerebrospinal fluid space; and 3 is spinal cord compression, deformation of the spinal cord, and obliteration of cerebrospinal fluid space. Grades 2 and 3 represent high-grade MSCC and should be considered an oncologic emergency. Step 3: Evaluate Life Expectancy, Performance Status, Extent of Disease, and Systemic Treatment Options The primary treatments aimed at relieving and controlling MSCC are radiation and/or neurosurgery. However, certain patients may be better served by best supportive care or low-dose single-fraction cEBRT. After a patient is started on corticosteroids, an evaluation of the patient’s performance status and life expectancy is required. Multiple prognostic tools have been created to estimate prognosis for patients with spine metastases.22–24 Important caveats exist for each system, due to differences in the studies’ underlying patient populations, histologies, and interventions.25 In patients with poor performance status, poor prognosis, limited effective treatment options, and widely metastatic disease, a conservative treatment approach (e.g., short-course radiation or hospice) is often ideal. However, patients with good performance status, life expectancy >2 months, minimal or moderate burden of disease, and/or effective systemic treatment options still available will likely benefit from radiotherapeutic or neurosurgical intervention. For these patients, the long-term deficits and declines in quality of life caused by MSCC often outweigh the burdens and side effects of therapy. In 2009, the Spine Oncology Study Group issued a “strong” recommendation to consider sSBRT over cEBRT for patients with solid-tumor spinal metastases.39 sSBRT is a method of delivering high doses to tumor while sparing adjacent normal tissues and is typically delivered over three to five treatments. The biologically effective dose is approximately three to five times higher than with cEBRT, which results in much higher durable local control. This holds true even for radioresistant tumors, such as renal cell carcinoma and sarcoma, where >85% long-term local control can be achieved.40–47 Importantly, the doses commonly used for sSBRT exceed spinal cord tolerance and, if delivered directly to the spinal cord, would have a high probability of causing radiation-induced myelopathy. Therefore, 1 to 3 mm of space between the spinal cord and tumor is typically needed to deliver effective doses of sSBRT. For this reason, grade 2 and 3 MSCC should not be treated with full-dose sSBRT. Select cases of grade 1 MSCC can be treated with sSBRT, but the ideal case is grade 0 MSCC. Therefore, sSBRT plays a small role in the upfront treatment of MSCC. However, the adjuvant or postoperative use of sSBRT is a critical component of managing MSCC. 4. Other therapies.
