Dr. AVR @ TMH 115 Metabolic Emergencies Stacey Stein and Hari A. Deshpande INTRODUCTION Metabolic emergencies continue to be an important challenge for practicing oncologists. Whereas many of these are well-known side effects of treatments and individual cancers, others have emerged because of new and innovative therapies. It is essential to anticipate and recognize early signs and institute appropriate treatment to avoid severe complications. TUMOR LYSIS SYNDROME AND HYPERURICEMIA Definition, Diagnosis, and Staging Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is a disorder involving electrolytes, renal function, and, in severe cases, cardiac and central nervous system abnormalities that result from rapid breakdown or lysis of cancer cells. It has been classified into two groups: laboratory and clinical.1,2 The laboratory abnormalities are as follows: 1. Increase in uric acid 2. Increase in potassium 3. Increase in phosphorus levels 4. Decrease in calcium levels A 25% change from baseline in two or more of these electrolytes within 3 days before or up to 7 days after the initiation of therapy is needed to satisfy the Cairo-Bishop laboratory definition.2 Clinical tumor lysis requires that the laboratory changes are accompanied by the following: 1. Increased creatinine level 2. Seizures 3. Cardiac dysrhythmia 4. Death It has been suggested that refinements, including the finding of any symptomatic hypocalcemia, may make the criteria more useful clinically.1 Incidence and Etiology Early reports of TLS occurred in patients with rapidly growing chemosensitive hematologic malignancies with a high tumor burden, including Burkitt lymphoma and acute leukemias,3–5 although solid tumors with similar characteristics were later also described.6,7 The incidence of laboratory and clinical TLS in patients with high- grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) is 42% and 6%, respectively,8 whereas in a retrospective European study, TLS occurred in 3.4%, 5.2%, and 6.1% of patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and NHL, respectively, with a mortality rate of 0.9%.9 Pathogenesis As the name implies, TLS occurs because the release of cell contents after lysis exceeds the body’s ability to regulate the changes in electrolyte levels. In addition to release of electrolytes from the cells, decreasing adenosine triphosphate (ATP) levels may also lead to potassium leakage,

decreased tubular reabsorption of phosphate. As the transport becomes saturated, however, phosphate levels rise with eventual precipitation of calcium phosphate in tissues resulting in hypocalcemia. This starts a vicious cycle of increased parathyroid hormone levels, decreased proximal tubule phosphate reabsorption, hyperphosphaturia, and risk of calcium phosphate crystal deposition causing tubular obstruction. Hyperuricemia can also contribute to renal failure. Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism, and crystals of urate and uric acid can obstruct renal tubules, collecting ducts, pelvises, and ureters when cellular breakdown is accelerated. Precipitation occurs more readily when pH becomes more acidic. Screening Any rapidly growing cancer or a cancer with a high tumor burden that is expected to respond rapidly to treatment should be considered a candidate for tumor lysis. Laboratory values of potassium, uric acid, phosphorus, and creatinine along with routine blood tests should be monitored twice daily until the risk of tumor lysis complications has passed. Lactate dehydrogenase levels may help determine the rate of breakdown of the tumor. Management Preventative measures are extremely important in managing the condition and should be started 24 hours before chemotherapy administration if possible. Aggressive hydration of at least 3,000 mL/m2/day is required, but urine alkalinization is controversial because, although it makes uric acid more soluble, calcium phosphate complexes are less soluble at an alkaline pH. Hyperkalemia should be treated aggressively with cation exchange resins, dextrose with insulin, calcium gluconate, and sometimes sodium bicarbonate and loop diuretics. Hemodialysis should be used in renal impairment and hyperkalemia not responding to the mentioned measures. Hyperphosphatemia is managed by hydration, oral phosphate binders, and sometimes dialysis. Oral calcium binders should be used with caution as they may cause precipitation of calcium phosphate crystals. Allopurinol (dose adjusted for renal insufficiency) should be started immediately to reduce the risk of hyperuricemia. Because allopurinol and its metabolite oxypurinol inhibit xanthine oxidase, levels of preexisting uric acid will not decrease for 2 to 3 days after treatment. If rapid lowering of uric acid is deemed necessary to avoid renal failure, rasburicase (Fast

Dr. AVR @ TMH HYPONATREMIA Incidence and Etiology Hyponatremia (serum sodium <135 mmol/L) is a common condition affecting up to 47% of hospitalized cancer patients.15 The incidence of moderate or severe hyponatremia (<130 mmol/L) is less common (7.8%)16 but represents levels that are more likely to be symptomatic (nausea, vomiting, pain, depression, fatigue, and coma). The causes of hyponatremia include the disease itself, concomitant comorbidities, physical stress, and medication.17 It may be a prognostic factor, not only in the case of small-cell lung cancer but also in other malignancies and is often the result of a syndrome of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (SIADH).18 This can occur due to ectopic secretion from the cancer itself or antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion induced by various medications including vincristine, cyclophosphamide, opioids, and antidepressants.19 Other causes of hyponatremia include diarrhea and vomiting-induced hypovolemic hyponatremia, which require volume repletion as a primary treatment.17 Plasma osmolality is closely related to sodium levels and is normally closely regulated in the range of 280 to 295 mOsm/kg through thirst perception, control of free water clearance in the kidney by ADH, and renal sodium excretion regulated by atrial natriuretic peptide and the renin–angiotensin system. Therefore, inappropriate or ectopic secretion of either ADH or atrial natriuretic peptide can result in hyponatremia. Figure 115.1 Risk assessment of tumor lysis syndrome (TLS). TABLE 115.1 Management of Tumor Lysis Syndrome Risk Group Management Low risk Allopurinol Hydration Monitor and correct daily electrolytes. Intermediate and high risk Aggressive hydration Ion exchange resins, dextrose and insulin, calcium gluconate (treatment of hyperkalemia) Consider sodium bicarbonate and loop diuretics. Oral phosphate binders (treatment of hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia) Allopurinol, urate oxidase (treatment of hyperuricemia)

Consider hemodialysis if mentioned not successful. Screening, Diagnosis, and Management The finding of hyponatremia on a serum chemistry panel does not necessarily constitute an emergency. However, an appropriate workup should ensue to determine the cause. Rapid onset of hyponatremia with refractory seizures and coma can have a significant mortality, and profound hyponatremia is a true oncology emergency. Traditionally, hyponatremia can be classified as hypovolemic, euvolemic, or hypervolemic; however, this is often difficult to assess in clinical practice. Often, more than one mechanism is involved in the disorder. The volume status can sometimes be determined on a clinical basis and can be aided by simple plasma and urine electrolytes. The acuity of onset of hyponatremia predicts for the risk of complications, and identifying patients with acute drop in sodium levels (<48 hours) is probably the most important factor in determining treatment. In patients with chronic hyponatremia, there is a higher risk of complications of overaggressive treatment, and it is probably in these patients that vasopressin antagonists tolvaptan and conivaptan should be used.20 Care should be taken with sodium replacement and the treatment of other forms of hyponatremia not to correct extremely low sodium levels too rapidly because of the risk of osmotic demyelination.21 Osmotic demyelination can be avoided by correcting sodium at a rate that does not exceed 8 mEq/L/day and, in high-risk patients, 4 to 6 mEq/L/day. High-risk individuals include those with a serum sodium level of <105 mmol/L, heavy alcohol intake, advanced liver disease, hypokalemia, and malnutrition. Although the risk of mortality is increased with all degrees of hyponatremia, deaths from neurologic complications including cerebral edema and osmotic demyelination are rare.22 Hypovolemic hyponatremia due to reduced intake, gastrointestinal losses, or renal losses can be determined on history and physical examination. The treatment is replacement of sodium via normal saline infusions. Isotonic saline should not be used to treat symptomatic hyponatremia or hyponatremia associated with intracranial disease. If vasopressin levels are elevated, isotonic saline may exacerbate hyponatremia as all sodium may be excreted in a small volume of urine.22 For symptomatic patients, hypertonic saline should be used. This is usual

Generally, all should receive hydration and bisphosphonates, but other measures such as calcitonin and dialysis are reserved for those with either mental status changes or renal insufficiency. Both bisphosphonates and rank ligand inhibitors are now used in the routine treatment of patients with cancers with evidence of bone metastases, and this should be considered when planning treatments. Bisphosphonates have an onset of action of approximately 48 hours and a nadir in calcium levels of 5 to 7 days. Zoledronic acid, the preferred agent, is given at a dose of 4 mg over 15 minutes and has been shown to be superior to pamidronate. The average duration of response is 32 days.26 Zoledronic acid can be given weekly for patients with persistent hypercalcemia. It is a well- tolerated agent, but adverse events of mild nephrotoxicity, flu- like syndrome, musculoskeletal pain, and hypocalcemia have been reported. Osteonecrosis of the jaw is a chronic side effect occurring in about 1% to 2% of patients. Figure 115.2 Hyponatremia classification and treatment. CTCAE, Common Terminology Criteria of Adverse Events. Calcitonin has the advantage of acting rapidly in 6 to 24 hours, can be given prior to hydration, and is not nephrotoxic. However, it exhibits rapid tachyphylaxis and can only be given for two doses. Therefore, it should be used in severe hypercalcemia or in cases of renal failure. Other agents such as gallium nitrate are rarely used today. LACTIC ACIDOSIS Lactic acidosis is defined as a pH ≤7.35 with plasma lactate concentration ≥5 mEq/L.27 It has been reported more frequently as a complication of hematologic malignancies but can be a rare event in solid tumors, often associated with liver metastases.28 Often, the acidosis is associated with an elevated anion gap, but in cancer patients with poor nutrition and low albumin levels, the anion gap may not be appropriately corrected. Lactic acidosis occurs when the production of lactate exceeds the ability metabolize it. Overproduction is a result of circulatory, respiratory, hematologic, or cellular dysfunction or collapse, whereas underutilization can be a result of poor hepatic perfusion.29 Lactate is generated largely by anaerobic glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway).30 Cancer cells produce energy primarily through

reprogramming designed to promote cancer cell survival (Warburg effect).31,32 TABLE 115.2 Risk Groups of Hypercalcemia High Risk (Usually Inpatient Management) Low Risk (Consider Outpatient Management) Serum calcium >12 mg/dL Serum calcium <12 mg/dL Severe nausea and vomiting Minimal nausea or vomiting Clinically dehydrated Able to ingest fluids easily Altered mental state Mild fatigue; otherwise neurologically stable Renal insufficiency Normal renal function Cardiac arrhythmia Stable cardiac rhythm Obstipation or ileus Mild, if any, constipation easily controlled with laxatives Lives alone or frail state Adequate social support Limited access to medical care Adequate access to medical facilities The treatment consists of effective management of the underlying malignancy and prevention of life- threatening acidemia. Lactic acidosis should be managed by providers with experience in acid-base balance and intensive care. Although cancer can result in lactic acidosis by itself, other serious causes may also be present and will need to be concurrently managed aggressively, including shock, heart failure, sepsis, hypoxia, anemia, and various medication side effects (Table 115.3). Bicarbonate infusions are sometimes used as a temporary measure to reverse acidemia, especially in patients with malignancies where the underlying cause may not be rapidly reversible.33 In the absence of proven outcomes data, however, such infusions should be used judiciously. HYPERAMMONEMIA Incidence, Etiology, and Diagnosis Cancer and its treatments can be causes of hyperammonemia and hepatic encephalopathy. This represents an impairment of mental state as a result of impaired hepatic function and accumulation of ammonia from the gut.34 The detailed pathogenesis and array of symptoms are varied and complex, but in cancer patients, disorder of the blood–brain barrier may be an important factor. Although the symptoms can be varied, severe findings such as asterixis, confusion, somnolence, and coma define states requiring emergent intervention.35 Patients suspected of having hepatic encephalopathy should also be checked for other reversible causes including hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis, uremia, medications (including rare side effects of novel agents),36 electrolyte abnormalities, central nervous system metastases or hemorrhage, and hypoglycemia.37 TABLE 115.3 Etiology, Pathogenesis, and

Because most patients show an improvement in clinical symptoms within 48 hours of initiation of therapy, those who do not recover should be evaluated for one of the differential causes listed above. TABLE 115.4 Treatment of Severe Symptomatic Hyperammonemia in Cancer Patients Treatment Comments Supportive care Control of agitation; avoid overuse of sedating medications. Reduce risk of falls. Consider restricting protein intake unless severely malnourished. Identify and treat underlying cause For example, gastrointestinal bleed, infection, constipation, hypokalemia, new hepatic metastases Lower ammonia levels Lactulose (up to 45 mL four times a day) can be given orally or as an enema. Rifaximin if no improvement with lactulose after 2 d Consider neomycin. Correct hypokalemia, which will reduce renal production of ammonia. Management The treatment is divided into supportive care, identifying and treating underlying causes, and decreasing the production of ammonia (Table 115.4). Some causes (e.g., gastrointestinal [GI] bleed), may require procedures such as endoscopic evaluation, whereas others, including rapidly growing hepatic metastases, may respond to early initiation of appropriate treatment such as chemotherapy. Specific treatment for lowering ammonia levels is usually achieved by the administration of lactulose, usually at a dose of 30 to 45 mL every 6 hours. This can be given orally or as an enema. Patients who do not respond rapidly may need to be moved to a more intensive care setting and require the assistance of hepatologists or transplant teams. Medications such as rifaximin and neomycin can be considered in refractory cases. Aggressive treatment of hypokalemia is important because this will reduce renal production of ammonia. SUMMARY The management of the metabolic emergencies described in this chapter has changed in recent years with the addition of new medication options for TLS and hyponatremia. As new agents for the treatment of cancers are developed, other metabolic syndromes may be discovered. The practicing oncologist should be aware of the possibility of metabolic side effects of cancers and their treatments, the management of which may often require a multidisciplinary approach

Dr. AVR @ TMH 116 Metastatic Cancer to the Brain John H. Suh, Rupesh Kotecha, Manmeet S. Ahluwalia, and Michael A. Vogelbaum INTRODUCTION Brain metastases represent the most common neurologic complication of cancer. Historically, the outcomes were very poor. Advances in neuroimaging, neurosurgery, radiation oncology, medical oncology, and supportive care have allowed for earlier detection, better local treatment, immune system modulation, and innovative strategies to mitigate potential complications, which have improved survival and quality of life for these patients. Given the heterogeneity of patients with brain metastases and evolving treatment approaches, their management is complex, evolving, and controversial. As a result, a number of clinical trials are ongoing to determine the optimal treatment strategy for these patients. EPIDEMIOLOGY The true incidence of brain metastases, which develop in nearly 30% of cancer patients,1 is not known, although autopsy estimates are as high as 170,000 cases annually in the United States.2 Brain metastases can be diagnosed at the same time or within 1 month of primary diagnosis, which occurs in about one-third of cases3 (synchronous), or after the primary tumor has been diagnosed (metachronous). An estimated 30% to 40% of patients present with a solitary lesion, which is defined as a single brain metastasis without any evidence of extracranial disease and controlled primary disease. Cancers of the lung and breast and melanoma, which represent 50%, 15% to 20%, and 10% of cases, respectively, are the most common primary tumors that spread to the brain. CLINICAL PRESENTATION The clinical presentation can vary widely. Historical data from the 1970s to early 1990s showed that 10% of patients diagnosed by computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were asymptomatic.4 Because screening scans are more frequently performed, a higher percentage of patients now present with asymptomatic disease. The majority of patients with brain metastases have neurocognitive deficits prior to the initiation of whole- brain radiotherapy (WBRT), with a comprehensive phase III trial reporting that >90% of patients have some decline in neurocognitive function (NCF) prior to WBRT.5,6 NCF is typically assessed with a battery of tests; the Hopkins Verbal Learning Test—Revised (HVLT-R) is the one most commonly used for trial end po

differential diagnosis includes nonmalignant causes such as abscess, infection, demyelination and hemorrhage, and primary brain tumors such as a malignant glioma. If uncertainty exists regarding diagnosis, biopsy or resection should be performed for confirmation. For patients with known cancer, restaging scans, which typically include CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, should be performed to assess systemic disease status. The use of fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography alone can be done only when the imaging is adjusted to account for the high background metabolic use of glucose by the brain.9 After surgery, postoperative MRIs should be performed within 48 hours to help differentiate residual tumor from blood. For patients undergoing primary stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS), MRI changes can be variable, with approximately one-third of lesions experiencing a transient increase in tumor volume.10 The Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology Working Group (RANO), an independent, international, collaborative effort, provided guidelines for the design of trials in patients with brain metastases with emphasis on radiographic response.11 In addition, RANO developed guidelines for the use of neurocognitive, neurologic, and quality-of-life outcomes for patients with brain metastases.12 PROGNOSIS One of the earliest prognostic scales was based on three consecutive Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (RTOG) phase III brain metastases trials from 1979 to 1993.13 Using recursive partitioning analysis (RPA), three well- defined prognostic groups (RPA class I, II, and III) were identified based on age (younger than 65 or 65 and older), Karnofsky performance status (KPS) of ≥70 or <70, absence or presence of extracranial metastases, and primary tumor status (Fig. 116.1A). To develop a less subjective and more quantifiable prognostic system, the graded prognostic assessment (GPA) was developed by analyzing data from five RTOG studies.14 The GPA, which is stratified into four prognostic groups, is the sum of scores (0, 0.5, or 1.0) based on age, KPS, presence of extracranial metastases, and number of brain metastases (Fig. 116.1B). Given the heterogeneity of outcomes for patients based on tumor type, an updated diagnosis-specific (DS) GPA was developed through a multi-institutional database.15 Given the impact of prognosis based on tumor heterogeneity mediated b

SYMPTOM MANAGEMENT Corticosteroids

Because brain metastases can cause peritumoral edema, corticosteroids are commonly used to help temporarily control brain edema. Dexamethasone, which has low mineralocorticoid effect, is typically used given its long half- life. Based on a prospective randomized trial of patients who were not at risk for cerebral herniation, higher dose dexamethasone (16 mg per day) demonstrated no advantage compared to lower dose dexamethasone (4 or 8 mg per day), but patients receiving higher doses of dexamethasone had more frequent side effects.19 Acute side effects may include insomnia, increased appetite, gastritis, fluid retention, mood swings, acne, and elevation of blood sugars. Long-term side effects may include weight gain, facial plethora, pedal edema, immunosuppression, proximal muscle myopathy, cataract formation, aseptic necrosis of the femoral head, and osteoporosis. Because most brain metastases trials have not assessed steroid use as end points, much controversy exists regarding specific indications and dosing.20 For patients who are neurologically asymptomatic, routine use of corticosteroids is not necessary.21,22 For patients with more severe symptoms from increased intracranial pressure, doses of 16 mg per day or higher should be considered.23 If possible, steroids should be tapered within 1 week of initiation and discontinued within 2 weeks.22 When tapering dexamethasone, it is important to recognize withdrawal symptoms such as headaches, lethargy, weakness, dizziness, anorexia, diffuse arthralgias, and myalgias. Anticonvulsants Although seizures are the presenting symptom in 10% of cases and can occur in up to 25% of brain metastases,24 the role of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) in these patients has very limited class I evidence.25 A meta-analysis of five randomized controlled trials in patients with intracranial disease as well as a systemic Cochrane review have both demonstrated that no immediate or long-term benefit exists to prophylactic use of AEDs in patients without a previous history of seizures.26,27 Alternatively, patients who present with seizures or who develop seizures during therapy should receive AEDs, preferably with agents that do not interact with hepatic cytochrome P450 (e.g., levetiracetam). For patients on dexamethasone, phenytoin levels can be affected by its use. In addition, phenytoin can affect clearance of chemotherapy agents and

Dr. AVR @ TMH from clinical trials. The RTOG has completed numerous phase III trials evaluating various fractionation schedules and dose schemes.36–39 Although these trials have shown that the majority of patients have partial or complete response of their neurologic symptoms ranging from 40% to 70%, the median survival only averages 3 to 5 months. Extended or hypofractionated WBRT has shown no survival benefit. The most commonly used fractionation schemes in the United States are 30 Gy in 10 fractions or 37.5 Gy in 15 fractions. Shortened fractionation schemes of 20 Gy in 5 fractions can be used for poor-prognosis patients. Recently, the Medical Research Council reported the results of the Quality of Life after Treatment for Brain Metastases (QUARTZ) trial, which randomized 538 patients with inoperable NSCLC brain metastases to supportive care with dexamethasone with or without WBRT. The mean quality- adjusted life-years and overall survival were similar between the two arms; therefore, supportive care alone should be considered in patients with extremely poor performance status and limited expected survival.40 The imaging response rates or stabilization of tumors after WBRT can range from 0% to 71%.41,42 Nieder et al.43,44 studied the CT responses in 108 patients with 336 measurable lesions after WBRT (30 Gy in 10 fractions) and found the overall response rate at up to 3 months was 59% (lesion complete response rate of 24%, partial response rate of 35%). The complete response rates were 37% for SCLC, 35% for breast cancer, 25% for squamous cell carcinoma, 14% for nonbreast adenocarcinoma, 0% for renal cell carcinoma, and 0% for melanoma. Smaller tumor volumes and absence of necrosis influenced complete response rates. The most common side effects that occur during or shortly following WBRT include alopecia, mild skin erythema, and fatigue. Other side effects may include headache, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, change of taste, serous otitis, and somnolence. Secondary to the effect of opposed tangential radiation beams on skin sparing, hair loss is variable and may be permanent in the superior and portion portions of the scalp. Skin reactions typically resolve after several weeks, and fatigue usually improves after 2 to 3 months and may respond to methylphenidate. The long-term and frequency of side effects from WBRT have not been well documented as th

and overall survival. A recent Japanese phase III trial randomized 224 patients to PCI or observation after chemotherapy with MRI of the brain performed prior to radiotherapy.51 This study demonstrated a reduction in incidence of brain metastasis without an improvement in overall survival. A randomized phase II study testing PCI versus HA-PCI is undergoing analysis to determine if accrual to the phase III should be completed for patients with limited- and extensive-stage SCLC (NRG-CC003). RTOG 0214 randomized patients with stage III NSCLC without disease progression after treatment with surgery and/or radiation therapy with or without chemotherapy to PCI (30 Gy in 15 fractions) or observation.52 The primary end point of the study was overall survival. Unfortunately, the study closed early secondary to slow accrual. The 1-year overall survival and disease-free survival were not significantly different. However, the 1-year rate for development of brain metastases was significantly less for PCI than for observation (7.7% versus 18.0%, respectively; P = .004). The impact of PCI on self-reported cognitive functioning and HVLT was analyzed based on the results of RTOG 0214 and RTOG 0212.53 At 6 and 12 months, significant declines in self-reported cognitive functioning and HVLT score were noted after PCI. Surgery Surgery plays an important role for some patients with brain metastases. It can provide immediate and effective relief from symptomatic mass effect and can confirm or establish the diagnosis, which is important for patients who have no prior cancer history. In addition, patients with larger tumors (diameter >2 cm) may also benefit from surgery compared to other treatment modalities. Advances in imaging and image guidance have improved the rates for complete resection.54 The data are mixed regarding the impact of the type of surgical resection on the rate of local recurrence. A retrospective review from MD Anderson Cancer Center of 570 patients undergoing surgical resection alone suggested that piecemeal resection compared with en bloc resection significantly predicted for higher local recurrence (hazard ratio, 1.7; P = .03).55 Larger tumor volumes exceeding 9.71 cm3, compared with smaller tumors, also predicted for higher local recurrence (hazard ratio, 1.7; P = .02). A subsequent prospective evaluation of the role of SRS versus observation from the same g

Dr. AVR @ TMH brain (18% versus 70%, P < .001). Survival was not different, although the study’s end point was local control and was not powered to demonstrate a survival advantage.64 Kocher et al.65 reported the results of a phase III EORTC study of 359 patients comparing SRS (199 patients) or surgery (160 patients) with or without WBRT. Survival and time to World Health Organization (WHO) performance status deterioration >2 were not different between the two arms. At 2 years after surgery, WBRT significantly decreased the risk of local and new brain relapse from 59% to 27% (P < .001) and 42% to 23% (P < .008), respectively. Health-related quality-of-life results were better for patients in the observation arm.66 Stereotactic Radiosurgery Unlike WBRT, SRS delivers high dose(s) of ionizing radiation to focal target(s) while greatly minimizing the dose to surrounding brain tissue. Features that make a brain metastasis an ideal target for SRS include its pseudospherical shape, location in the gray–white junction, and maximum diameter of <4 cm. The vast majority of brain metastases have distinct pathologic and radiographic margins, allowing for accurate target delineation, planning, and treatment delivery through the use of multiple intersecting radiation beams, which produce steep dose gradients (“dose falloff”).67 Since the 1990s, numerous institutional and multi-institutional studies have been published on the results of SRS as a primary, adjuvant, and salvage treatment for brain metastases. When doses of 15 to 24 Gy are used, the local control rates range from 70% to 95%.68–70 Freedom from local progression depends on dose, volume, histology, and pattern of MRI or CT enhancement at the time of radiosurgery.71,72 In addition, SRS is effective for all types of primary tumor including radioresistant histologies, such as melanoma and renal cell carcinoma.73,74 Although the ideal candidate for SRS is subject to debate, it generally consists of patients with controlled or absence of extracranial metastases and excellent KPS. Historically, the number (one to four) of brain metastases was considered a general contraindication, although recent publications refute this.75–77 RTOG 9005 was a phase I/II trial for patients with recurrent primary and metastatic brain tumors to study the relationship between maximum-tolerated SRS dose and maximum tumor diameter.78 The max

Unfortunately, this study closed early due to poor accrual, with 33 patients in the surgery and WBRT arm and 31 patients in the SRS-alone arm. Table 116.1 summarizes the advantages of SRS and surgery for patients with brain metastases. Whole-Brain Radiotherapy with or without Stereotactic Radiosurgery The first randomized trial of WBRT (30 Gy in 12 fractions) with or without SRS boost (16 Gy) enrolled functionally independent patients with two to four brain metastases measuring ≤2.5 cm in diameter and >5 mm from the optic chiasm.41 Secondary to early stopping rules, this trial enrolled only 27 patients. The two arms were well balanced with respect to known prognostic factors. The local control was 92% in the WBRT + SRS arm versus 0% in the WBRT arm (P = .002). Median survival was not significantly different in the two arms (7.5 months for WBRT versus 11 months for WBRT + SRS, P = .22). Recently, a phase III intergroup trial led by the North Central Cancer Treatment Group (N0574) randomized 213 patients with one to three brain metastases to SRS alone or SRS and WBRT.95 SRS alone resulted in less cognitive deterioration and improvement in overall quality of life. Stereotactic Radiosurgery to Resection Cavity Because patients undergoing surgical resection alone are at high risk for local recurrence, the use of radiosurgery rather than WBRT has been explored given the potential side effects of WBRT and the convenience of SRS.96 Mahajan et al.56 recently reported the results of a phase III trial of resection of a brain metastasis followed by observation or SRS to the resection cavity. At a median follow-up of 11.1 months, there was a significant improvement in local control (43% versus 72%) with SRS with no adverse events encountered. The North Central Cancer Treatment Group, in collaboration with RTOG, recently reported the results of a phase III trial (RTOG 1270/N107C) of postsurgical SRS compared with WBRT for resected brain metastases in patients with four or fewer brain metastases.97 The resection cavity measured <5 cm in maximal extent on the postoperative MRI (or CT) brain scan obtained ≤35 days prior to preregistration. In this study, cognitive deterioration-free survival was higher and cognitive deterioration less at 6 months in the SRS arm with no difference in overall survival. A concern regarding the use of postoperative SRS is that inadvertent tumor spillage during surgery might lead to a risk of leptomeningeal disease (LMD) that would have been previously treated with WBRT. A review by Patel et al.98 indicates that the risk of postsurgical SRS LMD may be as high as 17%, and the MD Anderson SRS versus observation study indicated an LMD rate as high as 28%.56 The risk of postoperative SRS-associated LMD may vary with histology as patients with breast cancer histology has been found to have a higher rate of leptomeningeal spread.99 An alternative approach to the combination of surgery and SRS has been to perform SRS followed by surgery.100 With this approach, early reports indicate a lower risk of postoperative LMD and radiation necrosis (3% and 5%, respectively). A multi-institutional retrospective comparison of preoperative SRS and postoperative SRS for resected brain metastases demonstrated similar local and distant brain recurrence, but lower rates of LMD and symptomatic radiation necrosis in the preoperative SRS group.98 Table 116.2 summarizes the various phase III trials of surgery or radiosurgery with and without WBRT for patients with brain metastases. LEPTOMENINGEAL METASTASES Leptomeningeal metastases (LM) or neoplastic meningitis is a serious complication in patients with advanced solid (leptomeningeal carcinomatosis or carcinomatous meningitis) or hematologic malignancies (leukemic meningitis or leptomeningeal leukemia). Because LM is often underdiagnosed, early management can be challenging, with treatment being mostly palliative. The overall prognosis is very poor, with median survival of 2 to 3 months and 1-year survival of 15%.126 For patients with leukemic and lymphomatous meningitis, the outcomes are better. Epidemiology Although the incidence of LM varies depending on the type of primary cancer and stage of disease (0.8% to 8 %), it is estimated that 5% to 15% of patients with cancer are diagnosed with this complication. In autopsy series, the estimated rate of LM has been reported to be as high as 19%.127 Clinical Presentation Given the subtle signs and symptoms, LM can be easily missed. Greater than 50% of patients have spinal cord dysfunction as the primary presenting symptom, followed by cranial neuropathies, hemispheric defects, and nonfocal presentations.128 If hydroce

Diagnosis Given the difficulty with diagnosing LM, a thorough neurologic history and physical examination, contrast- enhanced MRI of the brain, and examination of the CSF are important in establishing the diagnosis of LM.130 In addition, a contrast-enhanced MRI of the spine should be completed if signs and/or symptoms warrant. Radiographic presentations may include hydrocephalus without an identifiable intracranial lesion, partial or full obstruction of CSF flow, and LM enhancement. Approximately 50% of patients with LM and spinal symptoms have abnormal imaging studies using gadolinium-enhanced MRI.131 Figure 116.3 demonstrates MRI findings in the posterior fossa and ventricles in a patient with LM. B: One-year follow-up magnetic resonance imaging demonstrating excellent response to stereotactic radiosurgery and crizotinib. The patient is very functional and works full time. Examination of the CSF, which is usually performed via high-volume lumbar puncture, represents the sole diagnostic criteria for LM in approximately one-half of cases. The CSF is examined for opening pressure, appearance, glucose, protein, white and red blood cell counts with differential, and the presence of any abnormal cells by cytology or flow cytometry. Unfortunately, cytologic evaluation of the CSF is an insensitive test, with 40% to 50% of patients having negative CSF cytology.132 If the initial examination of the CSF is negative, up to two repeat CSF examinations should be performed to increase diagnostic sensitivity. Radiation Therapy Radiation therapy provides effective palliation in many cases of LMD, such as symptomatic sites and regions, cranial neuropathies, and cauda equina syndrome.133 Craniospinal irradiation is generally not recommended given the potential toxicity and amount of bone marrow irradiated, which may preclude the use of chemotherapy. As a result, the use of involved-field radiation therapy possibly followed by intrathecal chemotherapy is generally recommended.

Dr. AVR @ TMH Intra–Cerebrospinal Fluid Chemotherapy Given the BBB, the best approach to administer chemotherapy within the leptomeningeal space without bulky disease is through an intraventricular access device such as an implanted subcutaneous reservoir and ventricular catheter (Ommaya reservoir) with intrathecal delivery via lumbar puncture as an alternative. A limitation of this approach is impaired or obstructed CSF flow from bulky meningeal disease, which impairs or obstructs CSF flow. Generally, radiation therapy is delivered prior to intra-CSF therapy. Based on limited and older data, radiation therapy and intra-CSF therapies are not delivered concurrently secondary to concerns of increased neurotoxicity.134 Commonly used intrathecal chemotherapy agents include methotrexate, cytarabine, liposomal form of cytarabine, and thiotepa. Complications associated with intra-CSF chemotherapy include treatment-related meningitis that most frequently presents as a chemical arachnoiditis, with fewer than 10% of patients experiencing bacterial meningitis. A small percentage of patients may experience chemotherapy-related leukoencephalopathy, which appears to occur most commonly in patients who receive intrathecal methotrexate following cranial irradiation. Systemic Chemotherapy and Other Agents Unlike most water-soluble drugs, high-dose systemic administration of methotrexate results in therapeutic drug levels in the CSF, resulting in activity in neoplastic meningitis in lymphoma and some solid tumors. High-dose intravenous methotrexate administration is active even when there is obstruction of CSF flow, which sometimes compromises the subarachnoid administration of drugs. Its administration does require detailed inpatient monitoring of fluid status and renal function, urine alkalinization, and leucovorin rescue, which limits its use.135 Targeted therapies such as erlotinib (pulsatile doses), osimertinib, and ANG1005 have shown preliminary evidence of efficacy in oncogenic-driven tumors that needs confirmation in larger prospective trials. 117 Metastatic Cancer to the Lung John Yonge and Jessica Donington INTRODUCTION Ultimately, uncontrolled metastatic disease is the most frequent cause of cancer-related death. Whereas widespread disease is not amenable to localized therapy, metastatic spread that is limited to a single organ can be successfully treated with localized therapy. In 1882, Weinlechner performed the first surgical resection of metastatic pulmonary disease from a primary rib sarcoma.1 Pulmonary metastasectomy eventually gained popularity in the 1960s and 1970s after a series of patients who underwent repeated pulmonary resection for metastatic osteogenic sarcoma demonstrated a 5-year survival rate >30% compared with 17% in historical controls.2 Since that time, hundreds of studies have documented promising outcomes after pulmonary metastasectomy among numerous tumor types. However, most of these studies are small, single-institution retrospective reviews; large prospective data sets are not currently available to guide clinical decisions regarding which patients are most likely to benefit from resection. Furthermore, the increased efficacy of “targeted” molecular therapies and immune checkpoint modulators for specific histologies has heightened the importance of a multidisciplinary approach to the management of metastatic disease. Surgery may no longer be the best therapeutic option for a specific tumor type. Despite the lack of randomized data proving efficacy of pulmonary metastasectomy, its use is increasing. A recent analysis from the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) noted a significant increase from 2000 to 2011 in its application for the management of common cancers, including colorectal, breast, and melanoma.3 Control of pulmonary metastasis from colorectal carcinoma demonstrated the largest annual increase at 9.4%. The increased use of pulmonary metastasectomy for colorectal cancer highlights the synergy between improved tolerability for resection and more efficacious systemic therapies. Better drugs have dramatically slowed the pace of metastatic progression and allowed greater time for consideration of local interventions, whereas the minimally invasive approach has improved the safety of metastasectomy, increased the number of patients who can tolerate resection, and reduced breaks in systemic therapy for local intervention. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is in general a poor technique for imaging pulmonary tissue and not a useful modality for routine imaging of pulmonary metastases compared with CT. MRI is useful for demonstrating tumor invasion of the great vessels, heart, chest wall, or nervous structures, including the spine or brachial plexus, and in ruling out synchronous liver metastases. The classic CT appearance of pulmonary metastases is a smooth, well-circumscribed, peripheral nodule (a “gumball” or “cannonball”) (Fig. 117.1). Metastases also frequently appear in multiple sites throughout the lungs simultaneously. Despite radiographic appearance, it is important to differentiate suspected metastatic lesions from other pulmonary pathologies. Multiple simultaneous lesions may need to be differentiated from infectious processes, whereas single lesions require differentiation from primary lung cancer. The likelihood of pulmonary metastases relative to a new primary malignancy is related to the tissue type of the patient’s antecedent cancer, risk factors for lung cancers, and the interval between the previous malignancy and presentation. In patients with history of sarcoma or melanoma, a new pulmonary nodule is 10-fold more likely to be a metastasis than a new primary lung cancer. If the initial tumor was of genitourinary or colorectal origin, there is equal chance that the tumor is either a metastasis or new primary. If the primary tumor is of head and neck origin, the newly identified lesion is twice as likely to be a new primary lung cancer than a metastasis.6 These assumptions reflect relative differences in patterns of spread and predisposing risk factors (e.g., tobacco smoking) between lung cancer and the histologies in question. Patients with a history of non–small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) have a unique pattern for recurrence in the first 4 years after curative resection of early-stage NSCLC; the risk for recurrence is 6% to 10% per person-year but decreases to 2% thereafter. The risk for a second primary NSCLC ranges from 3% to 6% per person-year and does not diminish over time.7 In patients with a history of previous lung cancer, new primary lung cancers are more likely after 4 years and usually have a classic radiographic appearance of early tumors, such as spiculation or a mixed soli

Ultimately, determining whether a new pulmonary nodule is a metastasis or second primary tumor requires histopathologic confirmation. In specific circumstances where surgical removal will not be pursued, nonoperative biopsy is preferable. Techniques including image-guided percutaneous biopsy, fluoroscopic-guided transbronchial biopsy, endobronchial ultrasound, or navigational bronchoscopy are all reasonable approaches and should be used based on the location of the nodule, institutional expertise, and patient-specific concerns. Differentiating site of origin can be confounded by the histologic similarity between primary lung cancer and metastatic lesions, most commonly differentiating between primary squamous cell cancers and lung and metastatic head and neck tumors. Molecular analyses may be useful in these circumstances. In patients who cannot be diagnosed by nonoperative means, surgical exploration and biopsy, preferably by VATS, is appropriate. SURGICAL METASTASECTOMY Criteria for Surgical Resection Originally put forth by Ehrenhaft et al.9 in 1958 and modified by Thomford et al.10 in 1965, the following are generally accepted criteria for defining the patient population appropriate for pulmonary metastasectomy: (1) definitive control of the primary tumor has occurred (or is possible), (2) absence of (or ability to control) extrathoracic metastatic disease, (3) the lung metastases are amenable to complete resection, (4) the patient can tolerate the planned procedure, and (5) there is no better treatment alternative.11 Using these criteria, however, long-term survival after metastasectomy remains uncommon, reflecting the fact that in only a subset of patients does the resected disease represent the entire metastatic burden. The potential for extrathoracic spread of a tumor influences the likelihood of surgical management for pulmonary metastatic disease. This is demonstrated by the International Registry of Lung Metastasis (IRLM) database, in which the distribution of primary tumors in decreasing frequency was as follows: 751 soft tissue sarcomas, 734 osteosarcomas, 645 colorectal carcinomas, 396 breast cancers, 372 renal cancers, 282 melanomas, and 247 head and neck cancers.12 Sarcomas are relatively rare tumors compared to breast cancer, but their predilection for young patients and isolated spread to the lungs make use of pulmonary metastasectomy commo

The need to perform a second (repeat) metastasectomy in the IRLM analysis was associated with remarkably good 5-year survival (44%), which suggested that patients who experience recurrence and are still physiologically able to tolerate surgery should be offered re-resection. Subsequent outcomes studies after metastasectomy have corroborated the IRLM results and have continued to demonstrate the prognostic importance of complete resection, prolonged DFI, and lesser numbers of metastases. Additional prognostic factors include histologic variants, presence of lymph node metastasis, response to chemotherapy, and lesion size. However, these risk factors alone are insufficient to determine whether a patient should undergo surgery. The decision to operate must be individualized as the risk–benefit relationship is intimately tied to a patient’s specific histology, tumor location, and physiologic state. Furthermore, the role of metastasectomy must be considered in conjunction with current nonsurgical treatment options, which continue to advance and may offer similar benefit to resection. Breast and renal cell carcinoma exemplify this phenomenon. Several large but older retrospective studies demonstrated a benefit from pulmonary metastasectomy in these histologies. Currently, patients with pulmonary metastasis from these tumors demonstrate prolonged response with novel systemic therapies, and only highly selected cases are reserved for surgery. As targeted and molecular therapies continuously improve the treatment of solid tumors, the criteria for pulmonary metastasectomy also evolve. The decision to perform pulmonary metastasectomy must be part of a multimodality discussion between patients, surgeons, medical oncologists, pulmonologists, and radiation oncologists.

Large randomized trials provide the best evidence to direct efficacious treatment. A large trial of pulmonary metastasectomy for colorectal cancer is under way in Britain and will likely have a significant impact on clinical decision making in that histology.13 Unfortunately, randomized data mature slowly and can be nearly impossible to obtain for all clinical scenarios; therefore, the decision to operate often relies on the results of large retrospective series and databases. Ongoing advances in the treatment of metastatic disease should temper the use of these retrospective data to guide modern clinical practice. Open versus Minimally Invasive Surgery The surgical approach to metastasectomy is controversial, with retrospective studies supporting both open and minimally invasive approaches. The argument for a minimally invasive approach is based on decreased pain, shorter hospital stay, improved time to and tolerance for chemotherapy, and increased tolerability in patients with poor pulmonary function,14 relative to improved detection of small metastases (<5 mm) afforded by manual palpation of the lung with open surgery. As thoracoscopic techniques gain popularity for a wide range of thoracic procedures, surgeons have been keen to apply this technique to metastasectomy. Historical studies suggested that without manual palpation of the lung, small metastatic lesions would be missed, thus increasing the risk for incomplete resection. If the foundation for metastasectomy is resection of all disease, then a technique that potentially leaves disease behind is inappropriate. Convincing evidence in favor of an open approach and manual palpation of the lungs came from the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in 1996.15 In this prospective series, 18 patients underwent a VATS resection immediately followed by thoracotomy. A total of 10 (56%) patients had malignant lesions found at thoracotomy that were not identified on preoperative imaging or during thoracoscopy. The authors made the following conclusions: (1) CT scan of chest underestimated the number of lung metastases (that therefore would be unable to be found thoracoscopically) and (2) thoracotomy after VATS identified nodules missed during VATS. Although this study is criticized for not using “high-definition” imaging and modern thoracoscopic techniques, other studies have subsequently corroborated these re

Approach to Open Metastasectomy The controversy over surgical approach goes beyond the open versus minimally invasive debate. There is also controversy as to which open approach is ideal. In the setting of unilateral nodules, most advocate use of thoracotomy, but the decision is less clear in the setting of bilateral disease. Some advocate a single surgical procedure with a median sternotomy or clamshell for patients with bilateral metastases. Ideologically, it is appealing to limit the patient to one anesthetic and one recovery, but “one-stage” approaches have their drawbacks. Sternotomy affords poor exposure posteriorly and restricts manual palpation of the posterior aspect of the lower lobes, especially on the left side. The clamshell incision offers improved access to the entirety of both lung fields but is associated with increased pain and postoperative recovery. Given the poor prognosis for patients undergoing metastasectomy with positive lymph node involvement, radical lymph node dissection is unlikely to significantly lengthen survival. However, although the increased prognostic information received from lymphadenectomy appears to support its routine use, many surgeons believe that the primary role for lymphadenectomy is to determine the need for additional oncologic treatment; there are no widely accepted strategies for implementation. The lack of consensus is evident in the ESTS survey, where only 19% of respondents reported routinely performing complete mediastinal lymphadenectomy, 55% reported performing lymph node sampling, and 32% reported forgoing nodal sampling.31 Extent of Resection In general, the goal of metastasectomy is complete removal of all gross tumor. An R0 resection is essential for successful metastasectomy; debulking of disease carries no clinical benefit. A second, but equally important, goal is preservation of pulmonary function, which requires consideration for extent of surgical metastasectomy. Because approximately 50% of patients will present with recurrent disease after initial metastasectomy, an important objective is to remove as little functional lung tissue as possible to maintain physiologic function in case subsequent treatments are indicated.12 Nonanatomic wedge resections are ideal for removal of peripheral nodules and are generally associated with improved postoperative lung function relative to anatomic resection (segmentectomy, lobectomy, or pneumonectomy). Lobar and segmental anatomic resections can be safely performed with mortality of <1% but are usually associated with removal of more functional lung parenchyma than a wedge resection. Although lobectomy has been associated with lower rates of local recurrence in the treatment of primary NSCLC,37 no such data exist for resections for metastatic disease. On the contrary, because patients with pulmonary metastases frequently undergo multiple procedures (and additional other therapies), lung conservation is particularly essential. Pneumonectomy is rarely indicated for the treatment of metastatic disease, and many believe that the morbidity of a pneumonectomy is a relative contraindication to metastasectomy.31 Pneumonectomy should thus be reserved for patients with ideal circumstances, such as long DFI, single central lesion, and excellent performance status. ABLATIVE THERAPIES Image-guided ablative therapies are being used with great frequency in the lungs and are a popular alternative to surgical metastasectomy. These therapies attempt to provide equivalent local control to resection with less morbidity. Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or stereotactic ablative body radiotherapy (SABR) is a highly precise and dose-intensive form of external-beam radiation therapy that has been used to treat metastases in the thorax. Percutaneous CT-guided technologies include radiofrequency ablation (RFA), microwave ablation (MA), and cryoablation. Patterns of use for ablative therapies vary significantly according to practitioner and institutional expertise. These therapies have been applied most consistently in patients whose performance status precludes thoracic surgery or when complete surgical resection is not possible. In 2010, a prospective trial of percutaneous RFA of lung metastases demonstrated impressive long-term results among a group of patients with mixed tumor histology.45 Of 148 patients treated, 26% had complete radiographic response, 20% had partial response, 39% had stable disease, and 16% showed disease progression. The median overall survival was 51 months, and on multivariate analysis, DFI and response to treatment were independent predictors of overall survival. In 2015, de Baère et al.46 reported the results from 566 patients treated with RFA.46 The authors demonstrate a 5-year overall survival rate of 51%, inclusive of all primary sites of disease, which is consistent with survival for surgical metastasectomy. Although patients were not operative candidates, patients were only considered for treatment if all sites of disease could be ablated (Table 117.2). Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy SBRT is an additional ablative technique used to treat metastatic lung lesions. Unlike conventional fractionated radiation therapy, SBRT uses highly focused and intensive radiation to deliver ablative doses of radiation to specific areas with less radiation injury to adjacent tissues. Theoretically, the high-dose and tightly focused nature of SBRT provides an ablative response in the target area, which is particularly useful for treatment of pulmonary metastases where wide margins are not required to control disease. Dr. AVR @ TMH HISTOLOGIES Soft Tissue and Osteogenic Sarcoma Soft tissue and osteogenic sarcomas are relatively rare malignancies, but they have high rates of pulmonary metastases, without spread to other organ sites. Failure to control pulmonary metastatic disease is the most frequent cause of death in these patients. This combined with the young age of sarcoma patients has resulted in numerous retrospective studies testing the potential survival benefit afforded by pulmonary metastasectomy. Furthermore, the lack of efficacious chemotherapy suggests that metastasectomy should remain an important intervention in the treatment of sarcoma patients for the foreseeable future. Osteosarcoma is a histologic subtype with high predilection for pulmonary metastases. In 2003, the Cooperative Osteosarcoma Study Group found that of 202 patients with metastases at diagnosis, 81% had lung metastases, and in 62%, the lung was the only site of metastases.53 Patients with osteosarcoma are generally young and healthy, making them excellent candidates for pulmonary resection. Several reports have shown prolonged survival after surgical treatment of pulmonary metastases, with rates of 5-year survival ranging from 30% to 40% (Table 117.4).54 Although reports have been somewhat varied with respect to prognostic factors associated with good outcome, prolonged DFI, complete resection, and response to adjuvant therapy are noted consistently.55,56 Unfortunately, new lung metastases frequently recur after resection; therefore, close postoperative surveillance is mandatory for these patients. Although benign nodules can occur after metastasectomy, a recurrent nodule ipsilateral to the initial resection is almost always recurrence, and aggressive surgical management is warranted.57 Soft tissue sarcomas are a heterogeneous group of tumors with a predilection for metastatic pulmonary spread. Trunk and extremity sarcomas have higher rates of pulmonary metastasis than other soft tissue sarcomas.58 Based on multiple retrospective studies, 5-year overall survival rates of 30% to 40% can be achieved after pulmonary metastasectomy with eradication of all known disease (see Table 117.4).59 Conversely, patients not undergoing metastasectomy have an anticipated 3-year survival of 17%. Although adjuvant chemotherapy protocols are not usually associated with significant benefit for treatment of soft tissue sarcoma, some subtypes are chemosensitive and emerging therapies should be considered. Progression after receiving adjuvant chemotherapy is a marker for poor prognosis after metastasectomy, and preoperative identification of chemotherapy-resistant histologies may soon aid in stratification of surgical candidates.61,62 An MD Anderson Cancer Center study from 2011 demonstrated that 5-year overall survival after metastasectomy in patients whose disease progressed after chemotherapy was substantially reduced compared with patients without progression (0% versus 32%).63 Norwegian researchers demonstrated no overall or disease-free survival difference for 93 patients undergoing preoperative chemotherapy versus surgical resection alone. The authors did report a significant survival advantage in patients with histologic response to chemotherapy.61 These findings again demonstrate the improved survival of patients with indolent, lung-only, chemosensitive metastases. Overall, recurrence in the lung is common for soft tissue sarcoma after metastasectomy, and patients with reasonable performance status should be strongly considered for repeat metastasectomy due to the paucity of effective chemotherapy options. Melanoma Disseminated melanoma carries a dismal prognosis, typically with a median survival of ≤6 months and a 5-year survival for patients with pulmonary metastases of 9% to 35%.64 Although many chemotherapy and radiotherapy combinations have been attempted, few are successful. Biologic treatments, such as interleukin-2 (IL-2), interferon-α (IFN-α), and monoclonal antibodies, are associated with a survival benefit in only a minority of patients and significant systemic toxicity.65 Tremendous advances have been made in the treatment of melanoma using BRAF inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting the cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA- 4) and the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1); however, responses to these therapies are often heterogeneous and not always durable.66–68 Patients with disseminated melanoma often present with disease in multiple sites, and <10% have lung metastases alone.69 In patients with isolated pulmonary disease, surge

Colorectal Cancer Lung metastases develop in 5% to 15% of patients with colorectal cancer. Pulmonary metastasectomy has become an integral part of the multimodal treatment plan for these patients, offering 5-year survival rates ranging from 38% to 49%.93 Colorectal cancer treatment is a rapidly evolving field, and the benefit of metastasectomy in the era of targeted therapy is accepted yet somewhat unproven. To address this question, the previously mentioned randomized trial of metastasectomy for colorectal carcinoma (PulMiCC) is currently under way in Europe (NCT011062610).13 This trial compares “active monitoring” to “active monitoring plus pulmonary metastasectomy” and evaluates overall survival, relapse-free survival, lung function, and patient-reported quality of life. Metastasectomy in this trial can be either surgical or by ablation. Until these data are available, there is a considerable volume of retrospective data supporting a role for metastasectomy in selected patients. In a recent meta-analysis of lung metastasectomy for colorectal carcinoma, four parameters were associated with poor survival after metastasectomy: short DFI, multiple metastases, positive hilar and/or mediastinal lymph nodes, and elevated prethoracotomy carcinoembryonic antigen level (see Table 117.4).35 In this analysis, the presence of liver metastases was not associated with poor prognosis. Shiono et al.94 investigated the influence of histologic findings on overall survival. On univariate analysis, vascular invasion, pleural invasion, lymphatic invasion, and aerogenous spread with floating clusters of cancer cells (ASFC) were found to significantly reduce prognosis. On multivariate analysis, vascular invasion and ASFC were found to significantly influence survival.94 Patients with vascular invasion had reduced 5-year survival compared to patients without this histologic feature (39% versus 85%). In addition, patients with ASFC had reduced 5-year survival compared to patients without this histologic feature (46% versus 88%). Dr. AVR @ TMH 118 Metastatic Cancer to the Liver Clifford S. Cho, Sam Lubner, and Dawn Owen INTRODUCTION The development of hepatic metastasis is oncologically unique for three reasons. First, the nature of portal venous drainage makes the liver a common destination for hematogenously disseminated alimentary tract malignancies. Indeed, the most common metastatic tumors in the liver are derived from primary cancers of the alimentary tract and pancreas. Second, unlike other anatomic locations susceptible to hematogenous seeding (e.g., brain, lungs, bone), the liver is often the sole site of metastatic disease. Third, several aspects of hepatic anatomy and physiology make it particularly accessible to oncologic therapy. In this chapter, we explore the unique aspects of disease biology and treatment options as they relate to the two types of hepatic metastasis (colorectal adenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine carcinoma) most commonly treated with liver-directed therapy as well as a few less commonly treated forms of hepatic metastasis. Relevant Hepatic Physiology The venous drainage of the alimentary tract, pancreas, and spleen compose the portal venous circulation. Blood flow returning from these sites converges into the portal vein. At the microscopic level, portal venous blood enters into the hepatic sinusoids, where it interfaces with hepatocytes. Once the contents from the portal venous circulation are metabolized and filtered, blood is directed into the hepatic venous system, which then reenters the nonportal systemic venous circulation at the level of the inferior vena cava. A unique anatomic property of the liver is its dual blood supply. Hepatocytes derive the majority of their blood supply from the portal venous circulation; in contrast, the cholangiocytes that compose the biliary ductal system derive most of their blood supply from the hepatic arterial circulation. Importantly, it is believed that primary and metastatic tumors within the liver generally derive the large majority of their blood supply from the hepatic arterial circulation. This important physiologic contrast in circulatory perfusion between normal hepatocytes and abnormal cancer cells provides an opportunity for therapeutic intervention; as discussed later, many liver-directed therapies rely on the delivery of embolic particles, chemotherapy, or radiation into the hepatic arterial circulat

A comprehensive understanding of the treatment modalities available in hepatic oncology requires some familiarity with hepatic anatomic nomenclature.1 The liver is composed of two hemilivers, four sections, and eight segments. The right and left hemilivers are divided by the principal scissura, or Cantlie’s line, which runs between the inferior vena cava and the gallbladder fossa. The liver is also bisected by the middle hepatic vein, which runs through the principal scissura. The left hemiliver is divided into two sections separated by the umbilical fissure, a natural cleft that houses the left portal vein and remnant of the umbilical vein. The left lateral section, composed of segments II and III, is situated to the left of the umbilical fissure, and the left medical section, composed of segment IV, is situated between the umbilical fissure and the principal scissura. The venous drainage of the left hemiliver is via the left hepatic vein, which courses between segments II and III, and the middle hepatic vein. The larger right hemiliver is separated into a right anterior section and a right posterior section; the anatomic plane between the right anterior and posterior sections is defined by the course of the right hepatic vein. The right anterior section is composed of segments V and VIII, and the right posterior section is composed of segments VI and VII. Segment I, or the caudate lobe, is a centrally located structure that lies between the portal vein and inferior vena cava. Operative procedures are named according to the anatomic structures that are being removed. For example, resection of the left hemiliver (i.e., removal of segments II to IV) is referred to as a left hemihepatectomy; a right hemihepatectomy refers to removal of segments V to VIII. Resection of segments II and III is referred to as a left lateral sectionectomy; resection of segments VI and VII is referred to as a right posterior sectionectomy. Resection of segments IV to VIII is a right trisectionectomy. Resection of the caudate lobe is referred to as a segmentectomy I. At a minimum, the evaluation of patients with hepatic metastases requires high-resolution contrast- enhanced computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Ultrasonography

Dr. AVR @ TMH Hepatic Resection The determination of resectability of hepatic metastases centers around the concept of the future liver remnant (FLR), defined as the portion of the liver that will remain after hepatic resection. As stated previously, the FLR is generally capable of rapid postoperative hypertrophy; however, the FLR must be capable of a minimum level of function in order to avoid fatal postoperative hepatic failure. In order for hepatic resection to be performed safely, four criteria regarding the FLR must be met: (1) the FLR must be well vascularized (i.e., the portal venous and hepatic arterial inflow into the FLR must be retained); (2) the FLR must have adequate biliary drainage (i.e., the hepatic duct[s] emanating from the FLR must not be compromised); (3) the FLR must have adequate venous drainage (i.e., the hepatic vein[s] decompressing the FLR must remain intact; and (4) the FLR must be of an adequate size. Using cross-sectional CT or MRI, the volume of the FLR and the volume of the entire liver can be calculated. In this way, the ratio of the FLR volume to the total estimated liver volume (or, alternatively, to the total ideal liver volume based on patient size) can be calculated.7 The minimal FLR–to–total liver volume ratio necessary to sustain sufficient postresection liver function and hypertrophy depends on the condition of the underlying liver. In patients with normal liver function, the ratio can be as small as 20%. In patients with severe underlying liver dysfunction (e.g., resulting from cirrhosis), the minimal ratio may be 50%. As outlined in the following text, iatrogenic impairment of hepatic function resulting from prolonged chemotherapy may require a minimal FLR of 40%. In cases of advanced disease with large or multifocal tumors, adjustments to operative planning may become necessary in order to preserve a sufficient FLR. These so-called “parenchymal sparing” approaches to hepatic metastasectomy may invoke the use of adjuncts such as thermal ablation or portal vein embolization, as discussed later. Although the safety of hepatic surgery has greatly improved in recent decades (with operative mortality risk after major hepatic resections approximating 1% to 3% in large-volume centers), it remains a considerable undertaking. Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) is a noninvasive technique of providing local therapy for liver malignancies with ablative intent. This technique uses high doses per day (6 to 10 Gy) delivered over a course of three to five fractions such that very high biologically effective doses are achieved. Patients are simulated with various techniques to minimize tumor motion, including breath hold and abdominal compression, and highly conformal radiation plans are created such that there is very high dose falloff from the edge of the planning target volume (PTV) and into normal tissue. Liver SBRT was initially studied in prospective dose-escalation studies using a critical volume method that is conceptually similar to the FLR notion mentioned earlier with respect to hepatectomy. The critical volume method works backward from the premise that for any given organ, a certain amount of functional tissue must remain after a course of radiation therapy to avoid severe late sequelae. In the case of liver SBRT, the proposed initial good faith estimate was that at least 700 mL of normal liver must receive a dose less than 15 Gy in a three-treatment regimen, a threshold below which organ functionality was expected to be preserved. With this type of constraint in place, it was possible to escalate the prescription dose to individual lesions to 60 Gy in three fractions in the initial University of Colorado study10 and in five fractions in the University of Texas-Southwestern study,11 thus achieving actuarial rates of local control of 93% to 100% at 18 to 24 months. In the setting of liver metastases, the rate of radiation-induced liver disease after SBRT is extremely low in the absence of preexisting liver disease, primarily because the mean normal liver dose is kept low. In the first stage, operative resection and/or ablation is used to clear the anticipated FLR (most commonly the left hemiliver or left lateral section). This is often undertaken in a minimally invasive manner to facilitate recovery and progression to subsequent therapy. Very shortly after this procedure, contralateral PVE is performed to induce hypertrophy of the newly cleared portion of the liver. If post-PVE imaging verifies satisfactory hypertrophy of the FLR, completion hepatectomy is then performed to clear all remaining sites of disease. Transarterial Therapy Transarterial therapies take advantage of the aforementioned unique physiologic characteristic of hepatic metastases. Unlike normal hepatocytes, which derive approximately 75% of their blood supply from the portal venous circulation, hepatic metastases derive 80% to 90% of their blood supply from the hepatic arterial circulation. As a result, a number of therapeutic interventions targeting hepatic metastases have been designed to be delivered intra-arterially (via the hepatic arterial system). Hepatic arterial infusion (HAI) chemotherapy involves the delivery of chemotherapeutic agents directly into the hepatic arterial system. HAI typically uses chemotherapeutic agents that undergo high first-pass hepatic metabolism. Once metabolized by hepatocytes, negligible quantities of chemotherapy are then exposed to the rest of the body; in this way, HAI enables the administration of vastly higher concentrations of chemotherapy to hepatic metastases than can be delivered systemically. Transarterial embolization (TAE) involves the selective administration of polyvinyl alcohol or microspheres into the small arterial vessels that perfuse hepatic tumors. Once delivered, these agents induce thrombosis in small-diameter arteries that results in selective ischemia of tumors but not of the surrounding hepatic parenchyma. Extrahepatic Disease One special circumstance of liberalizing indications for hepatic metastasectomy that deserves mention is that of extrahepatic metastases. The presence of metastatic disease outside of the liver (e.g., pulmonary, peritoneal, retroperitoneal) was once universally considered to be an absolute contraindication to hepatic resection. At the very least, care should be taken to limit the duration of preoperative chemotherapy to minimize the risk of chemotherapy-associated hepatotoxicity; based on retrospective analyses, it appears that the risk of perioperative complications increases after six or more cycles of preoperative chemotherapy. Identification of chemotherapy-associated hepatotoxicity can be challenging because routine laboratory assessment of hepatic function is typically not sensitive enough to identify these changes. Thrombocytopenia can be suggestive of hypersplenism resulting from hepatic fibrosis-induced portal hypertension. Radiographic evidence of steatosis (as estimated by a decrease in hepatic parenchymal attenuation on CT imaging or signal dropout on in-phase and out-of-phase MRI sequences) or fibrosis (as indicated by alterations in hepatic segmental atrophy or hypertrophy or irregularities in parenchymal contour) can also be suggestive of hepatotoxicity.64 Because of the inconsistency with which these preoperative diagnostics identify significant hepatotoxicity, some have argued for the routine use of percutaneous liver biopsy (to evaluate for steatosis, fibrosis, or sinusoidal obstruction) in patients who have received intensive systemic chemotherapy.65

Hepatic Artery Infusional Chemotherapy As stated previously, hepatic metastases preferentially derive their perfusion from the hepatic arterial circulation. Floxuridine (FUDR) is a derivative of FU that is rapidly metabolized by the liver. HAI of FUDR has therefore been developed as a means of delivering extremely high doses of chemotherapy to hepatic tumors with negligible systemic exposure. Clinical trials have demonstrated impressive benefits with the use of adjuvant and neoadjuvant HAI chemotherapy.66–68 Follow-up studies from the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center have shown that the efficacy of HAI chemotherapy persists even with the use of modern systemic chemotherapy in properly selected patients.69 The use of HAI chemotherapy requires familiarity with proper techniques for infusion pump placement and care. Complications of HAI chemotherapy include hepatic arterial thrombosis and off-target effects of FUDR chemotherapy including gastritis and duodenitis if the catheter becomes dislodged or if collaterals form into the celiac arterial vasculature. In addition, patients receiving HAI chemotherapy must be closely monitored for signs of biliary sclerosis. Like metastases, cholangiocytes of the biliary tree also derive their blood supply from the hepatic arterial system; as a result, prolonged arterial infusion of chemotherapy can result in biliary strictures. The “Disappearing Metastasis” Because of the risk of chemotherapy-associated hepatotoxicity, patients with advanced disease undergoing preoperative systemic chemotherapy must undergo serial imaging surveillance so that operative intervention can be undertaken before the onset of liver damage. Introduction Like colorectal adenocarcinoma, neuroendocrine carcinoma arising from the gastrointestinal tract and pancreas commonly metastasizes to the liver via the portal venous circulation. As a result, therapies to target hepatic metastases have been developed and pursued aggressively. Unlike colorectal adenocarcinoma, comparatively little progress has been made in the development of systemic chemotherapy for neuroendocrine carcinoma. Somatostatin analogs and targeted therapies such as everolimus and sunitinib have demonstrated improvements in PFS but little to no response rates.91–93 Emerging technologies such as peptide receptor radiotherapy have the potential to change the landscape of treatment for metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma,94 but the role of operative therapy for symptom management and cytoreduction has been explored for some time. The motivation and rationale for aggressive liver-directed therapy for patients with hepatic neuroendocrine carcinoma center on the generally indolent and often highly symptomatic nature of its disease course. Well- differentiated forms of neuroendocrine carcinoma often grow and progress slowly, with median survival of patients with even widely metastatic disease measured in years. In addition, the hormones that are often elaborated by neuroendocrine neoplasms escape hepatic metabolism when they arise from tumors located in the liver; as a result, patients with hepatic metastases can suffer from highly symptomatic syndromes of hormonal overproduction that can quickly become refractory to pharmacologic suppression. The effort to prolong survival and/or improve quality of life has led to a variety of treatment options for patients with hepatic neuroendocrine carcinoma metastases. An important difference between hepatic metastases from colorectal adenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine carcinoma is that neuroendocrine metastases tend to be more diffuse and multifocal in their dissemination. Indeed, it is not uncommon to find innumerable, miliary liver lesions in patients with metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma. Not surprisingly, the likelihood of performing a complete resection and the durability of hepatic recurrence-free survival are much lower for hepatic neuroendocrine metastases. This important difference informs decision making when considering the various treatment options available for this disease. TABLE 118.3
