Whereas the goal of surgical treatment for hepatic colorectal metastases is invariably a complete resection, subtotal resection (also referred to as debulking) is occasionally advocated in the management of hepatic neuroendocrine metastases. The circumstance in which this is most appropriately pursued is in the palliation of patients with refractory symptoms of hormonal overproduction. Operative cytoreduction of a majority of hepatic disease burden has been associated with a magnitude and duration of symptomatic improvement that compare favorably with nonoperative modalities of treatment. When cytoreduction is undertaken for this reason, therapy is typically directed at eliminating the largest tumors and resecting the maximal amount of total disease burden possible. However, there are no clear data to support the specific manner (e.g., the target tumor size or percentage of tumor bulk elimination) in which cytoreduction should be best performed. Although some centers have argued that operative cytoreduction also prolongs survival for patients with metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma,97 it is important to recognize that patients with even significant hepatic tumor burden often survive for years without any form of tumor-directed therapy. Therefore, in the absence of randomized controlled data, the extent to which operative cytoreduction (resulting in gross residual disease) prolongs survival remains unclear. However, in light of the often diffuse manner in which neuroendocrine carcinoma metastasizes to the liver and the near inevitability of hepatic recurrence after surgical resection, one can make the argument that all hepatic resections for metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma are inherently cytoreductive. Prognostic Factors It is evident that the most informative prognostic variable for neuroendocrine carcinoma is the degree of histologic differentiation. Neuroendocrine carcinoma is characterized into three levels of histologic differentiation based on mitotic activity as assessed by mitotic figures or by Ki-67 immunohistochemical proliferative index. Classification of well-differentiated, moderately differentiated, and poorly differentiated disease permits stratification of oncologic outcomes. Coleman INTRODUCTION Bone metastases are most frequent in breast and prostate carcinomas and affect two-thirds to three-quarters of patients with advanced disease from these tumors. In addition, lung, thyroid, and renal carcinoma metastasizes to bone in approximately 30% to 40% of cases.1 Mean survival ranges from a low of less than 12 months for those with lung carcinoma, to several years for those with bone metastases from prostate, thyroid, or breast carcinoma.1 If patients have skeletal metastases only, their average survival is even longer. PRESENTATION The morbidity associated with metastatic bone disease, often referred to as skeletal-related events (SREs), includes pain that may require opiates, the need for radiotherapy and/or surgery, hypercalcemia, pathologic fractures, and spinal cord compression. The most common symptom is pain. Pain initially may be either a well- localized focus of pain or a diffuse ache, typically worse at night and often not relieved by lying flat. Pain from extremity lesions tends to be well defined, in contrast to spine and pelvic sites, which produce vague, diffuse symptoms. Eventually, the pain worsens with weight-bearing activity. Initially, pain results from the physical presence of tumor in the bone; with the release of inflammatory mediators, neuropeptides, and cytokines; as well as from elevation of the intraosseous pressure from tumor mass effect, causing irritation of intraosseous and periosteal nerve endings.2 Functional pain is caused by the mechanical weakness of the bone, which can no longer support the normal stresses of daily activities. Mechanical pain is more typically associated with the focal bone loss within lytic lesions; however, radiographically blastic lesions may also weaken the bone through associated areas of osteolysis that are sufficient to compromise structural integrity. The development of functional pain may be a marker for bone at risk for fracture. Pathologic fractures may be the first sign of metastatic bone disease. In breast carcinoma, as many as 35% of patients with bone disease experience a fracture.3 Breast, lung, renal, and thyroid cancers have been the most common cancers with pathologic fracture, but even in endocrine-resistant prostate cancer where osteoblastic metastases

Osteoclastic activity has been shown to be increased by tumor expression of a wide range of cytokines and growth factors, resulting in an increased rate of bone resorption.5 This in turn leads to the release of bone-derived growth factors, notably transforming growth factor β, which in turn may react with receptors on the tumor cells. This sets up the so-called vicious cycle whereby the stimulation of bone cell activity produces a favorable microenvironment for the neighboring tumor cells and facilitates the metastatic process. The new bone formation associated with osteoblastic lesions has been associated with endothelin 1 and insulin-like growth factor stimulation of osteoblasts, but typically even in osteoblastic lesions, there is also an associated increase in osteoclastic bone resorption.6 DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION Radiographs and bone scans are the first lines of imaging supplemented by computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and, in some disease settings, positron emission tomography (PET) to document the presence or absence of an osseous lesion and to identify whether these are solitary or multiple lesions. In the spine, plain films classically show absence of a pedicle with the “winking owl sign” (Fig. 119.1). A CT scan is the best modality to define the size of an osseous lesion and to evaluate the extent of cortical involvement. In the spine, CT scan is most useful to evaluate aspects of bony stability as measured by pedicle and/or posterior body wall integrity. These factors are important in establishing risk of burst fracture and for planning and assessing the safety of vertebroplasty as a treatment alternative.7 CT-guided biopsy can be used for obtaining tissue samples. MRI is valuable for evaluating marrow disease and is most sensitive in identifying metastatic deposits in the spine and pelvis. In patients with neurologic compromise, MRI is best for assessing epidural disease and extent of vertebral involvement (solitary versus multifocal). THERAPEUTIC MODALITIES Optimal management requires a multidisciplinary team. Medical treatment, radiation therapy, surgery, and bone- targeted treatment with the bisphosphonates and denosumab are combined depending on the biology of the disease, extent of the skeletal involvement, and the life expectancy of the patient.

Systemic Therapy In addition to systemic treatments for the disease, which can be found in disease-specific chapters, there are several bone-specific agents, as discussed in the following text. Bisphosphonates for Metastatic Bone Disease Over the past 20 years, bisphosphonates have become established as a valuable additional approach to the range of current treatments. Bisphosphonates are analogs of pyrophosphate, characterized by a phosphorus-carbon- phosphorus–containing central structure that binds to bone and a variable side chain that determines the relative potency, side effects, and precise mechanism of action.8 Bisphosphonates bind avidly to exposed bone mineral, and during bone resorption, bisphosphonates are internalized by the osteoclast and subsequently cause apoptotic cell death. After intravenous administration of a bisphosphonate, the kidney excretes approximately 25% to 40% of the

injected dose, and the remainder is taken up by bone where it is retained for months or even years. All bisphosphonates suffer from poor bioavailability when given by mouth and must be taken on an empty stomach, as they bind to calcium in the diet. It is generally accepted that osteoclast activation is the key step in the establishment and growth of bone metastases. Biochemical data indicate that bone resorption is of importance not only in classic “lytic” diseases such as myeloma and breast cancer but also in prostate cancer.6 As a result, the osteoclast is a key therapeutic target for skeletal metastases irrespective of the tissue of origin.9 Although radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for localized bone pain, the bisphosphonates provide an additional treatment approach for the relief of bone pain across a range of tumor types.10 Oral Bisphosphonates The absorption of bisphosphonates from the gut is poor, variable, and dramatically inhibited by food intake. Nevertheless, oral clodronate and ibandronate have been shown in randomized trials to have useful efficacy in breast cancer.9 Intravenous Bisphosphonates There is extensive experience with intravenous bisphosphonates in breast cancer, with zoledronic acid, pamidronate, and ibandronate all showing useful clinical activity.9 Comparative data are few, but in a double- blind randomized trial of 1,130 patients with advanced breast cancer, an additional 20% reduction in the risk of SREs was seen with zoledronic acid compared with pamidronate (P = .025).11 Ibandronate was licensed in Europe for the treatment of metastatic bone cancer after a placebo-controlled trial of monthly infusions showed a significant reduction in skeletal-related morbidity.12 Intravenous bisphosphonates have become routine clinical management for most patients with multiple myeloma, with zoledronic acid and pamidronate the agents of choice.9,11 Improved survival with the inclusion of zoledronic acid in first-line myeloma treatment, as well as fewer SREs, have been shown in a large randomized comparison of zoledronic acid versus oral clodronate.11 In advanced castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), zoledronic acid was shown to reduce the overall risk of skeletal complications by 36%.13 In addition, zoledronic acid significantly reduced the risk for SREs by approximately 30% (P = .003) in the management of bone metastases from s

Several large-scale prospective randomized trials were subsequently performed. The United Kingdom Bone Pain Trial Working Party randomized 765 patients with bone metastases to either an 8-Gy single fraction or a multifraction regimen (20 Gy in 5 fractions or 30 Gy in 10 fractions).30 There were no differences in the time to first improvement in pain, time to complete pain relief, or time to first increase in pain at any time up to 12 months from randomization. Re-treatment was twice as common after 8 Gy than after multifraction radiotherapy. There were no significant differences in the incidence of nausea, vomiting, spinal cord compression, or pathologic fracture between the two groups. The study concluded that a single 8-Gy fraction is as safe and effective as a multifraction regimen for the palliation of metastatic bone pain for at least 12 months. The Dutch Bone Metastases Study included 1,171 patients and found no difference in pain relief or the quality of life after a single 8-Gy or 24- Gy dose in six daily radiation treatments.31 However, the re-treatment rates were 25% in the single 8-Gy arm and 7% in the multiple-treatment arm, respectively. In the cost-utility analysis of this randomized trial, there was no difference in life expectancy or quality-adjusted life expectancy. The estimated cost of radiotherapy, including re- treatments and nonmedical costs, was statistically significantly lower for the single-fraction schedule than for the multiple-fraction schedule.32 One critical review included a systematic search for randomized trials of localized radiotherapy of bone metastases using different dose fractionations.33 The authors suggested that protracted fractionated radiotherapy, given over 2 to 4 weeks, results in more complete and durable pain relief. A prospective randomized trial in 270 patients with painful bone metastases compared efficacy of 4- or 8-Gy single doses.41 At 4 weeks, the actual response rates were 69% for 8 Gy and 44% for 4 Gy (P < .001), but there was no difference in complete response rates at 4 weeks or duration of response between the two arms. It was concluded that 8 Gy gives a higher probability of pain relief than 4 Gy but that 4 Gy can be an effective alternative in situations of reduced tolerance. Another randomized trial of three single-dose radiation therapy regimens in the treatment of metastatic bone pain consisted of single fractions of 4, 6, or 8 Gy.42 The authors confirmed that 8 Gy could be considered as probably the lowest optimal single-fraction radiation treatment for painful bone metastases, although a single fraction of 4 Gy should not be easily discarded because of its applicability in specific cases. Wide-Field or Half-Body External-Beam Radiation Wide-field or half-body irradiation (HBI) differs from localized external-beam radiation mainly in the volume of tissues and bone metastases covered as a single treatment field. It is more useful for patients with multiple painful bone metastases. HBI is usually delivered either to the upper half or to the lower half of the body. Single-fraction HBI has been shown in retrospective and prospective phase I and II studies to provide pain relief in 70% to 80% of patients.43,44 Pain relief is apparent within 24 to 48 hours, suggesting that cells of the inflammatory response pathway may be the initial target tissue, as tumor cell activities are unlikely to be halted so quickly. Toxicities include minor bone marrow suppression and gastrointestinal side effects such as nausea and vomiting in upper abdominal radiation and may be controlled with ondansetron or dexamethasone. Pulmonary toxicity is minimal provided the lung dose is limited to 6 Gy.45 Fractionated HBI was investigated in a randomized phase II study involving 29 patients that compared a single fraction with fractionated HBI (25 to 30 Gy in multiple fractions). Pain relief was achieved in >94% of patients. At 1 year, 70% of patients in the fractionated group and

patients who did not respond initially, there were 12 responses (46%). The authors concluded that the lack of response to initial single-fraction radiotherapy should not deter repeat irradiation. Toxicity in their series was low and gastrointestinal only. No acute toxicity of grade 3 or greater was reported. Pathologic fractures were reported in 3 of 135 (2%) patients and spinal cord compression in 3 of 135 (2%) patients in their series. The same group reported the efficacy of reirradiation with the second single 4-Gy fraction for painful bone metastases after the previous two single fractions. The overall response rate of the 25 patients (19 responders and 6 nonresponders to the two prior single fractions) was 80%, with both complete response and partial response rates of 40%. No acute or late high-grade toxicity (≥3) was observed in their study. No pathologic fractures or spinal cord compression were seen in any of these patients during the follow-up.51 The Dutch Bone Metastases Study Group presented the efficacy of reirradiation of painful bone metastases.52 For patients not responding to the initial radiation who were reirradiated, 66% of patients who initially received a single 8-Gy fraction responded to the re-treatment versus 33% of patients who received the initial multifraction regimens. Re-treatment for patients with progression was successful in 70% of single-fraction patients versus 57% of multifraction patients. In general, re-treatment was effective in 63% of all re-treated patients. A recent intergroup randomized trial on dose fractionations in repeat radiation for painful bone metastases in 850 patients concluded that a single fraction of 8 Gy appears to be noninferior and less toxic than 20 Gy in multiple fractions, with 2-month response rates in evaluable patients of 45% versus 51%, respectively (P = .17).53 SYSTEMIC RADIONUCLIDES Patients with bone metastases often have diffuse bony disease. Administration of a systemic radionuclide has the advantage of targeting all bony lesions simultaneously and can be given as a single administration on an outpatient basis. Osteoblastic bone metastases can be detected by a technetium-99 methylenediphosphonate bone scan. Dr. AVR @ TMH discussed earlier.26 Controlling Side Effects of Treatment Radiation treatment planning is the most critical aspect of reducing radiation side effects. Management of the acute effects of radiotherapy requires attentive medical management that prevents expected side effects. Radiation side effects are specific to the area treated. Careful radiation treatment planning that avoids critical structures like mucosal surfaces can prevent most side effects. Patients should be reassured that the unavoidable side effects that they experience will resolve after the completion of radiotherapy. Skin reactions are usually minimal during radiotherapy for bone metastases and are limited only to the radiation portal. Nausea and vomiting, resulting from a radiation portal that includes the abdomen, will usually respond to antiemetic therapy, but ondansetron or dexamethasone also is commonly used, especially if patients have recently received emetogenic chemotherapy. Diarrhea, resulting from abdominopelvic radiation, will respond to antidiarrhea medications such as loperamide. Local irritation from mucositis of the oropharyngeal region may be relieved by soluble aspirin, analgesics, or benzydamine mouthwashes. Secondary infections, such as Candida, should be treated. The side effects of electron-beam radiation are more limited because it only treats superficial structures such as the ribs, skin lesions, and superficial lymph nodes. Underlying structures are spared with the selection of the proper electron-beam energy. The most prominent side effect of electron-beam radiation is an erythematous skin reaction. Other side effects listed here do not occur with electron-beam radiation because the radiation beam does not penetrate to these structures. No side effects, other than a possible flare of pain in the first 2 weeks after administration, are observed with systemic radioisotope therapy because all the radiation is localized to the bone. This is an important consideration for patients who have significant symptoms of the disease or other treatments. Side effects from external-beam radiation also are more severe when the radiation fields are large because more normal tissues are treated. Pain flare is common after palliative radiotherapy for osseous metastases.57 The use of dexamethasone has been shown to be effective in the prophylaxis of pain flare.58 Systemic r

Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy of Spinal Metastases Technologic advances in radiation oncology have resulted in the development of stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT), and one of the most common indications has been for spinal metastases.62 Typically, spine SBRT refers to focal high total dose and dose per fraction (>5 Gy) conformal radiation, delivered such that the tumor is dose escalated while maintaining the surrounding normal tissues to a lower and safe dose threshold. Millimetric precision in treatment delivery, MRI for target and spinal cord delineation, and stringent quality assurance of the treatment plan are required.63,64 For spine metastases, SBRT represents a major shift in the therapeutic intent as doses such as 16 to 24 Gy in a single fraction, 24 Gy in two to three fractions, and 30 to 35 Gy in five fractions represent two to six times the biologically equivalent dose as those investigated in the conventional radiotherapy literature. The ideal candidate for spine SBRT has oligometastatic disease, no mechanical instability, no epidural disease, and radioresistant disease (e.g., renal cell, melanoma, lung cancer) or progression after prior conventional radiation. Spine The spine is the most common site of metastatic bone disease. Spinal complications are due to loss of mechanical stability creating pain and spinal cord compression causing paralysis. Neurologic compression occurs due to direct tumor load in the epidural space or from a pathologic fracture causing bony compression or vertebral instability. The goals of spinal surgery in metastatic disease are to preserve or restore spinal stability for pain and to restore or protect neurologic function. Because of immunosuppression, poor nutritional status, and medical comorbidities, surgery to the spine may be associated with significant complications. Considerations in decision making are life span of the patient, general medical condition, number of spinal levels involved, age, cancer type, and radiation status.96 The significance of the primary cancer type on survival is well established. After detection by bone scan of spine involvement, Tatsui et al.97 reported a 1-year survival of 0% and 22% for gastric and pulmonary can

surgery. For overall survival, each year of advancing age had a 1% increased risk of dying. Lung primary had a 2.65 relative risk of mortality within 30 days. The beneficial effect of surgery with adjuvant radiation for solitary solid tumors compared to radiation alone was demonstrated by Patchell et al.99 in their landmark randomized study. A subsequent multicenter observational cohort study by the AOSpine North American Clinical Research Network again noted the beneficial effect of surgery for solitary solid tumors on the health-related quality-of-life outcomes (HRQoL).100 Surgical intervention as an adjunct to radiation and chemotherapy provided lasting pain relief and improvements in neurologic function and HRQoL. The effect of a preoperative neurologic deficit on survivorship has been evaluated by a number of authors. In a multicenter study by Argenson et al.,101 patients with a preoperative deficit had significantly lower mean survival at 1 and 3 years after surgery. We have shown that patients with preoperative neurologic deficits were 71% more likely to get a postoperative infection, likely from the administration of preoperative radiation. Other authors have likewise found increased infection rates and poorer outcomes after surgery in the presence of preoperative radiation.98,102–104 In 2003, Wai et al.96 prospectively evaluated the efficacy of surgery in patients with metastatic spinal disease with respect to quality of life using a validated outcome measure specific for palliative patients. This study demonstrated the largest improvement to be in pain after surgery. There were significant improvements in six other domains and trends toward improvement in another one. There was no significant deterioration in any domain. The major benefit of surgery occurs within the first month and remained stable until death or for at least 6 months (length of follow-up).

Principles of open surgical techniques and considerations are beyond the scope of this chapter. In general, tumor location within the vertebrae, spinal level, radiation status, neurologic deficit, and number of levels involved affect decision making. SINS is a classification system that may also be used to assist the radiation oncologist and spinal surgeon in evaluating spinal instability. The SINS criteria consist of classifying the involved spinal segment according to the location along the spinal axis, the presence of mechanical pain, bone lesion type (lytic, blastic, or mixed), spinal alignment, degree of vertebral body collapse, and involvement of posterior elements. A score is calculated from a total of 18 possible points, and a SINS score of 0 to 6 is stable, 7 to 12 is potentially unstable, and >13 is unstable.105 Surgical approaches for addressing spinal instability and neurologic compression can be from either an anterior or posterior approach. Instrumentation is required after decompression. Most cases can be performed posteriorly, and a vertebral column resection (VCR) has more recently been advocated for addressing the anterior instability from a posterior approach only. VCR eliminates the need for a transthoracic or retroperitoneal approach, which can create significant morbidity in these patients.106 More minimally invasive approaches for management of metastatic spinal disease are percutaneous vertebroplasty (PV) and kyphoplasty. These are an alternative to open surgery for restoring stability to the spine.107,108 PV may be applied to a greater number of candidates with pain due to instability. These same patients may not be suitable for invasive spinal surgery because of medical comorbidities, multilevel disease, or presence of a profound neurologic deficit. PV is performed under intravenous sedation in the radiology suite or in the operating room. Taylor Ripley MALIGNANT PLEURAL EFFUSIONS Malignant pleural effusions (MPE) are diagnosed in greater than 150,000 patients annually in the United States.1 In a series of over 3,000 patients who underwent a diagnostic thoracentesis, 27% of the patients had MPE (Fig. 120.1).2 In this series, the most common causes of MPE were lung cancer (37%), breast cancer (16%), lymphoma (10%), and unknown origin (10%). A retrospective analysis of over 126,000 hospital admissions for MPE in the United States reported similar incidences (Table 120.1).3 Typically, patients with MPE have a poor prognosis; however, survival is highly dependent on the underlying pathology. For patients with MPE secondary to lung cancer, the presence of even a small effusion was associated with worse overall survival compared to no effusion (7.49 versus 12.65 months, respectively).4 Based on the poor survival of patients with MPE, the seventh edition of the tumor, node, metastasis (TNM) lung cancer staging system upstaged patients with MPE from stage IIIB to IV (M1a disease).5 Survival rates for patients with breast cancer and MPE are slightly higher, with a median overall survival of approximately 13 months.6 Patients with MPE secondary to hematologic malignancy have a median survival of about 7 months.7 The vast majority of MPE are caused by metastatic disease; however, malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) arises from the pleural surface and may also result in MPE.8 Even though MPM is a primary disease of the pleura, the median survival is about 9 months, and the long-term prognosis remains uniformly poor.9 The pleura of the chest cavity is fibrous tissue formed from a single layer of mesothelium that is divided into the parietal and visceral layers.10 The visceral pleura is adherent to the lung, whereas the parietal pleura lines the remainder of the thoracic cavity. A small amount of fluid is secreted and reabsorbed between the parietal and visceral surfaces to assist in respiration by helping to maintain a negative intrathoracic pressure. An estimated 0.01 mL/kg/h of fluid is produced and cleared at the same rate to maintain a constant volume.11 The parietal pleura is likely more important in maintaining fluid homeostasis given that the vessels are closer to the pleural lining and lymphatic stomata are more abundant compared to the visceral p

Diagnosis and Evaluation Radiologic Examinations Pleural effusions can be detected in the costophrenic sulcus by erect posterior-to-anterior chest radiographs (CXRs) when as little as 200 mL of fluid collects in the subpulmonic area. This fluid forms a meniscus when in contact with the parietal pleura. Supine CXRs are much less useful. If the diaphragm is obscured, then about 500 mL of fluid has collected; if the effusion is as high as the fourth rib, then about 1,000 mL of fluid is present. Massive MPE can appear as complete opacification of the hemithorax with mediastinal shift. If fluid is loculated, then it will not move to dependent areas and may appear anywhere on the film. Small amounts of fluid can be detected with decubitus imaging; however, computed tomography (CT) has replaced decubitus imaging for evaluation beyond upright CXR.15 MPE is often associated with other malignant features on CXR including irregular pleural thickening and nodular opacities. If MPE is suspected or established, CT is indicated to better characterize the effusion and to identify pleural thickening or masses, loculations, lung parenchymal processes, pulmonary emboli, and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy (Fig. 120.2).16 Parietal pleural thickening, mediastinal pleural thickening, and nodularity are classic features of malignancy that are often associated with MPE. CT should be a multislice section (2.0 mm or less) with intravenous contrast and reviewed in mediastinal and lung window settings with multiplanar reconstruction.17 MPEs are easily identified by CT, although occasionally distinguishing the effusion from ascites can be difficult. CT is usually not necessary for management; however, CT is particularly useful for assessment of treatment response or evaluation of interventions. Ultrasound (US) is often used when MPE is suspected because it is portable, making it particularly useful in the intensive care unit.18 The normal pleura is an echogenic line or “pleural stripe,” which is both the visceral and parietal pleura.19 “Comet tails” are echogenic bands beyond the pleural stripe that can be any object, and “lung sliding” describes the appearance when the pleural stripe is shimmering. Both comet tails and lung sliding disappear with pleural air or fluid accumulation. Pleural fluid including MPE is dark or hypoechoic.20 L

Similarly, MRI is rarely warranted with MPE; it is limited in the chest by cardiac and respiratory movement and poor special resolution.21 Invasive Diagnostic Procedures Prior to the establishment of MPE, the fluid should be analyzed based on appearance such as straw colored, milky, bloodstained, or turbid and for the presence of food particles. Next, laboratory analysis should include protein, lactate dehydrogenase, pH, white and red blood cell counts, cytology, and cultures.22 MPE usually presents as an exudate that is hypercellular and bloodstained; cytologic positivity confirms malignancy. Importantly, cytology may be positive in only 40% of cases of pleural fluid with an underlying malignancy; therefore, a negative result does not rule out an MPE.23 Thoracentesis is a straightforward method to obtain fluid for biochemical and cytologic analysis. Often, 8- to 14-Fr small catheters are inserted instead of needle thoracentesis to obtain both fluid for analysis and to drain a large effusion slowly to avoid reexpansion pulmonary edema (RPE). Although relatively rare, RPE can occur with lung expansion when large-volume effusions are rapidly drained.24 Avoidance of draining >1,500 mL at one setting, stopping with chest pain or shortness of breath, and draining periodically can usually avoid RPE. Efficacy of pleurodesis is defined as complete success with absence of fluid reaccumulation, partial success with some reaccumulation without additional therapeutic procedures, and failure when the two prior definitions are not met.1 Pleurodesis is preferable to repeated thoracentesis except in patients who have an extremely short life expectancy, are too frail, or have a trapped lung. Apposition of the visceral and parietal pleural surfaces is critical for pleurodesis. If a lung cannot expand secondary to undrained pleural loculations, visceral adhesions that “trap” the lung, or persistent air leak, the lack of apposition may result in a failed pleurodesis.27,28 A thoracentesis or tube thoracostomy can be used not only to drain the MPE but also to determine whether reexpansion of the lung occurs. Lung reexpansion is predictive of success with pleurodesis. In the situation in which the lung will not expand, the underlying problems needs to be corrected. Debridement of the loculations, decortication of the trapped lung, or relief of an endobronchial obstruction may be required. These procedures are often possible; however, the performance status of the patient or the need to rapidly restart systemic therapy must be considered carefully. If the patient is too frail or needs to be started on therapy quickly, the patient may be served better by a tunneled indwelling pleural catheter (IPC). Trapped lung occurs when the lung cannot expand to fill the pleural space secondary to restriction of the visceral pleura. This restriction, or “peel,” occurs secondary to fibrosis from inflammation or direct tumor spread on the visceral pleura. In this situation, dyspnea secondary to the decreased lung volume and a perfusion mismatch may not improve with pleural drainage by any method. In addition, pleurodesis requires apposition of parietal and visceral pleura to induce pleural symphysis, which cannot occur if the lung is trapped. Relief of a trapped lung requires surgical management by decortication by either open thoracotomy or VATS. As opposed to benign disease, management of trapped lung from metastatic disease requires a visceral pleurectomy instead of decortication alone. A decortication typically removes a fibrous peel secondary to an infection, whereas the surgical plane for a visceral pleurectomy is one layer lower, which exposes the underlying lung parenchyma. Decortication can prevent repeated pleural interventions with the potential risk of empyema. Palliation by pleurectomy and decortication via thoracotomy are rarely indicated for MPE except for MPM. If a thoracotomy is considered, the patient should have an expected survival of greater than 12 months and expect significant symptom relief.41 Given the morbidity of an open thoracotomy in patients with limited life expectance and the relative ease of performing a partial parietal pleurectomy via VATS, the role of thoracotomy with MPE is quite limited. Tunneled Indwelling Pleural Catheter IPCs are approximately 15-Fr silicone tubes that are inserted in the pleural cavity and tunneled subcutaneously. The tube has a profibrotic cuff in the tunneled segment that induces adhesions to secure the catheter subcutaneously and a one-way valve that can be accessed intermittently to drain the space. The most widely used IPC is the PleurX by Denver Biomedical (Golden, CO) that was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 1997 (Fig. 120.5). Vacuum bottles are attached to the valve to drain the space intermittently. The Aspira pleural drainage system by Bard Access Systems (Salt Lake City, UT) is the primary competitor in the United States that uses a manual pump instead of a vacuum bottle for drainage. Either IPC can be placed as an outpatient. Patients often tolerate up to 1,500 mL of drainage,

Catheter dysfunction may require intermittent thrombolysis to maintain patency.50 TREATMENT ALGORITHM Often, MPEs are diagnosed in patients with an established diagnosis of metastatic disease. In this situation, establishment of a diagnosis is not always necessary. However, treatment-related pleural effusions do occur; therefore, diagnostic evaluation may be warranted. Diagnosis can be established with a thoracentesis and aspiration; however, negative results are often false negatives. In this situation, VATS biopsy may be warranted for diagnosis as well as treatment. In many patients with MPE who require treatment, proceeding directly to a treatment algorithm without further diagnostic evaluation is reasonable. Despite substantial literature and recommendations for management, treatment decisions require a personalized approach in which one strategy r

by VATS, with CT guidance, or with local anesthesia only. VATS is necessary if concomitant biopsies are required, but otherwise, the method of placement is usually institution specific. For patient who do not want an IPC and have reasonable survival expectations, surgical intervention is appropriate. In almost all cases, these patients undergo VATS, and open thoracotomy is almost never required. The first step during VATS pleurodesis is to determine the ability of the lung to fill the pleural space if unknown from preoperative imaging. If the lung can adequately inflate, then VATS pleurodesis with sclerosants, mechanical abrasions, or partial pleurectomy is performed. If the lung cannot inflate, a decortication to allow expansion of the trapped lung is required. If a decortication cannot be performed, then an IPC is placed and the procedure is terminated. An additional option in addition to this practical algorithm includes bedside talc slurry or sclerosants. The usefulness of IPC, relative low morbidity of VATS, and need to repeat installations of talc slurry or sclerosants make the bedside procedures less useful. Often, patients need to start systemic therapy or resume therapy between cycles, therefore, repeated interventions can delay treatment. Achievement of adequate pleurodesis and resolution of an MPE, even if a short hospitalization is required, is often the fastest method to facilitate systemic options. MALIGNANT PERICARDIAL EFFUSIONS Malignancy is one of the most common causes of pericardial effusions; however, only 15% to 20% of patients with pericardial metastases have pericardial effusions.51,52 Malignant pericardial effusions (MPCEs) are the most common manifestation of pericardial tumors that results in symptoms. However, pericardial effusions in patients with known malignancy may be secondary to other causes such as treatment-related complications; therefore, diagnosis of the etiology of the effusion is critical. Jama et al.53 reviewed the literature and noted that 60% (1,339 of 2,322) of patients with symptomatic effusions had malignancy. Gornik et al.54 reported that 43.8% (96 of 219) of patients with pericardial effusions had MPCE in a single-institution series. Similar to the pleura, the pericardium is much more frequently a site of metastatic cancers than primary pericardial tumors.55,56 Primary tumors of the pericardium, including mesot

In patients with slowly developing MPCE, the first sign may be atrial fibrillation. Other patients may present with cardiac tamponade or pericardial constriction, which constitute an emergency.52 The classic presentation of the Beck triad with hypotension, tachycardia, and muffled heart sounds may be present; however, subacute tamponade from accumulation of fluid usually does not lead to hypotension and is much more common with MPCE.59 Symptoms range from severe, such as chest pain, palpitations, or syncope, to more subtle, such as dyspnea, chest discomfort, and fatigue. Distended neck veins and pulsus paradoxus may be present. Pericarditis may occur secondary to disease progression, infection, or treatment-related complications of chemotherapy and radiation. The pericardial sac becomes rigid at a fixed volume, which may impair ventricular filling. These patients present with fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. Kussmaul sign is uncommon, but pulsus paradoxus may be present.60 Diagnosis and Evaluation Radiologic Examinations MPCE is suspected in an asymptomatic patient with a known malignancy in whom a “water bottle” pericardial silhouette is noted on CXR. CXR has a low sensitivity and specificity. This imaging finding may be missed if mediastinal masses or left pleural effusions are present. More commonly, CT will distinguish pericardial fluid, pleural fluid, and tumors, but the hemodynamic significance cannot be ascertained based on the size of the effusion from CT. MRI can be substituted in patients with a contrast dye allergy. Echocardiography is the most useful imaging technique to evaluate MPCE. It can define the presence and distribution of the effusion as well as tumor size and location. More importantly, echocardiography helps assess hemodynamic consequences of the effusion. Signs such as right chamber collapse, flow velocity across the mitral valve, and dilatation of the inferior vena cava help assess the hemodynamics. The apical approach decreases risk of injury to the cardiac chambers, but it is a more difficult approach and is not suitable for emergencies. The parasternal approach is the most direct route but may cause a pneumothorax or injury the internal mammary artery. Dr. AVR @ TMH SUMMARY Patients with MPCE usually have advanced disease and short expected survivals. Treatment to relieve symptoms with minimal morbidity and prevention of recurrence is the overall goal. Usually, patients are best managed with a surgical, subxiphoid window. If the patient is unstable, a percutaneous tube pericardiostomy can alleviate hemodynamic compromise in preparation for surgery. Pericardial sclerosants can be instilled in surgically or percutaneously placed tubes. For patients with recurrent MPCE after subxiphoid window, VATS window is indicated in the stable patient. 121 Malignant Ascites Thuy B. Tran and Ajay V. Maker INCIDENCE AND ETIOLOGY Ascites is the accumulation of serous fluid in the abdominal cavity. Malignant ascites (MA) is a pathologic condition secondary to either primary peritoneal neoplasms or advanced-stage cancers resulting in increased abdominal fluid production, inhibited reabsorption, or both, accounting for 10% of ascites cases. Abdominal malignancies commonly associated with MA include ovarian, endometrial, appendiceal, colorectal, gastric, primary peritoneal, and pancreatic tumors, whereas breast, lung, and hematologic malignancies are the main nonabdominal tumors responsible. Ascites may be found in 52% of patients at the time of cancer diagnosis.1 Although nonmalignant etiologies for ascites should be considered, such as malnutrition, cirrhosis, portal hypertension, congestive heart failure, pancreatitis, infectious processes, and nephrosis, the majority of patients with newly diagnosed ascites and cancer will have MA. ANATOMY AND PATHOLOGY Ascitic Fluid Homeostasis Lining the abdominal cavity is the parietal peritoneum, a thin layer of mesothelium that contains multiple foramina. The amount of fluid and solutes that are secreted through this layer are tightly controlled, first by the capillary endothelium, then the capillary basement membrane, followed by the interstitial stroma between the capillaries and the peritoneum, and then the mesothelial basement membrane. The capillary endothelium contains anionic charges within an extracellular glycocalix that discourages anionic proteins and albumin from extravasating. This maintains plasma oncotic pressure. The capillary basement membrane is also lined with negatively charged proteoglycans, acting as a selective barrier against transit of anionic proteins. The interstitial space is a negatively charged filter of connective tissue, fibroblasts, and hyaluronic acid that is lined by the mesothelial cell basement membrane and also coated with anionic glycosaminoglycans. The peritoneal mesothelial cells also maintain a glycocalix of anionic charges, thereby forming a multilayered matrix that functions to inhibit transgression of intravascular proteins into the abdominal cavity. The total peritoneal surface area is approximately 2 m2, and fluid is continually secreted into the abdomen. At least two-thirds of peritoneal fluid reabsorbs into the open lympha

For example, carcinomatosis increases capillary permeability through a process of cytokine release and growth factor–driven angiogenesis, including fibroblasts, interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor (TNF), and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) as well as increased production and secretion of matrix metalloproteinases by tumor cells. Advanced malignancy can also result in chronic protein malnutrition, resulting in a catabolic state with reduced intravascular protein, thereby creating an oncotic pressure gradient that favors fluid extravasation from the vessels into the peritoneal cavity and lack of fluid reabsorption. The combination of these forces increases the extravascular oncotic pressure and decreases the rate of lymphatic uptake, thereby driving fluid into the interstitium and increasing intra-abdominal fluid. DIAGNOSIS Comprehensive history taking combined with physical exam will diagnose ascites in most patients. In patients with known malignancy, increasing abdominal girth, bloating, abdominal discomfort, and weight gain are concerning for carcinomatosis and MA. Imaging, usually computed tomography (CT) scan or ultrasound, can confirm the presence of ascites (Fig. 121.1). The CT findings of peritoneal nodules, thickening, omental caking, solid organ metastases, or intraperitoneal nodules raise the suspicion that ascites is malignant as opposed to secondary to benign etiologies. In over 100 patients studied with MA or cirrhotic ascites, CT signs significantly associated with a malignant etiology were fluid in the omental bursa, higher ascitic density (11.5 HU versus 6.7 HU), thickening of the parietal peritoneum, and, in patients with at least a moderate amount of ascites, a tethered bowel sign.4 As most patients with abdominal pain or malignancy are undergoing cross-sectional imaging as part of the workup or for surveillance, attention to these radiographic signs are important as they can help direct treatment and streamline further workup. Cross-sectional imaging confirmed recurrence and malignant ascites. The gold standard to diagnose MA is positive peritoneal cytology. This can be obtained percutaneously and safely under image guidance. For advanced gastrointestinal and hepatopancreaticobiliary malignancies without metastases on cross-sectional imaging, diagnostic laparoscopy is often used for evaluation of occult carcinomatosis. If incidental low-volume ascites is found in these patients, then ascites can be aspirated and sent for cytology, as can peritoneal washings. This is a standard approach for advanced gastric cancer in some centers, including our own, as positive peritoneal cytology carries a prognosis similar to stage IV disease. For those without carcinomatosis but still with MA, cytology is diagnostic in only 50% to 60% of patients. For these patients, perhaps the most useful single test is the serum to ascites albumin gradient. Calculated as the difference between serum and ascites albumin concentrations, values <1.1 g/dL are suspicious for carcinomatosis as opposed to portal hypertension or other cardiopulmonary causes. The use of ascitic fluid protein and other chemistries to discriminate between malignant and nonmalignant causes is variable and not reliable. If negative for malignancy, cell counts with >250 neutrophils per μL are suggestive of infection, and Gram stain should be performed. Ascitic fluid fibronectin levels have been reported to be 100% sensitive and specific for malignancy, but this is not a standard test currently, nor is sialic acid, telomerase, or human chorionic gonadotropin-β, all of which have shown discriminatory promise.5 In the absence of a known primary tumor or imaging revealing evidence of malignancy, serum tumor markers can be helpful. Elevated carcinoembryonic antigen values are traditionally associated with colorectal cancer but can also be elevated in breast, lung, pancreas, gastric, or breast cancers. Hepatopancreaticobiliary tumors can often reveal elevated cancer antigen (CA) 19-9 levels. Increased CA 125 levels are most suspicious for ovarian carcinoma, although they can be elevated in pancreas, lung, and breast cancers. α-Fetoprotein is another helpful serum marker that, when elevated, can be indicative of hepatocellular carcinoma. Randomized studies have demonstrated no difference in survival between patients treated with albumin and patients treated with other plasma expanders, and for patients with MA, no definitive trials on this subject have been performed. Reports of 5 L per 1 to 2 hours were demonstrated to be safe without hypovolemia or renal dysfunction, and volumes up to 20 L per session have been reported, although there is no consensus on the rate of withdrawal, ranging from 30 minutes to 24 hours. Peritoneovenous Shunting Shunting involves removing fluid from the peritoneal cavity and returning it to the venous circulation (superior vena cava) with the goal of maintaining electrolytes and proteins, as compared to drainage procedures. The most commonly employed options include the LeVeen catheter and the Denver shunt (Denver Biomedical, Denver, CO) (Fig. 121.2).17 Peritoneovesicular shunts were attempted; however, peritonitis and occlusion limited their utility. There is no level 1 evidence comparing shunt efficacy in MA. Contraindications to shunt placement include hemorrhagic ascites, loculations, heart disease, renal failure, jaundice, portal hypertension, pleural effusion, and clotting disorders.12,14 Theoretically, there is a risk of systemic seeding from positive peritoneal cytology, but this has not been found to be clinically significant. Although shunt placement would be advised only in select patients with prolonged life expectancy, survival has been found to be approximately 30 days in one study and ranged from 52 to 266 days in a comprehensive review, with perioperative mortality as high as 20%.12 A review of 27 studies evaluating the LeVeen and Denver shunts found 78% control of ascites with 70% subclinical and approximately 3% clinical disseminated intravascular coagulation, a mean patency of 10 weeks, and lowest response rates in patients with gastrointestinal cancers (10% to 15%).8 Therefore, their use in gastrointestinal malignancies is relatively contraindicated. Complication rates of 25% to 40% are reported, with kinking or occlusion occurring in almost one-third of patients.10,18 In summary, in highly selected patients with prolonged life expectancy, surgical shunting may provide palliation with known procedure-related morbidity and mortality. Although repeat paracentesis carries the risk of significant protein loss and decreased circulatory volume, CART allows for preservation of important proteins such as albumin and globulin by removing cells from ascitic fluid and returning proteins from the drained ascitic fluid back into the patient. Waqar, and Ramaswamy Govindan INTRODUCTION Paraneoplastic syndromes are disorders caused by systemic effects occurring remotely from the cancer primary site or metastasis.1 The most commonly involved systems in paraneoplastic syndromes are the neurologic, endocrine, hematologic, dermatologic, and rheumatologic systems. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) is the malignancy most commonly associated with paraneoplastic syndromes, with lymphoproliferative disorders, thymoma, gynecologic and breast cancers accounting for the majority of the other causes. The two main mechanisms for paraneoplastic syndromes are ectopic production of humoral factors, such as hormones, peptides, or cytokines, and immune cross-response between malignant and normal tissues. Paraneoplastic syndromes may be the first manifestation of a malignancy, and their timely detection may allow the diagnosis of tumors at an early stage. Therefore, these malignancies that would likely be otherwise clinically occult may be detected at an earlier stage with increased probability of cure. The successful treatment of the underlying malignancy usually results in resolution of the paraneoplastic syndromes caused by ectopic hormone production. However, the tumor-directed treatment is less effective in the immune-mediated syndromes. PARANEOPLASTIC NEUROLOGIC SYNDROMES Paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes (PNSs) are a rare complication of malignancy, observed in approximately 0.01% of all patients with cancer.1,2 In the Euronetwork database for patients with PNS, the most common tumors were SCLC, ovarian cancer, breast cancer, and non-small cell lung cancer.3 PNSs occur when the immune system cross-reacts with antigens on the tumor cells and proteins expressed in the neurologic system.4 The two categories of antigens are intracellular and extracellular, with the pathophysiology differing according to the antigen.5 Diagnosis The initial diagnostic workup depends on whether the patients have a known malignancy. For patients with a known malignancy, the workup includes radiologic imaging to evaluate for brain metastases, leptomeningeal disease, or spinal cord compression and a review of previous radiation therapy or chemotherapy treatments that are associated with neurologic toxicity. Patients with symptoms consistent with PNS and without a known diagnosis of cancer should undergo workup for an underlying malignancy including history, physical exam, and imaging tests.4 If the malignancy is not detected by computed tomography (CT) scans, one option is the use of fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET).10 Classical Syndromes Syndromes that are commonly associated with underlying malignancy are called classical and include encephalomyelitis, limbic encephalitis, subacute cerebellar degeneration, opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome, sensory neuronopathy, chronic gastrointestinal pseudo-obstruction, Lambert-Eaton myasthenia syndrome (LEMS), and dermatomyositis. Encephalomyelitis is characterized by the involvement of several areas of the nervous system and is often associated with anti-Hu antibodies.4 The most commonly associated malignancy is SCLC. Limbic encephalitis is characterized by subacute onset of short-term memory loss, seizures, and cognitive decline.9 Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is abnormal in the majority of patients, with involvement of the temporal lobes, hypothalamus, and brain stem.4 Antineuronal antibodies include anti-Hu, anti-Ma2, anti- amphiphysin, and anti-CV2/CRMP5. The most commonly associated malignancy is SCLC. Subacute cerebellar degeneration typically presents with symptoms of ataxia, diplopia, dysphagia, and dysarthria. Typically, the first symptom is isolated gait ataxia, with subsequent development of truncal and hemispheric cerebellar dysfunction.7 MRI of the brain initially does not reveal any significant cerebellar atrophy. Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is a disorder of sodium and water balance characterized by a hypotonic euvolemic hyponatremia. The nonapeptide antidiuretic hormone (ADH), or arginine vasopressin (AVP), is synthesized in the hypothalamic magnocellular neurons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and stored in the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland. There are three known receptors for ADH at the cell membrane: V1a, V1b, and V2.22,23 V1a receptors are found in the vascular smooth muscle, uterus, platelets, and hepatocytes where the main functions include vasoconstriction, uterine contraction, platelet aggregation, and glycogenolysis, respectively. V1b receptors are located in the corticotroph cells of the anterior pituitary gland where they are involved in the release of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and β-endorphin. V2 receptors are located in the basolateral membrane of the renal collecting duct principal cells, vascular smooth muscle, and vascular endothelium, where they are involved in the synthesis and insertion of aquaporin 2 (AQP-2) channels into the apical membrane, vasodilation, and release of von Willebrand factor and factor VIII. Binding of ADH to the V2 receptor in the basolateral membrane of the collecting duct cells leads to activation of adenylate cyclase, with increased production of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), which in turn leads to activation of protein kinase A (PKA). PKA phosphorylates vesicles containing preformed AQP-2, leading to their movement to the apical membrane where AQP-2 is inserted and works as selective water-conducting channels according to the gradient from the tubular lumen to the medullary interstitium. V2 receptor activation also leads to increased synthesis of AQP-2. The water enters the cells through AQP-2 channels in the apical membrane and exits through the constitutively active aquaporin 3 (AQP-3) and aquaporin 4 (AQP-4) in the basolateral membrane. The two main stimuli for the ADH secretion are the increased plasma osmolality and decreased intravascular volume, which are regulated by the hypothalamic central sensing system and baroreceptors, respectively. Clinical euvolemia is defined as the absence of signs of volume depletion (dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, and orthostasis) caused by renal or extrarenal sodium loss or volume overload (edema and ascites) caused by renal failure, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, or heart failure. Patients with symptomatic acute hyponatremia should be treated with continuous intravenous infusion of hypertonic saline (3% NaCl) with a maximal correction rate of 8 to 12 mmol/L during the first 24 hours.35 It is estimated that an initial increase of plasma sodium of 5 mmol/L can reduce intracranial pressure and reverse the clinical signs of cerebral herniation.45 Therefore, a goal of a 4 to 5 mmol/L increase in the first 4 hours has been recently recommended. Patients with severe symptoms may be treated with a fixed bolus 3% NaCl regimen with 100 mL over 10 minutes or 150 mL over 20 minutes, up to three times as needed.46 Patients with known cardiovascular disease should receive 20 to 40 mg of intravenous furosemide to avoid volume overload. The main goal of therapy is to achieve safe serum levels with symptomatic relief, rather than completely normal levels. Therefore, acute treatment can be discontinued once the symptoms are resolved, a safe serum sodium usually defined as ≥120 mmol/L is reached, or the total magnitude of correction reaches 18 mmol/L. Dr. AVR @ TMH 123 Autologous Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation Hillard M. Lazarus, Mehdi Hamadani, and Parameswaran N. Hari INTRODUCTION Many decades ago, researchers determined that bone marrow cells transplanted from one animal to another could restore blood production.1 As these preclinical investigations were taken into the clinical arena, hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) evolved as a potentially curative modality for selected malignant and certain nonmalignant diseases. Many malignancies show a steep dose-response curve to cytotoxic therapy (i.e., small increments in dose of drug or radiation markedly increase the number of cancer cells killed). Cure or effective disease control depends on delivering intensive doses of chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy. This intensity often exceeds the tolerance of bone marrow, necessitating restoration of hematopoietic marrow function in such patients to prevent irreversible and fatal marrow aplasia. This is accomplished by restoring blood production using either autologous (“self”) cells (i.e., autologous HCT) or cells collected from another individual (i.e., allogeneic) donor cells (i.e., allogeneic HCT). Autologous HCT depends entirely on high-dose therapy to eradicate malignancy, in contrast to allogeneic HCT in which the immunocompetent infused cells exert an “allogeneic effect” against the tumor (i.e., graft-versus-tumor effect). The phases of autologous HCT include collection of autologous hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) and their cryopreservation; administration of high-dose therapy (also called conditioning or preparative regimen); thawing and intravenous administration of the autologous cells; and then vigorous supportive care including antibiotics, blood transfusions, and other measures such as electrolyte replacement while awaiting recovery of hematopoiesis. Careful patient selection is crucial to successful outcomes after autologous HCT. Patients with poor performance status (Karnofsky performance score ≤60) or significant comorbidities (e.g., poor cardiac reserve [left ventricular ejection fraction <40%], compromised pulmonary function [forced expiratory volume in 1 second and/or adjusted diffusion capacity <40% of predicted normal], advanced renal insufficiency) are not suitable candidates for high-dose therapies. Similarly heavily pretreated and chemotherapy-refractory patients are un

colony-stimulating factor either alone (“cytokine only” strategy) or in combination with chemotherapy agents such as cyclophosphamide (“chemomobilization” strategy). Another agent, plerixafor, works by disrupting the chemokine receptor type 4 and stromal-derived factor tether between the HPCs and the marrow stromal cells. Most patients have an adequate amount of HPCs collected after one or two apheresis procedures. Prior chemotherapy or radiation therapy can impair mobilization, which may affect HPC collection strategy. AUTOLOGOUS HEMATOPOIETIC CELL TRANSPLANTATION TOXICITIES AND SUPPORTIVE CARE Specific regimens used for high-dose therapy vary depending on the indication for HCT and are discussed in coming sections in detail. HPCs infused after high-dose therapy require time to regenerate hematopoiesis; during this time, the patient requires intensive supportive care to prevent complications arising from prolonged cytopenias and organ damage induced by conditioning regimen. Breakdown of the normal mucosal barriers in the gastrointestinal tract leading to oral mucositis, pain, diarrhea, and increased susceptibility to infectious complications is common. Hematopoietic recovery takes approximately 2 to 3 weeks, and recombinant hematopoietic growth factor support early after HPC infusion can reduce the duration of severe neutropenia by 2 to 4 days. Red blood cell and platelet transfusions are essential to prevent or treat complications and symptoms of profound cytopenias. All blood products must be irradiated to prevent inadvertent engraftment of “contaminating” allogeneic lymphocytes from the transfused unit that may cause lethal transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease. Major infections encountered in autologous HCT are due to gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria (e.g., Clostridium difficile toxin–associated diarrhea), herpes simplex virus, and fungi, particularly Candida and Aspergillus species. The use of prophylactic antibacterial, antiviral, and antifungal agents; recombinant hematopoietic growth factors; and blood HPCs has decreased the incidence of severe infections. Other common and reversible toxicities include nausea, vomiting, alopecia, poor appetite, rash, edema, and flushing.2 Figure 123.1 Causes of death after autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (U.S. data, 2011 to 2015). Indications for Autologous Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation The predominant indication for autologous HCT is the treatment of cancer, although it is sometimes performed for nonmalignant diseases (Fig. 123.2). This chapter focuses on the oncologic indications of autologous HCT. AUTOLOGOUS HEMATOPOIETIC CELL TRANSPLANTATION FOR PLASMA CELL MYELOMA In the United States, myeloma and other plasma cell disorders are the most common indication for autologous HCT (Figs. 123.3 and 123.4). Two large randomized trials in the 1990s3,4 and four others5–8 from the modern era of myeloma therapy have demonstrated the efficacy of autologous HCT in prolonging event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS) (in four of these studies) compared with a variety of nontransplant therapies. Nonrandomized comparisons and meta-analyses have confirmed the EFS advantage and the importance of an HCT-based intensification in eligible patients for sustaining initial remissions.9,10 The majority of autologous HCTs for myeloma are performed in newly diagnosed patients after induction therapy (early or upfront HCT). Because myeloma is incurable, even patients who do not receive an upfront autograft may undergo HCT at relapse (delayed autologous HCT). Similarly, those who have benefited from an upfront autograft may receive a second autologous HCT after a subsequent relapse (sometimes referred to as a salvage second autologous HCT). Figure 123.2 Indications for autologous transplantation in the United States. MM, multiple myeloma; NHL, non-Hodgkin lymphoma; HL, Hodgkin lymphoma; AML, acute myeloid leukemia; ALL, acute lymphoblastic leukemia; CLL, chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

Figure 123.3 Survival after autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation in myeloma. Autologous Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation for Myeloma: The Pre–Novel Agent Era The Intergroupe Francophone Myeloma (IFM) and Medical Research Council led randomized clinical trials comparing autologous HCT to the then available conventional chemotherapy in newly diagnosed patients and demonstrated that patients randomized to receive autologous HCT had significantly higher complete remission (CR), EFS, and OS rates compared with traditional alkylating agent–based chemotherapy. Other randomized studies from this period failed to demonstrate an OS benefit, although most showed an improvement in EFS. A randomized French study Myeloma Auto Greffe 95 (MAG 95) reported comparable OS between early versus delayed autologous HCT.11 In general, the early studies indicated that an upfront autologous HCT (immediately after initial therapy) improved CR rates and EFS, whereas OS benefit was not readily apparent in studies that permitted or planned for delayed autologous HCT. Many clinicians therefore used the so-called “collect and hold” approach of harvesting autologous HPC in first remission with an intent to transplant at relapse. Autologous Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation for Myeloma: The Modern Era In the two-decade period since IFM 90, several classes of new drugs with considerable single-agent activity emerged, most notably the immunomodulatory drugs (thalidomide, lenalidomide, pomalidomide), proteasome inhibitors (bortezomib, carfilzomib, ixazomib), and monoclonal antibodies (daratumumab). These “novel” agents in doublet or triplet combinations used as initial induction therapy for multiple myeloma have resulted in excellent CR rates comparable to those of HCT recipients. Modern clinical trials therefore readdressed the role of HCT in the setting of novel agent–based induction. Data from three published studies and one presentation are available.5–8 These trials were designed with the study patients receiving novel agent induction followed by an early HCT versus HPC collection followed by nontransplant consolidation and late autologous HCT at relapse among controls (Table 123.1). All four of these trials demonstrated an EFS benefit for upfront HCT. The multicenter trials RV-MM-209 and EMN-441 used the doublet induction of lenalidomide plus dexamethasone followed by tandem H

Dr. AVR @ TMH 84% for the early HCT cohort versus 70% for the nontransplant cohort.12 Figure 123.4 Survival after autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation in common B-cell non- Hodgkin lymphoma subtypes. In the IFM 2009 study, patients received three cycles of lenalidomide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (RVD) triplet induction followed by randomization to upfront versus delayed HCT. In the upfront HCT arm, autologous HCT was followed by two cycles of RVD consolidation and subsequently lenalidomide maintenance for 1 year. Patients in the delayed HCT arm underwent HPC cryopreservation followed by five additional cycles of RVD consolidation and lenalidomide maintenance. At 44 months of follow-up, the study indicated a significant EFS benefit for the upfront HCT arm, although with no survival advantage.8 Another study (EMN02-HOVON95) by the European Myeloma Network (EMN) and Hemato-Oncologie voor Volwassenen Nederland (HOVON) randomized patients after initial induction therapy with bortezomib plus cyclophosphamide and dexamethasone to upfront HCT (single or tandem) versus chemotherapy consolidation with four cycles of bortezomib, melphalan (MEL), and prednisone. Results presented in abstract form indicate that the 3-year EFS was superior for the transplant arm (66% versus 57.5% in the nontransplant arm; P = .003) with no OS difference. In conclusion, even in the era of combination novel agent therapies as induction, EFS benefit from an early autologous HCT has been redemonstrated across multiple large randomized studies. Longer follow-up will be necessary for OS results to mature. Notably, the majority of patients in the nontransplant arms of these studies proceeded to delayed HCT at relapse, indicating the importance of early HPC collection after induction. Novel agent–based triplet induction, frontline early autologous HCT, and maintenance therapy currently remain a preferred standard of care for transplant-eligible patients with myeloma. Conditioning Regimens for Autologous Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation in Myeloma A randomized phase III trial evaluating conditioning regimens for MM compared intravenous MEL 200 mg/m2 (MEL200) to a combination of MEL 140 mg/m2 (MEL140) and 8 Gy of total-body irradiation (TBI). The MEL140-TBI regimen caused significantly more mucositis, delayed hematologic recovery, and resulted in higher

transfusion requirements and longer hospitalization, whereas the OS and EFS were similar. Current Center for International Blood and Marrow Transplant Research (CIBMTR) data indicate that most centers (>90%) use MEL200 as conditioning therapy for myeloma. An attempt to dose reduce MEL to 100 mg/m2 (intermediate-dose MEL) was not associated with a meaningful reduction in TRM and resulted in shorter EFS.13 Numerous studies have proposed combining agents such as busulfan, bortezomib, carfilzomib, and bendamustine with MEL140 or MEL200, but none of these regimens is currently standard. A new propylene glycol–free formulation of intravenous MEL was approved in the United States in 2016, although head-to-head clinical comparisons with older formulations of MEL are lacking. MEL200 is associated with severe toxicity, and a MEL dose of 140 mg/m2 is preferred.18 In the context of renal failure, residual dimethyl sulfoxide in the thawed HPC infusion can cause toxicity, including histamine release, abdominal pain, hypotension, and worsening renal function, which can be mitigated by washing the HPC product.19 MAINTENANCE THERAPY AFTER HEMATOPOIETIC CELL TRANSPLANTATION Various consolidation and maintenance strategies have been evaluated to delay the inevitable progression or relapse of myeloma after autologous HCT. Thalidomide maintenance after tandem autologous HCT has been studied in several randomized studies but has been replaced by lenalidomide maintenance due to better tolerability and superior efficacy data. Both the Cancer and Leukemia Group B 100104 and IFM 05-02 trials20,21 demonstrated a superior progression-free survival (PFS) and EFS with lenalidomide maintenance, whereas the Cancer and Leukemia Group B 100104 trial also demonstrated an OS benefit, which has now been sustained at long-term follow-up.22 A meta-analysis that pooled individual patient–level data from 1,811 patients from lenalidomide maintenance (versus placebo) studies indicated a 25% risk reduction in the risk of mortality and a median EFS of 52.8 months for recipients of maintenance therapy (versus 23.5 months for controls). A two- to threefold increase in second primary malignancies has been observed with lenalidomide maintenance and was confirmed by the meta-analysis. Based on these data, the risks and benefits of lenalidomide maintenance should be discussed with autologous HCT recipients. Numerous other approaches to post-HCT therapy are being studied in myeloma, including newer maintenance, consolidation, and tandem HCT. TANDEM AUTOLOGOUS HEMATOPOIETIC CELL TRANSPLANTATION Barlogie and coworkers pioneered the tandem autologous transplant approach in their Total Therapy program, which involved multiple applications of high-dose MEL and HPC support.10 The IFM 94 randomized trial compared single versus tandem autologous HCT in patients with previously untreated myeloma and demonstrated superior 7-year EFS and OS benefits for the tandem autologous HCT arm (10% versus 20% for EFS, and 21% versus 42% for OS, sin

UNIQUE CONSIDERATIONS FOR HEMATOPOIETIC PROGENITOR CELL COLLECTION IN MYELOMA In patients with myeloma who are autologous HCT candidates, it is important to avoid upfront factors that impair HPC mobilization (e.g., MEL-based induction regimens, prolonged use of lenalidomide, and radiation therapy to significant volume of bone marrow). The availability of plerixafor has improved mobilization yields in difficult- to-mobilize patients with myeloma, and international consensus guidelines have been developed for rational mobilization choices.27 Given the increasing use of salvage autologous HCT after relapse, it is prudent to target collection of ≥6 to 10 million CD34+ cells per kilogram in order to obtain adequate product for at least two transplants. There seems to be no additional antimyeloma benefit for the use of chemotherapy in mobilization.28 SALVAGE SECOND OR THIRD TRANSPLANTS AT RELAPSE Salvage second autologous HCT is an option at relapse after a prior transplant and appears to especially benefit those with a long (>24 to 36 months) remission from their first transplant.29 Cook et al.30 treated patients in first relapse with bortezomib-based reinduction followed by randomization to salvage second HCT versus oral cyclophosphamide. Salvage HCT consolidation after reinduction was associated with superior OS (67 versus 52 months; P = .017) in this study. FUTURE DIRECTIONS IN AUTOLOGOUS HEMATOPOIETIC CELL TRANSPLANTATION FOR MYELOMA Recent advances in supportive care have made autologous HCT relatively safe and cost effective. Current (2010 to 2015) CIBMTR data suggest a day 100 mortality of <1% in upfront HCT for myeloma. Median cost for autologous HCT in the United States is approximately $100,000 U.S. dollars and largely represents the cost of hospitalization. Autologous HCT can be entirely performed in the outpatient setting with excellent results and lower costs. Current directions being explored in HCT for myeloma include changes to conditioning regimens and novel maintenance or consolidation strategies that aim to induce deeper minimal residual disease–negative responses; at the same time, pretransplantation induction strategies continue to improve. For patients who relapse after HCT, there is increasing interest in second salvage HCT followed by additional maintenance. Conventional and Novel Conditioning Regimens Commonly used conditioning regimens for lymphomas include cyclophosphamide, etoposide, and carmustine; carmustine, etoposide, cytarabine, and MEL (BEAM); carmustine, etoposide, cytarabine, and cyclophosphamide; and TBI-containing regimens. TRM is generally lower and survival superior outcomes after TBI-free conditioning. Several uncontrolled studies have reported efficacy and feasibility of combining rituximab with high-dose therapy, but convincing randomized evidence for this approach is lacking. RIT with monoclonal antibody–radionuclide conjugates is effective in B-cell NHL. Incorporation of RIT into pre–autologous HCT conditioning has been studied, either alone or in combination with high-dose therapy. In the BMT CTN 0401 trial, iodine-131 tositumomab was prospectively compared against rituximab, both in combination with BEAM conditioning for relapsed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Another European study compared BEAM plus yttrium-90 ibritumomab tiuxetan with BEAM alone in aggressive NHL. Neither study favored a RIT-based conditioning regimen (reviewed in Kharfan-Dabaja et al.33). Disease-Specific Indications for Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation in Lymphomas The indications of autologous HCT in lymphoid neoplasia are dependent on patient age, comorbidities, chemosensitivity, histologic subtype, and remission status at the time of HCT. HEMATOPOIETIC CELL TRANSPLANTATION FOR FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA First Remission The role of autologous HCT as consolidation for advanced-stage follicular lymphoma (FL) in first remission was examined in four randomized trials, including three trials conducted in the prerituximab era34–36 and one in the rituximab era37 (Table 123.2). Autologous HCT provided a PFS benefit in three of these four trials. OS, however, was not improved as this therapy was associated with a higher risk of second malignancies, including myelodysplastic syndrome/acute myeloid leukemia (AML). With the advent of rituximab maintenance or retreatment and a myriad of targeted therapies, the routine use of upfront HCT consolidation in FL is not recommended.
