Berger INTRODUCTION Effectiveness of cancer treatment modalities designed to increase cure rates and to extend disease-free survival and survival time, including chemotherapy (CT), radiation therapy (RT), and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), is tempered by treatment-related side effects and associated symptoms as well as impaired health-related quality of life (HRQOL). Oral complications are one such side effect category that includes oral mucositis; oral chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD); and associated oropharyngeal pain, xerostomia, and oral infection. Pathogenesis of and management strategies for these oral complications and future clinical research directions are presented in this chapter. ORAL MUCOSITIS Oral mucositis is an inflammation of the mucous membranes of the oral cavity and oropharynx characterized by tissue erythema, edema, and atrophy, often progressing to ulceration.1 The clinical significance of CT- and RT- related oral mucositis as a dose- and treatment-limiting side effect is related to pain and impairment in a patient’s HRQOL and functional status.2–4 Oral mucositis presents clinically with asymptomatic erythema and progresses from solitary, white, elevated desquamative patches that are mildly painful to large, contiguous, pseudomembranous, painful ulcers. Clinical oral sequelae of stomatogenic CT agents’ mechanism of action typically include epithelial hyperplasia, collagen and glandular degeneration, epithelial dysplasia, atrophy, and localized or diffuse mucosal ulceration. Nonkeratinized mucosal areas are most affected. The loss of basement membrane epithelial cells exposes underlying connective, innervated tissue stroma, which contributes to more severe oropharyngeal pain. Healing of oral lesions in nonmyelosuppressed patients occurs 2 to 3 weeks after cancer treatment, with decrease in oropharyngeal pain seen in parallel with mucosal healing. The frequency and severity of oral mucositis are influenced by patient- and treatment-related risk factors (Table 129.1).5,6 Risk factors for CT-related oral mucositis are complex. Although women have reported more frequent severe oral mucositis than men and children are three times more likely than adults to develop mucositis, Driezen7 reported no age or gender risk for this oral condition. Chemotherapy-Induced Mucositis Approximately 40% of patients receiving CT develop oral mucositis,11 and approximately half of these patients develop painful oral lesions requiring parenteral analgesia or total parenteral nutrition (TPN) and CT treatment type or dose modification.12 Oral mucositis and ulcerative oral mucositis incidence rates of 60% and 78%, respectively, are seen in the HSCT setting.13 Importantly, oral mucositis is a risk factor for life-threatening infections in neutropenic patients. Oral infections, such as herpes simplex virus (HSV), may increase oral mucositis severity. There is a reported four times greater relative risk of septicemia in patients with oral mucositis and oral infections due to mucosal barrier injury. The relationship between severe oral mucositis and clinical outcomes in patients who receive conditioning CT has been reported.14,15 McCann et al.14 conducted an observational study in 197 patients with multiple myeloma (MM) or non-Hodgkin lymphoma treated with either high-dose melphalan or BEAM CT, respectively. RADIATION THERAPY–RELATED COMPLICATIONS Long-term effects of RT delivered to the head and neck include soft tissue fibrosis, trismus, nonhealing or slow- healing mucosal ulcerations, and slow-healing dental extraction sites. RT-induced fibrotic changes may occur in the masticatory muscles or the temporal mandibular joint up to 1 year after RT. Early phases of fibrogenesis after RT are observed as wound healing characterized by upregulation of tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α and other proinflammatory cytokines.20 As RT-related fibrogenesis continues, it functions as a nonhealing wound.20 Osteoradionecrosis is a relatively uncommon condition related to hypocellularity, hypovascularity, and tissue ischemia. Higher incidences are reported with total doses to the bone exceeding 65 Gy.21 Osteoradionecrosis is usually related to trauma and is reported following tooth extractions not timed to allow extraction site healing for 10 to 14 days before the start of RT. Osteonecrosis of the jaw bone is strongly associated with bisphosphonate use.22,23 PATHOGENESIS OF CHEMOTHERAPY- AND RADIATION THERAPY– INDUCED ORAL MUCOSITIS Current understanding of oral mucositis pathogenesis is being informed by translational research that applies advances in molecular-genetic techniques and cell biology to this oral condition.24 Cancer therapy affects rapidly dividing cells including oral basal epithelium with a 7- to 14-day cell turnover rate, thus placing these cells at risk for CT targeting. Sonis et al.25 reported a “burst” of cyclooxygenase (COX)-2 expression observed with RT- related oral mucositis progression, suggesting that COX-2 plays an amplifying role. CHRONIC GRAFT-VERSUS-HOST DISEASE ORAL MANIFESTATIONS Patients who have undergone allogeneic HSCT (alloHSCT) frequently develop graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), an alloimmune condition derived from an immune attack mediated by donor T cells recognizing antigens expressed on normal tissues. GVHD occurs following alloHSCT due to disparities in minor histocompatibility antigens between donor and recipient, inherited independently of human leukocyte antigen (HLA) genes.30 Systemic corticosteroids are the primary treatment for cGVHD. In 2017, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the use of ibrutinib (Imbruvica) for the treatment of cGVHD in adult patients after failure of one or more systemic treatment strategies.31 cGVHD was historically defined as occurring >100 days after HSCT32 and is now classified based on characteristic clinical presentation. cGVHD is reported to occur in 30% to 60% of patients 100 days after alloHSCT.33 Approximately 80% of patients with extensive cGVHD have oral involvement,34 which is a major contributing factor to patient morbidity seen with alloHSCT. Although oral lesions are most commonly seen with extensive cGVHD organ involvement, patients may also present with only oral cGVHD, thus making comprehensive oral assessment important. Oral cGVHD presents with tissue atrophy and erythema, lichenoid changes, angular stomatitis, pseudomembranous ulcerations that occur typically on buccal and labial mucosa and the lateral tongue, and xerostomia.34 Treister et al.35 correlated the distribution, type, and extent of oral cGVHD lesions with oral pain and discomfort. The buccal and labial mucosa and tongue were the most frequently observed oral sites of ulcerations (93%), erythematous lesions (72%), and reticular lesions (76%). Ulcerations in the soft palate, although uncommon, were associated with increased pain intensity. Functional impact was significant with restriction of oral intake due to discomfort. SEQUELAE OF ORAL COMPLICATIONS Oropharyngeal Pain Oral mucositis is the principal etiology of most pain experienced during the 3-week post-BMT time period. Patients have described this oral pain as the most unforgettable ordeal of BMT. McGuire et al.42 reported in a sample of patients undergoing autologous and allogeneic BMT that oral pain was reported before observed oral mucositis, that pain intensity did not correlate directly with extent of mucosal injury, and that some patients reported limited or no pain after BMT. A descriptive, cross-sectional study of women with breast cancer undergoing autologous HSCT conducted by Fall-Dickson et al.43 showed a significant positive correlation between oral pain intensity and oral mucositis severity. The sensory dimension of oral mucositis–related pain reported with general mucosal inflammation and breakdown ranges from mild discomfort to severe and debilitating pain requiring opioids.44 Oral pain is associated strongly with cGVHD and has been described as severe, burning, and irritating with dryness and loss of taste. Mucositis-related oral pain reported with CT usually lasts <3 months, in contrast with the usually chronic oral pain accompanying oral cGVHD. Gender differences have been reported for oral mucositis–related pain. Women reported higher pain intensity scores in a study examining capsaicin efficacy for oral mucositis–related pain. Pain management is critical to avoid suffering and psychological distress.45 Adequate assessment of oral pain requires a comprehensive pain assessment tool such as the Painometer (Dola Health Systems, Baltimore, MD),46 which assesses overall intensity, sensory, and affective dimensions of pain. Xerostomia Xerostomia is a major clinical problem experienced by patients who receive head and neck RT, with severity dependent on RT dosage and volume of exposed salivary glands. Patients may also develop xerostomia as a late oral complication of HSCT. Brand et al.47 reported in a cross-sectional study of patients with a history of autologous HSCT or alloHSCT significantly higher levels of xerostomia than seen in the comparison group. Dr. AVR @ TMH COMPLICATIONS Pretherapy Dental Evaluation and Intervention Oral and dental stabilization prior to CT or RT is critically important to avoid serious sequelae and requires an experienced dental team and informed patients working together for appropriate oral hygiene and elimination of oral infection. Patients scheduled for CT or head and neck RT should undergo a dental screening to promote optimal mucosal health before, during, and after cancer treatment. Ideally, this should occur at least 2 weeks before therapy starts to allow for recovery from soft tissue manipulations, restoration of teeth, and proper healing of potential extraction sites. The initial dental appointment includes examination of dentition for caries and defective restorations, the periodontium, pulp vitality, and denture fit to avoid ill-fitting dentures causing irritation of irradiated tissue and ulceration to underlying bone.51,52 A panoramic radiograph combined with intraoral radiographs as needed is necessary to screen for periodontal disease, periapical infections, cysts, third-molar pathology, unerupted or partially erupted teeth, and residual root tips. Dental caries, repair of defective restorations, removal of orthodontic appliances, remediation of ill-fitting prostheses and periapical or third molar pathologies need to be addressed before cancer treatment begins. Bacterial load should be reduced prior to cancer treatment via root planning, scaling, and prophylaxis, excluding visible tumor located at the site of anticipated dental manipulation. The decision to extract asymptomatic teeth prior to the commencement of RT is related to radiation exposure, type, portal field, fractionization, and total dosage in addition to tumor prognosis and expediency of control of the cancer.51,53 Teeth that are class II or III mobility without use as abutment teeth for prosthetic retention should also be considered for extraction before RT. Extractions of residual root tips and impacted teeth should be performed atraumatically. Alveolectomy and primary wound closure eliminate sharp ridges and bone spicules that could project to the overlying soft tissues. This is important for prosthetic consideration because negligible bone remodeling is anticipated after RT. Kaner INTRODUCTION Pulmonary disease can be caused by a wide spectrum of pathogenic mechanisms in patients with cancer. These include a variety of infectious agents and neoplastic disorders as well as pulmonary thromboembolic disease, pulmonary hemorrhage, pulmonary edema (cardiogenic and noncardiogenic), and leukocyte agglutinin reactions. Pulmonary toxicity caused by antineoplastic agents is being recognized more frequently, and the number of drugs known or suspected to cause lung disease is steadily increasing. Because continuing the offending agent may cause death and because withholding the agent may result in resolution of the pulmonary toxicity, it is important to recognize radiation- and drug-induced pulmonary disease. In this chapter, parenchymal lung disease caused by irradiation and chemotherapy is discussed. Mechanisms of lung injury, histopathologic findings, clinical and laboratory features, diagnosis, and treatment of the abnormalities produced by these agents are reviewed. RADIATION-INDUCED PULMONARY TOXICITY Mechanisms of Lung Injury and Histology Radiation can affect dividing and nondividing cells and can cause genetic and nongenetic damage. The first phase of radiation-induced lung injury (RILI) is the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species. These species cause oxidative damage to cellular proteins, lipids, and DNA. Nonlethal ionizing radiation also activates a stress response in cells, which leads to upregulation of specific nuclear transcription factors such as nuclear factor-κB and transcription of specific early response genes such as c- abl, c-jun, egr-1, and c-fos. This leads to sloughing and denudation of type I pneumocytes, which make up 90% of alveolar epithelium, whereas type II pneumocytes proliferate in an effort to replace dying type I cells. In addition to pneumocyte injury, capillary endothelial cells are also injured, leading to the loss of barrier function. This microvessel damage leads to ongoing tissue hypoxia as well as chronic inflammation. The second phase of RILI includes inflammation in response to injury. Abnormalities in the intermediate stage (2 to 9 months after radiation) are characterized by obstruction of pulmonary capillaries by platelets, fibrin, and collagen. Alveolar-l

Furthermore, isolevuglandin-mediated adduction of collagen 1α1 impaired its degradation by matrix metalloproteinase-1, suggesting that adduction may diminish resolution of established fibrosis occurring after radiation. New evidence also points to a dysregulated radiation-induced IL-13 response that activates profibrotic macrophages, resulting in fibrosis.4 Indeed, modulation of IL-13 has been successful in alleviating fibrosis that results from many pathogenic stimuli, including irradiation in animal models. Impairment of the regulation of the inflammatory response is thought to contribute to late RILI. Although bronchiolitis obliterans with organizing pneumonia (BOOP) is an unusual histopathologic pattern for cancer therapy–related lung injury, radiation damage resulting in BOOP has been reported.5 The last stage of RILI is characterized by a process of repair. These cellular changes include capillary regeneration and alveolar epithelium repopulation by type II cells as well as fibrosis, a process that is dominated by TGF-β release. Activation of latent TGF-β in the extracellular space by radiation, ROS and reactive nitrogen species, and cell death–associated molecule patterns allows dissociated TGF-β to bind to cell surface receptors and activate downstream SMAD signaling, which mediates transcription of genes involved in fibroblast function, differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis. Several cytokines mediate chemoattraction of fibroblasts and recruitment of myofibroblast precursors from the circulation followed by differentiation into myofibroblasts as well as direct epithelial to mesenchymal transition. If the initial injury is severe, damage to extracellular matrix components of the lung, such as basement membrane glycoproteins and proteoglycans, takes place. Due to previous damage from the first phase of RILI, endothelial cells are unable to respond fully to VEGF and continue to die. Hypoxia is thought to be an important component of chronic injury. If the radiation injury is mild, these changes may subside entirely; however, when the injury is severe, a chronic phase (≥9 months after radiation) ensues that may persist or progress for months or years. Clinical Features Signs and Symptoms The clinical syndrome of radiation pneumonitis develops in 5% to 15% of patients receiving high-dose external- beam radiation for treatment of lung cancer. No significant difference is seen in the incidence of radiation pneumonitis between the young and elderly, but the pneumonitis is inclined to be more severe in the latter. Underlying chronic obstructive pulmonary disease does not appear to potentiate radiation damage. Symptoms of acute radiation pneumonitis usually become evident 2 to 3 months after the completion of therapy; rarely, they occur within the first month and occasionally as late as 6 months after irradiation. Early onset of symptoms often implies a more serious and more protracted clinical course. The cardinal symptom of radiation pneumonitis is dyspnea. It may be self-limited or progress to severe respiratory distress. Patients may also have a nonproductive cough or a cough productive of small amounts of pinkish sputum. Frank hemoptysis early in the clinical course is distinctly uncommon. Fever is unusual but can be high and spiking; in severe cases, other constitutional symptoms may occur. Chest pain, which is rarely a prominent feature, may be due to fractured ribs, pleural changes, or coughing. Symptoms of airway obstruction can occur in the first few days of radiation therapy and are usually associated with swelling of a central bronchogenic carcinoma. Hemoptysis and other manifestations of radiation pneumonitis may also occur in patients given palliative endobronchial brachytherapy or after surgical implantation of radioactive seeds. Whereas dyspnea is the hallmark of radiation-induced pneumonitis, fever and cough are the predominant features of radiation-related BOOP. On physical examination, signs of pulmonary involvement are minimal. Occasionally, rales, a pleural friction rub, or evidence of pleural fluid may be heard over the area of irradiation. In severe cases, tachypnea and cyanosis may be present, and occasionally, evidence of acute cor pulmonale appears, usually predicting a fatal outcome. Finger clubbing due to radiation is distinctly unusual and is

Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) changes can differ from those of standard radiation therapy; however, lung toxicity is rare due to the small fields. Several different patterns of early (acute pneumonitis) and late changes (fibrosis) have been described, including GGOs, consolidations, and patchy or diffuse patterns, as well as late bronchiectasis and scar formation.8 Due to the hypofractionated dose of radiation used in stereotactic radiotherapy and the delivery of radiation in a spherical volume with a gradient between the high dose and the low dose within normal adjacent tissue, the shape of the SBRT-induced injury mimics the tumor and does not have a linear pattern that may be seen with conventional radiation therapy. Similar to conventional therapy, late fibrosis may develop after 6 to 9 months without a preceding acute pneumonitis. Pulmonary Function Tests Prediction of changes in pulmonary function after high-dose irradiation to the lung has proven to be problematic. No gross physiologic changes occur in the lung until 4 to 8 weeks after completion of irradiation, usually coincident with the period of clinical pneumonitis. Then, there is a decrease in lung volumes, which can progress. These changes persist indefinitely, with little evidence of recovery. Small changes in spirometric values and gas exchange abnormalities, which include a decrease in diffusing capacity and arterial hypoxemia, especially with exercise, occur at approximately the same time but show some tendency toward recovery after 6 to 12 months. A fall in compliance coincident with the clinical pneumonitis is seen in most subjects. Accordingly, the elastic work of breathing is increased, and dyspnea, resulting from the increased workload, ensues. Airflow parameters remain close to normal in most studies. Diagnosis The diagnosis of radiation pneumonitis can sometimes be made clinically based on the timing of irradiation in relation to symptoms and the typical chest radiographic appearance (i.e., infiltrates corresponding to the margins of the irradiated portal). CHEMOTHERAPY-INDUCED PULMONARY TOXICITY The list of chemotherapeutic agents reported to cause cytotoxic drug-induced lung disease continues to grow. The true incidence of toxicity is unknown, but the reported frequency of pulmonary toxicity ranges from 10% to 30%. Distinguishing lung toxicity from other factors affecting the lung such as pulmonary edema, infection, lymphangitic carcinomatosis, and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage is very challenging. With the development of targeted monoclonal antibodies used in cancer treatment, new toxicities are continuously being reported. Mechanism of Pulmonary Injury and Histopathology Except for a few chemotherapeutic drugs (e.g., bleomycin), the details of the pathophysiology of lung injury are unknown. Various mechanisms of pulmonary toxicity have been proposed based on the mechanism of action of different classes of chemotherapeutic agents. These include a direct toxic effect on alveolar epithelial cells, the induction of an inflammatory immunologic response, and endothelial cell injury or activation causing capillary leak syndrome. These events can result in a variety of clinical presentations including nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis, hypersensitivity reaction syndrome, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (capillary leak syndrome), infusion reaction, eosinophilic pneumonia, organizing pneumonias, bronchospasm, acute lung injury (diffuse alveolar damage), and fibrosis. One of the potential determinants of bleomycin toxicity is the bleomycin hydrolase, which is the major enzyme responsible for metabolizing bleomycin to a nontoxic molecule. Interestingly, the two organs that are the most common targets for bleomycin toxicity (lung and skin) have the lowest levels of the enzyme. Studies are needed to determine if genetic variability of this enzyme accounts for individual susceptibility or immunity to bleomycin pulmonary toxicity in humans, as it does in animals. Because the lung is exposed to many substances that can activate its immune system, there appears to be a pulmonary immune tolerance state to avoid overreactions. This tolerance state may be part of an effector and suppressor cell balance. Cytotoxic drugs can alter the normal balance, which may cause tissue damage. For example, lymphocytic alveolitis is a consistent finding in methotrexate pneumonitis, with an imbalance of the CD4+ to CD8+ ratio.58 Bronchoalveolar lavage studies in patients with methotrexate pulmonary toxicity have shown the presence of T lymphocytic alveolitis, whereas studies on some patients with bleomycin toxicity have shown a polymorphonuclear alveolitis.58,59 Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) is also implicated in pulmonary toxicity through its effect on neutrophil activation. G-CSF toxicity is thought to be secondary to activation of inflammatory pathways and ROS within the neutrophils, causing pulmonary edema and acute respiratory distress syndrome.60 IL-2, used to treat metastatic melanoma and renal cell cancer, stimulates the immune system by stimulating CD4+ T cells and increasing natural killer cell activity. These effects likely contribute to a generalized inflammatory state, contributing to the capillary leak syndrome and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema associated with this drug. IL-2 has also been shown to directly increase endothelial permeability and indirectly increases vascular leak by increasing cytokine levels, particularly TNF-α, leukocyte adhesion, and inflammation, and altering the extracellular matrix. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), although generally well tolerated, can cause serious pulmonary toxicity. EGFR inhibitors are some of the newer molecular targeted chemotherapies including gefitinib and erlotinib. Treatment The most effective way to manage pulmonary toxicity associated with a chemotherapeutic agent is to prevent it. Animal studies of bleomycin toxicity showed a beneficial preventative effect of dietary supplementation with taurine and niacin; no comparable human studies have been reported. G-CSF should be discontinued as soon as the leukocyte level reaches >1,000 cells/μL. Hypersensitivity reactions can be mitigated with the administration of steroids and H2 receptor blockers prior to dosing. If toxicity occurs, withdrawing the offending agent is the cornerstone of therapy. Although no controlled studies in humans have systematically examined the effectiveness of corticosteroids, a trial of these agents is probably warranted in most cases. The optimal dose and duration of therapy are not known; however, 1 mg/kg/day is usually initiated with a slow and careful tapering schedule because clinical deterioration after tapering has been reported. The use of lung transplant in the treatment of advanced lung-induced pulmonary fibrosis should be considered in appropriate patients. Lunning INTRODUCTION Chemotherapy, monoclonal antibodies, targeted therapy, and radiotherapy (RT) may have deleterious effects on the cardiovascular system.1,2 Within these categories exist agents that have well-described cardiotoxicity: chemotherapeutics (anthracyclines, alkylators, taxanes, fluoropyrimidines), targeted therapy, and monoclonal antibodies. Each are discussed in detail. A more comprehensive list is shown in Table 131.1. The effects of RT on the cardiovascular system are detailed in a later section. CHEMOTHERAPEUTICS Anthracyclines Reversible acute cardiotoxicity and delayed irreversible dilated cardiomyopathy (CM) are not common with the use of anthracyclines. When discovered, reversible acute toxicity presents as a myocarditis and occasionally with evidence of pericarditis and may lead to nonischemic CM (NICM) with or without concomitant arrhythmias. The acute toxicity is rarely a fatal complication of anthracycline therapy. To reduce the incidence and/or severity of delayed CM, keen clinical recognition of factors that may lead toward a NICM includes monitoring cumulative dose (CD) of anthracycline used, early detection strategies, limiting total CD, use of adjunctive cardioprotective agents, and use of modified infusional or pegylated regimens or drugs. The risk of anthracycline-induced CM depends on CD received. Historically, a 5% risk of CM is seen at 400 to 450 mg/m2 for doxorubicin, 900 mg/m2 for daunorubicin, 800 to 935 mg/m2 for epirubicin, and 223 mg/m2 for idarubicin.3 Cofactors for cardiotoxic risk include mediastinal irradiation fields encompassing the myocardium, older (particularly older than 70 years) or younger (younger than 15 years) age, known coronary artery disease, antecedent valvular disease, and hypertension. Concurrent monoclonal antibodies (i.e., human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 [HER2] antibodies) appear to potentiate anthracycline-induced CM, whereas other chemotherapeutic agents may have independent or synergistic cardiac effects when used in combination. The diagnosis of an NICM in the setting of a history of anthracycline exposure is made by comparing serial left ventricular function studies. Several modalities can be used, including multigated radionuclide imaging (multigated acquisition scan [MUGA]), two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (cMRI).4–6 Nevertheless, it is imperative that an ischemic CM be excluded. Regardless of the modality used, a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of ≥50% is within normal range. A threshold CD has not been identified below which left ventricular dysfunction is not seen.7 A low LVEF regardless of symptom burden remains a relative contraindication for bolus anthracycline use. Echocardiograms and cMRI can also evaluate other structural changes of the myocardium in the setting of CM. Typical progression of CM on serial imaging includes left ventricular diastolic dysfunction and, later, left ventricular systolic dysfunction, particularly affecting septal wall motion. Rather, the CM may become progressive despite these agents after more than 5 years. The only curative therapy if encountered remains cardiac transplantation. The mechanism of anthracycline CD is not fully elucidated, but there is emerging evidence that cardiomyocyte apoptosis may play a major role.20 The production of free radicals generated during cardiomyocyte metabolism of the anthracycline results in membrane lipid peroxidation, with the consequent activation of the extrinsic and intrinsic apoptotic pathways. It is thought that free radicals are generated by enzymatic reduction of the anthracycline quinone ring and by formation of iron–anthracycline complexes. The intrinsic antioxidant defense of the cardiomyocyte is more limited than other organs, leading to its apparent selective toxicity profile. A knockout mouse model has suggested that a deficiency of the HFE gene (associated with hereditary hemochromatosis) confers increased susceptibility to doxorubicin CD.21 The investigators studied wild-type, HFE (+/−), and HFE (−/−) mice that were chronically treated with doxorubicin. Survival was significantly decreased in the HFE-negative mice, and cardiac iron concentration was significantly elevated. The mechanism of fluoropyrimidine cardiotoxicity is not well understood. It is possibly related to vascular spasm in reaction to the parent drug and its catabolites (fluoro-β-alanine and fluoroacetate). In an in vitro model, 5-FU causes vasoconstriction in smooth muscle rings, which is reversible with nitrates.37 On electron microscopy, the changes appear to be in the small arterial endothelium.37 Coronary angiography after the 5-FU–induced angina did not reveal ongoing cardiac spasm, and in fact, on autopsy evaluation, patients were found to have myocarditis.38 Brachial artery ultrasound was performed prospectively in 60 patients receiving regimens containing 5-FU (n = 30) versus regimens not containing 5-FU (n = 30).39 Fifty percent of the patients showed artery contraction with 5-FU and none with other therapy. Interestingly, arterial tone recovered within 30 minutes but reoccurred with retreatment in a high proportion of patients. Pretreatment with glycerol trinitrate, a vasodilator, abrogated the contractions in five patients. Nevertheless, there is no known prophylactic regimen that can be provided to prevent the cardiotoxicity, and despite evidence to the contrary, vasodilators do not necessarily relieve the symptoms once apparent. As a result, the optimal treatment is discontinuation of the fluoropyrimidine infusion and supportive measures with keen attention toward likely myocardial damage, with available cardiac support.40 Nevertheless, a rechallenge strategy after cardiac toxicity after 5-FU has been reported.41 Monoclonal Antibodies Trastuzumab and Lapatinib Trastuzumab and lapatinib are humanized monoclonal antibodies that target p185HER2 (ErbB2 or HER2 receptor), a transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase of the epidermal growth factor family. CHD Although the pathologic and clinical manifestations of radiation-induced heart disease may overlap in many patients, they are discussed separately in the following paragraphs. Pericardial Disease Incidence The risk of radiation-induced pericardial disease depends on the dose given and on the volume of the heart irradiated.59 Even when a large volume of the heart (≥60%) is irradiated with ≤40 Gy, the risk for mild pericarditis is <5%, and severe pericarditis is rare. Smaller heart volumes (20% to 30%) may tolerate up to 60 Gy, with an expected 2% risk of mild pericarditis. In the past, when the whole pericardium was irradiated, the pericarditis incidence was 20%, but when most of the left ventricle was excluded, it was reduced to 7%.60 An updated analysis of these patients showed a sharp decrease in the risk of death from cardiac complications other than acute MI for patients who received mediastinal irradiation after 1972, reflecting the change in cardiac shielding.55 With current RT techniques for HL and breast cancer, pericarditis is an infrequent event. Acute Pericarditis during Radiation Acute pericarditis during the course of RT is rare. It is almost always associated with massive mediastinal tumors adjacent to the heart. The signs and symptoms are of acute nonspecific pericarditis with chest pain, fever, and often ECG abnormalities. It does not lead to a significant risk of late pericardial damage and is not an indication for interrupting the radiation course. Delayed Pericarditis Radiation-induced pericarditis typically occurs within the first year after mediastinal irradiation. The common range is from 4 months to several years after treatment.61 Pericardial disease presents as an acute pericarditis, as a pericardial effusion that may be asymptomatic, or as a combination of both. The symptoms of delayed acute pericarditis are indistinguishable from those of other types of pericarditis and usually consist of fever, pleuritic chest pain, pericardial friction rub, ST-T segment changes, and a decrease of the QRS voltage in the ECG. Pericardial effusion may be large and manifest as an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Most cases of radiation-induced pericarditis and pericardial effusion resolve spontaneously, usually within 16 months. Dr. AVR @ TMH 132 Hair Loss and Other Hair Changes Hoyoung M. Maeng and Ann M. Berger INTRODUCTION Hair is often a reflection of one’s identity. During many cancer treatments, hair can be adversely affected, which may lead to emotional trauma in both male and female patients. Even though alopecia has been ranked the third most common adverse event (AE) of cancer treatment, no official management guidelines or recommendations are present. Hair loss or alopecia can be an immense burden, serving as a stressful visible reminder of the patient’s disease and negatively impacting social function; it also results in a loss of privacy because it reveals the patient’s medical condition.1 In several health-related quality-of-life (HRQL) research, patients reported hair loss as a reason for the refusal of chemotherapy, and hair loss was reported as more difficult than losing the breast in some breast cancer patients.2,3 With the growing use of biologics and targeted agents such as monoclonal antibodies and tyrosine kinase inhibitors along with recent progress in immuno-oncology that has led to the use of several immune checkpoint inhibitors and adoptive cell therapies, more hair-related side effects have arisen, including issues related to not only hair loss but also quality and color. This chapter describes the general principle of evaluation and diagnosis of hair loss and attempts to decrease such adverse reactions followed by a review of cancer treatment–associated hair changes due to both conventional chemotherapy and newer noncytotoxic agents. ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF HAIR The hair follicle is divided into three parts, called the upper portion (infundibulum), the middle portion (isthmus), and the lower portion (bulb and suprabulb). The hair fiber is the product of the hair follicle that consists of the medulla, cortex, and hair cuticle (Fig. 132.1).4 Hair growth is cyclical. On average, the human scalp has 100,000 hair follicles, and each hair undergoes the hair growth cycle, which involves anagen (growth), telogen (regression), and catagen (rest) followed by exogen (shedding). For more than 90% of the cycle, hair is in the anagen phase when hair undergoes mitosis and rapid cell growth over 3 to 5 years at the speed of 0.3 mm per day. During anagen, the hair becomes most vulnerable to chemotherapy-induced alopecia due to the suppression of cell proliferation, maki

Figure 132.1 Anatomy and physiology of hair. More than 90% of the time, hair is in the anagen phase undergoing mitosis in the bulb and becomes vulnerable to chemotherapy-induced alopecia. However, quiescent stem cells that can reinstate the hair growth reside in the bulge, and cancer treatment damaging the stem cells or the bulge can cause potentially permanent and cicatricial hair loss. Melanocyte stem cells in the bulge migrate down to hair follicles during anagen to differentiate into melanocyte-producing melanin. CLASSIFICATION OF HAIR LOSS Traditionally, hair loss is divided into cicatricial or noncicatricial types in dermatologic fields. Cicatricial type includes lymphocytic primary cicatricial alopecia, neutrophilic primary cicatricial alopecia, and tinea capitis. The loss of hair follicle stem cells in the bulge is observed in the cicatricial type of hair loss.7 The noncicatricial type is often divided into three categories depending on the pattern of involvement, namely, focal, patterned, and diffuse types. Alopecia areata, alopecia syphilitica, and hair loss related to mechanical pressure including traction alopecia and postoperative hair loss fall into the focal type. Trichotillomania and male pattern or female pattern alopecia are examples of patterned alopecia. Diffuse type is subdivided into anagen effluvium, telogen effluvium, loose anagen syndrome, hypotrichosis simplex, and atrichia with papular lesions. Most of the chemotherapy-induced hair loss or alopecia (CIA) falls into the telogen effluvium or anagen effluvium categories of the diffuse type. In CIA, immediate anagen release is the most important mechanism inducing telogen effluvium or hair breakage. The affected hair is prematurely forced into telogen, leading to a greater amount of shedding. Intravenously administered chemotherapy and combination chemotherapy increase the risk and extent of hair loss.5,8 In most cases, losing scalp hair becomes the biggest concern for the patients, but eyebrow, eyelash, axillary, and pubic hair and hair on any other body part can be affected. Hair loss begins approximately 2 to 4 weeks after starting treatment, and hair usually begin to return 3 to 6 months after cessation. Full recovery occurs within 6 to 12 months. Hair can be more brittle, curled, or hypopigmented when it returns, even though it gradually becomes

Depending on the goal of the treatment, expected changes in the hair should be counseled when discussing the options, and any regimen that can cause potential permanent hair changes should be chosen carefully, especially when treating patients with curative intent. A majority of patients report that planning whether or not to shave and when to do so and ordering a wig or a hairpiece in advance helped them to cope with the challenges associated with hair loss. DIAGNOSIS OF HAIR LOSS A complete personal and family history and physical examination including cancer treatment history and chemical or radiation exposure will be essential for an accurate diagnosis. Providers should question patients about the onset and location of any scalp symptoms. A thorough review of medication and treatment history is critical to diagnose CIA and rule out any other causes. The pattern of hair loss (i.e., diffuse or patchy) is a helpful physical finding for the differential diagnosis. Hair loss might not be noticeable to the provider until more than 50% of hair is lost. A workup should include a complete blood count, thyroid function studies, rapid plasma reagin (RPR), Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) test, and antinuclear antibody. Bacterial or fungal infections on the scalp and zinc, iron, vitamin D, or other nutritional deficiencies should be ruled out because these conditions can be medically managed. OTHER HAIR-ASSOCIATED CHANGES Many patients report changes in hair quality after cancer treatment. Hair can be more brittle, curly, or straight compared to the original hair. Returned hair can be lighter or bleached looking; however, with some agents, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitors, regrowing hair may be darker or thicker. EGFR inhibitors such as cetuximab,36,37 erlotinib,38,39 and gefitinib40,41 and multikinase inhibitors such as sorafenib42 have been reported to cause abnormal hair growth, including eyelash trichomegaly with or without hypertrichosis. Small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitors are well known to cause depigmentation. A change in the stem cell factor (SCF)/c-Kit interaction affecting the critical step in melanogenesis during early anagen has been proposed as a potential mechanism. Multikinase inhibitors affecting c-Kit or downstream signaling pathways can cause hair color change, which is sometimes coupled with skin pigmentation issues. In almost all cases, the hair depigmentation or hypopigmentation is fully reversible after cessation of treatment. Imatinib is known to cause both hypopigmentation and hyperpigmentation, but the mechanism is not well understood.43–46 Repigmentation has been described, although rarely, with the use of thalidomide, lenalidomide, erlotinib, and adalimumab.47–50 Recently, 14 cases of hair repigmentation have been reported with different immune checkpoint inhibitors including nivolumab, atezolizumab, and pembrolizumab in non–small-cell lung cancer patients with favorable response to therapy; interestingly enough, vitiligo, the loss of skin pigment, has also been reported as an autoimmune adverse reaction with use of immune checkpoint inhibitors.51,52 FUTURE CONSIDERATIONS Although CIA is not a life-threatening AE, patients identify CIA as a disturbing and stressful event that might even affect their choice of the treatment. Providers are observing a growing number of different hair changes with the expanded use of small-molecule inhibitors and biologics, including hypertrichosis and hair color changes. To meet the growing need for HRQL research, a quantitative grading scale should be used to standardize hair changes and the impact of such changes on quality of life. REFERENCES 1. DeCherney INTRODUCTION The increased survival associated with oncologic treatment has made the late-term effects, such as gonadal failure, increasingly important. When the cancer is controlled, quality of life, which often includes the ability to have a normal child, then becomes a major issue.1–3 The 5-year survival rate of young cancer patients is over 85%, and more than 75% of children with cancer will have a 10-year survival.3,4 Furthermore, the number of women younger than age 50 years, and thus likely premenopausal, who are estimated to be diagnosed with invasive breast cancer in 2017 is 48,080.5 These statistics signify that gonadal dysfunction from the effects of treatment is becoming even more important. Both neoplastic disease and its treatment can interfere with normal sexual and reproductive function (Table 133.1). Testicular and ovarian cancers directly involve the gonad, and prostate, endometrial, and cervical cancers directly involve the reproductive tract. Surgical treatment for any of these diseases results in damage or loss of these important reproductive organs. Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) for testicular and colon cancer, prostatectomy, and surgery involving the bladder neck may result in loss of the ability to ejaculate. Primary and metastatic tumors in the hypothalamus and pituitary can directly affect gonadotropin secretion, resulting in secondary hypogonadism. Both chemotherapy and radiation cause toxic effects on the male and female gonads. Cytotoxic therapies delivered to women during pregnancy can have teratogenic effects on the fetus. If fertility is maintained or recovers, there remains the concern about the heritability of cancer and at least a theoretical risk of mutagenic alterations to germ cells caused by cytotoxic therapies. The literature on the safety of male reproduction just after and during treatment is still unclear largely because of methodologic differences and different end points assessed by studies.6 More well-controlled studies are needed in this area to address these concerns. The seminiferous tubules contain the germ cells, which consist of stem and differentiating spermatogonia; spermatocytes; spermatids; sperm; and the Sertoli cells, which support and regulate germ cell differentiation. Sperm Cryopreservation Semen cryopreservation is an important procedure for preserving the fertility potential of men after cytotoxic treatment for cancer.94 The significance of notifying the patient of the potential risk of iatrogenic sterility as early as possible cannot be overemphasized.95 Physicians often are aware early during the diagnostic process that the patient will most likely need to receive potentially sterilizing cytotoxic therapy, although the exact diagnosis, stage, and treatment regimen may not have yet been decided. About 95% of providers mention fertility preservation prior to treatment to pediatric and adolescent cancer patients, with over 50% recommending sperm banking.96 This time should be used to initiate and complete the cryopreservation procedure. The number of samples to be banked may depend on how much time is available before starting therapy, sperm quality, and the cost of storing samples. A collection of three or four samples with approximately 48-hour periods of abstinence between sampling (a total of more than 5 days) is ideal. PHARMACOLOGIC ATTEMPTS AT PRESERVING FERTILITY IN WOMEN Although studies have been performed to assess the efficacy of oral contraceptive pills and GnRH analogs in girls, adolescents, and women, no comparative studies have been done using progestins in these age groups. Most studies do not support the use of hormonal therapy for the prevention of premature ovarian failure in girls and premenarchal adolescents receiving chemotherapy because prior to the onset of menarche, the ovaries are thought to be quiescent and less likely to be subject to damage by cytotoxic agents. Therefore, there would be no additional benefit to giving hormonal therapy to an already suppressed hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis. Furthermore, the use of estrogen may be associated with an increased risk of venous thrombosis. There is also concern regarding the side effect profile of hormonal therapy in premenarchal girls. Longhi et al.106 performed a small, observational study that examined the effects of oral contraceptive pills on ovarian function in premenarchal girls and postmenarchal women undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy treatment for osteosarcoma. They concluded that age and alkylant dose were the most predictive factors for early menopause and that oral contraceptives during high-dose alkylant-based chemotherapy did not prevent chemotherapy-induced premature ovarian failure. The follow-up time of this study was too short to rule out any positive long-term effects on the preservation of ovarian function. In addition, this study did show greater risk than benefit because two patients in the group receiving chemotherapy plus oral contraceptive pills developed thrombophlebitis. Similar findings have been observed in other studies.107 The majority of the evidence suggests that children and premenarchal adolescents do not benefit from hormonal suppression to preserve their ovarian function while undergoing chemotherapy. These agents induce both single-gene and chromosomal mutations in germ cells of animals,185 both of which cause genetic disease in the offspring. Mutations induced in stem spermatogonia cause the continued production of mutation-carrying sperm for the lifetime of the male, whereas those induced in later stages of spermatogenesis result in the production of mutation-carrying sperm for only a few months. Berger INTRODUCTION Fatigue is recognized as one of the most common symptoms in patients receiving treatment for cancer, often persisting beyond the conclusion of active treatment and at the end of life. Longitudinal and comparative studies indicate that fatigue may also be a significant problem for cancer survivors, with many survivors reporting fatigue scores higher than that of an age-matched general population. Depending on how fatigue is defined and measured, prevalence estimates of fatigue vary across the cancer continuum from 25% to 99%.1–5 Cancer-related fatigue (CRF) is a multifaceted condition characterized by diminished energy and an increased need to rest, disproportionate to any recent change in activity level, and accompanied by a range of other characteristics, including generalized weakness, diminished mental concentration, insomnia or hypersomnia, and emotional reactivity. Fatigue is often found to occur as a component of a cluster of symptoms such as depression, pain, sleep disturbance, and menopausal symptoms. Consequences of CRF include decrements in physical, social, cognitive, and vocational functioning; mood and sleep disturbances; and emotional and spiritual distress for both the patient and the family members.6 This chapter reviews the state of the science concerning CRF, addressing (1) the definition, risk factors, and mechanisms of CRF; (2) screening and evaluation of the patient with CRF; and (3) evidence-based pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions to prevent and manage CRF during and after cancer and its treatment. DEFINITION, RISK FACTORS, AND MECHANISMS OF CANCER-RELATED FATIGUE The etiology and clinical expression of CRF is multidimensional. An inherently subjective condition, fatigue may be experienced and reported differently by each individual. Qualitative studies of fatigue underscore the fact that the cancer fatigue experience is unlike any other fatigue patients have previously experienced, and patients emphasize that its unpredictability and refractoriness to self-management strategies that were previously effective make fatigue a particularly distressing symptom. Personality and coping style may also influence the experience of CRF. Some patients complain of a loss of efficiency, mental fogginess, and inertia and that sleep is not restorative; others de

(HPA) disruption, altered circadian rhythmicity, diminished heart rate variability, immune dysfunction, serotonin dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, 5-hydroxytryptophan (5-HT) dysregulation, and proinflammatory cytokine activity are among the mechanisms that directly or indirectly contribute to CRF.10–12 Studies also suggest that fatigue may be related to impairments in neuromuscular metabolism and function, the presence of concurrent symptoms such as pain and dyspnea, psychological and coping responses, and imbalanced neuroendocrine– immune stress responses.9,13 Evidence also suggests associations between CRF and comorbidities including anemia; mood disorder; electrolyte disturbances; cardiopulmonary, hepatic, or renal dysfunction; hypothyroidism; hypogonadism; adrenal insufficiency; infection; dehydration; protein-calorie malnutrition; cachexia, asthenia, and deconditioning; and the side effects of drugs such as opioid analgesics or anticonvulsants that act on a central nervous system. Altered energy metabolism within skeletal muscle has also been postulated to cause CRF. The tumor itself and the cancer- directed treatment can produce anemia, cachexia, and/or sarcopenia, and these may contribute to altered skeletal muscle energy metabolism, disrupted mitochondrial synthesis of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), or diminished oxygen delivery to muscle cells.14 In any one individual, the etiology of CRF is likely to be multifactorial, and the mechanisms and contributors to CRF may fluctuate across the disease and treatment trajectory. For example, fatigue may be present during treatment due to cytopenias but may persist through survivorship due to asthenia, sarcopenia, and physical deconditioning. Dr. AVR @ TMH RELATED FATIGUE Studies suggest that CRF is underdiagnosed, that the assessment of fatigue in patients with cancer is suboptimal, and that health-care professionals may not fully appreciate the degree of distress and functional loss that fatigue produces.15,16 Identified barriers to communication between patients and their clinicians about fatigue include a tendency to view fatigue as an inevitable consequence of illness, clinicians’ failure to offer interventions, patients’ lack of awareness of effective treatments for fatigue, a desire on the patient’s part to treat fatigue without medications, and a tendency to be stoic about fatigue to avoid being labeled as a “complainer” and to avoid prompting a change in therapy toward less active or aggressive treatments. Instruments to evaluate patient-derived barriers to fatigue management, self-efficacy for fatigue management, and the contributing factors to fatigue have been proposed.17,18 Identifying patients with CRF is the first key step in improving fatigue evaluation and management. Although there is currently no consensus concerning the optimal method or frequency to screen for CRF in the clinical or research setting, evidence of the widespread occurrence of CRF suggests that routine screening for CRF at regular intervals throughout treatment, follow-up, and long-term follow-up is warranted. There is accumulating evidence that brief one- or two-item measures to screen for fatigue are rapid and sensitive and can be applied efficiently in the clinic to identify patients who would benefit from more systematic evaluation.19,20 Based on National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines, fatigue should be assessed quantitatively on a 0 to 10 scale (0 = no fatigue and 10 = worst fatigue imaginable); patients with a severity of >4 should be further evaluated by history and physical examination.6 Although a brief measure may provide rapid assessment of general fatigue or serve as a screening tool, evidence suggests that brief measures do not fully capture all the dimensions of fatigue.21 It is theorized that fatigue generally consists of a sensory dimension (fatigue severity, persistence), a physiologic dimension (e.g., leg weakness, diminished mental concentration), and a performance dimension (reduction in performance of needed or valued activities), although evidence is mixed whether measures

In evaluating the patient with CRF, it is important to screen for treatable etiologic or potentiating factors including hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, adrenal insufficiency, cardiomyopathy, pulmonary dysfunction, anemia, sleep disturbance, fluid and electrolyte imbalances, emotional distress, physical inactivity, deconditioning, and uncontrolled concurrent symptoms.29–32 The medication profile should also be reviewed to identify specific classes of medications, such as opiates, antidepressants, anticonvulsants, antiemetics, antihistamines, and β-blockers, and drug–drug interactions that can also intensify fatigue.33 Evaluation should also include whether disease progression or recurrence could be among the causes of fatigue. INTERVENTIONS FOR CANCER-RELATED FATIGUE Because fatigue typically has several different causes in any one patient, the treatment plan needs to be individualized. Open communication between the patient, family, and caregiving team will facilitate discussion about the experience of fatigue and its effects on daily life. General supportive care recommendations for patients with fatigue include encouraging a balanced diet with adequate intake of fluid, calories, protein, carbohydrates, fat, vitamins, and minerals and balancing rest with physical activity and attention-restoring activities such as exposure to natural environments and pleasant distractions such as music. Targeted anticytokine therapy67 and thyrotropin-releasing hormone68 have shown preliminary evidence of effectiveness in reducing CRF; however, small sample sizes and the nonrandomized uncontrolled study design limit the strength of the conclusions that can be drawn. Several nutritional and herbal supplements (e.g., guarana, Essiac, valerian, vitamin supplements, zinc, levocarnitine, coenzyme Q10, mistletoe extract) and combined-modality interventions that incorporate several complementary therapies (e.g., megestrol acetate and omega-3 fatty acid supplementation) have also been evaluated with mixed evidence for efficacy.6,34,69 Interpretation of the study outcomes in these trials is limited by small sample sizes and the predominantly single-arm, open-label study design. NONPHARMACOLOGIC INTERVENTIONS Exercise, Physical Activity, and Structured Rehabilitation Meta-analyses of randomized trials support the benefits of physical activity and exercise in the management of fatigue during and after cancer treatment in patients with breast or prostate cancer, patients with other solid tumors, or patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, although effect sizes are generally small and positive results for the outcome of fatigue have not been uniformly observed across studies.26,70–73 The exercise modalities that have been applied differ in content (walking, cycling, swimming, resistive exercise, or combined exercise), frequency (ranging from two times per week to two times daily), intensity (with most programs at 50% to 90% of the estimated maximal oxygen consumption and heart rate), degree of supervision (fully supervised group versus self-directed exercise), and duration (from 2 weeks up to 1 year). Additional knowledge about the type, intensity, and duration of physical exercise that is most beneficial in reducing fatigue at different stages of disease, and treatment is needed to support tailored exercise prescription. At present, national guidelines recommend that patients aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate- intensity physical activity each week and that they incorporate strength training twice weekly.74 Comorbidities and the adverse effects of treatment may require exercise adaptations.75 Referrals to community-based exercise programs, comprehensive rehabilitation programs, or an exercise professional should be considered.6 Other types of p

Dr. AVR @ TMH Energy conservation and activity management are self-management interventions that teach patients to apply the principles of energy conservation and activity management and provide coaching to integrate these activities into patients’ daily lifestyle.6 Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) approaches (with or without hypnosis) directed specifically to fatigue, depression, or pain have also shown generally promising results for the relief of CRF in a variety of cancer patient populations during and after treatment.34,93,94 There is emerging evidence that psychoeducational and self-management interventions for CRF can be effectively delivered using mobile health approaches,95–97 which may increase access. Interventions to Improve Sleep Quality and Circadian Rhythmicity Studies indicate that cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), an intervention approach specifically designed to improve sleep quality, also has a beneficial effect on fatigue.34,98 In contrast, the efficacy of pharmacologic therapies in treating fatigue by reducing insomnia has had very little systematic study. CBT to improve sleep quality can be delivered individually, in a group setting, or via the Web. Components of CBT for sleep include relaxation training along with sleep-consolidation strategies (avoiding long or late afternoon naps, limiting time in bed to actual sleep time), stimulus control therapy (going to bed only when sleepy, using bed and bedroom for sleep and sexual activities only, having a consistent time to lie down and get up, avoiding caffeine and stimulating activity in the evening), and strategies to reduce cognitive-emotional arousal (taking at least an hour to relax before going to bed and establishing a presleep routine to be used every night).99 Morning exposure to bright light has been shown to prevent deterioration in CRF during chemotherapy for breast cancer, potentially by protecting recipients from circadian rhythm desynchronization during cancer treatment.100–102 Bright light therapy also improved fatigue outcomes in posttreatment survivors.103,104 COMPLEMENTARY AND INTEGRATIVE THERAPIES There is an expanding body of evidence supporting the efficacy of complementary and integrative therapies in the management of CRF, including progressive muscle relaxation with or without imagery, relaxation breathing, coping skills training, meditation, mind

designed randomized trials include physical activity and exercise; psychoeducational interventions; measures to optimize sleep quality; management of concurrent symptoms; comprehensive rehabilitation, yoga; mindfulness- based stress reduction; bright light therapy; and integrative and behavioral approaches such as acupuncture, progressive muscle relaxation, and massage. Travis INTRODUCTION Second primary cancers (SPCs) are one of the most serious and potentially lethal complications of cancer and its therapy. Subsequent malignancies now compose almost one in five incident cancers in the United States, superseding first cancers of breast, lung, and prostate.1 Whereas the number of first primary cancers increased by 70% over the past four decades, the number of SPCs increased by more than 300% during the same period.1 These increases mirror advances in cancer survival and reflect improvements in early detection, treatment, and supportive care. For all cancers combined, the 5-year relative survival rate has advanced steadily over the past few decades and is approximately 69% for patients diagnosed between 2005 and 2011.2 There are presently over 15.5 million cancer survivors in the United States, representing approximately 4.8% of the population.3 By 2026, it is anticipated that this population will expand to 20.3 million.3 Commensurately, it is expected that the number of patients with subsequent and higher order malignancies will increase. Aside from recurrence or progression of a primary cancer, SPCs have remained the most common cause of death among childhood cancer survivors despite decreases in SPC mortality rates over the past few decades attributable to reductions in treatment exposures.4 A population-based investigation within the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) program found that adolescent and young adults with a second Hodgkin lymphoma; sarcoma; or breast, thyroid, or testicular cancer (TC) had a greater than twofold increased risk of cancer-specific death compared with patients with the same primary malignant neoplasm.5 Possible explanations for these outcomes may include an inferior response to treatment, limitations on the types or doses of therapies that can be administered, or impaired physiologic reserves that impact the ability to tolerate further cancer therapies. Moreover, a number of patients may develop third and higher order cancers after therapy for either childhood6 or adult-onset cancers.7 SPCs may not necessarily be due to the late sequelae of cytotoxic treatment but rather reflect shared etiologic influences (including tobacco and excessive alcohol intake), envi

Most data on the carcinogenic effects of radiation in the higher dose range were derived from cancer survivors given therapeutic radiation.11,24 In assessing radiation-related SPCs in these patients, it is important to take into consideration other potential contributing factors. These include exposure to cytotoxic drugs (refer to “Chemotherapy” section), genetic predisposition (refer to “Genetic Susceptibility to Second Primary Cancers” section), immunosuppression, infections, environmental exposures, and heightened surveillance in cancer survivors.8,9 Tobacco use increases the risk of treatment-related lung cancer in a multiplicative manner as demonstrated in a case-control study of Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) survivors.25 Younger age at irradiation is associated with a significantly increased risk of breast cancer26 and thyroid cancer,27 as shown in survivors of HL, breast cancer,28 and childhood cancer.11 However, early menopause has a protective effect on breast cancer after radiotherapy in HL survivors,29,30 suggesting that ovarian hormones play an important role in promoting tumorigenesis once radiation has induced an initiating event. Risk of radiation-related cancer has been shown to increase with increasing dose for cancers of the breast,29–32 esophagus,33 lungs,25 and stomach34,35; meningioma36; sarcoma37,38; and pancreatic cancer,39,40 with no evidence of a downturn in risk at high doses. An exception to these trends is thyroid cancer risk, which has been shown to decrease after high doses (also see “Pediatric Malignancies” section).41 The radiation dose–response relationship in SPC development, therefore, appears to be tissue specific. A systemic review of data on the radiation dose– response relationship for 11 second solid cancers found that for most SPCs (except thyroid cancer), the dose– response curve was linear, even at doses of 60 Gy or higher.24 In addition to radiation dose, radiotherapy fields, which directly reflect the volume of normal exposed tissue, can affect SPC risk. However, shared risk alleles for pathologically independent cancers72,73 can make it difficult to identify true risk alleles for treatment-induced cancer. As such, the inclusion of reference groups controlling for shared risk in genetic epidemiology studies of therapy-induced cancer is a high priority.74 Further, specific therapeutic exposures can be associated with the acquisition of defined somatic alterations, and the presence of these can increase confidence that an SPC is treatment related. Phase I involves activation of substrates into reactive electrophilic intermediates that can damage DNA, a reaction principally performed by the cytochrome P450 family of enzymes. Phase II enzymes (conjugation) function to inactivate genotoxic substrates and include glutathione S-transferase (GST) and NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase-1. High phase I activity and low phase II activity can result in DNA damage from excess harmful products of chemotherapy. Expression of these enzymes is highly variable among individuals because of several functionally relevant genetic polymorphisms, some of which are reported to impact on SPC risk via gene–exposure interactions.74 For example, a functional polymorphism in GSTP1 is associated with a significantly increased risk (odds ratio [OR], 4.34) of developing t- AML after exposure to chemotherapy with a leukemogenic GSTP1 substrate (chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, melphalan, or doxorubicin) but does not influence the risk of radiogenic leukemia.84 DNA damage signaling and repair protects cells from mutations that can lead to cancer initiation and progression. It is also possible that somatic telomere shortening is a risk factor for treatment- induced SPC whereby precancerous cells are primed for transformation on exposure to genotoxic radiotherapy or chemotherapy, just as clonal hematopoiesis is an SPC risk factor.78 These studies highlight the importance of gene–exposure interactions in SPC studies and also demonstrate that genetic risk is multifactorial, with both constitutional and somatically acquired genetics likely defining risk. Evidence suggests that gene–gene interactions can also impact on SPC risk. Moreover, precise estimates of the magnitude of the effect(s) are required in order to develop personalized risk-adapted clinical strategies, including dose modification, alternative treatments, and posttherapy surveillance. Risk management could prove particularly important in children or young adults with primary cancers where cure rates are high and the risk of a subsequent cancer is associated with substantial morbidity or premature mortality. Studies have consistently shown that young age at radiotherapy is associated with a significantly higher risk of breast cancer. In a large population-based cohort study,111 the absolute risks of breast cancer in women diagnosed with HL at ages 15 to 25 years were higher than the absolute risks of women in the general population between 50 and 54 years old, a standard age when mammography screening is recommended. Travis et al.122 developed estimates of the cumulative absolute risk of breast cancer, taking into account age and calendar year of HL diagnosis, current age, radiation dose, and competing causes of mortality. Thus, for an HL survivor with history of mantle field radiation therapy to a dose of ≥40 Gy at age 25 years, the cumulative absolute risks of breast cancer at 10, 20, and 30 years were estimated to be 1.4%, 11%, and 29%, respectively. There is a clear radiation dose–response relationship for breast cancer risk after HL. In an international case- control study of breast cancer after HL that included 105 cases of breast cancer and 266 matched controls,29 radiation dose to the area of the breast where the tumor developed in the case (and a comparable area in controls) was estimated. Familial RB is caused by inherited mutations in the RB1 tumor suppressor gene.229 Approximately 90% of hereditary RB patients have bilateral disease. In a large cohort of 1,601 RB survivors in Boston and New York, SPC risk was increased 19-fold in hereditary RB survivors; risk was not elevated in nonhereditary patients.174 The 50-year cumulative incidence of an SPC was 36% and 5.7% in hereditary and nonhereditary patients, respectively. Among hereditary RB patients, radiotherapy increased the 50-year cumulative incidence of an SPC to 38.2%, compared to 21.0% in nonirradiated patients. In an extended follow-up of the 906 hereditary RB survivors in this cohort, 33% of RB survivors developed at least one SPC (median follow-up, 26.3 years; range, 0.6 to 63.0 years), and 6% developed more than one SPC.230 Similar risks among hereditary RB survivors have been reported in Dutch176 and British231 nationwide cohorts. The 50-year cumulative mortality from any SPC for hereditary RB survivors has ranged from 17.3% to 25.5%.232,233 The majority of SPCs are bone and soft tissue sarcomas occurring in the most heavily irradiated areas (i.e., head and neck region). Cerhan INTRODUCTION Cognitive dysfunction occurs in most patients with brain tumors, often at presentation, and is frequently progressive. In non–central nervous system (CNS) cancers, there is a growing understanding of the potential cognitive impact of the cancer process itself and of systemic cancer therapies. Treatment options for cognitive deficits remain quite limited. Therefore, it is crucial to consider the cognitive risks and benefits associated with specific interventions when making clinical decisions in cancer care. Fortunately, preventive measures and therapeutic innovations are emerging that aim to lessen cognitive impact. ASSESSMENT OF COGNITIVE FUNCTION Cognition is integral to virtually all activities of daily living, and even small changes in cognitive function can have significant impact on quality of life and independence. Patients and caregivers alike often find cognitive problems more challenging to manage than physical problems, contributing to illness burden and stress. Cognitive changes with significant impact on daily functioning may not be evident on casual observation or detectable via routine medical evaluations such as bedside mental status exams. Furthermore, patient self-report is important but does not routinely correlate with objectively measured cognitive function or functional outcomes.1 If unrecognized, cognitive deficits can lead to inaccurate judgment on the part of the medical team regarding the patient’s capacity for self-care or return to activities such as school, work, or driving. Failing to detect cognitive changes could also lead providers to have inaccurate perceptions about treatment effectiveness and safety. A formal neuropsychological assessment provides quantitative, objective measurement of potentially subtle, yet clinically significant, changes in cognitive function. The testing involves administration of standardized psychometric instruments that evaluate various aspects of brain function such as attention, learning and memory, processing speed, expressive and receptive language, executive function (e.g., abstract reasoning, planning, decision making), visual perception and construction, and mood and personality. Whether the predominant cause of cognitive decline in patients with brain tumors is the treatment or the tumor itself is an important question and has a significant impact on treatment recommendations. Older studies have emphasized the late neurotoxicity of treatment, especially radiotherapy. However, these studies have suffered from a number of deficiencies; most importantly, they have lacked baseline cognitive testing and thus missed the fact that the brain tumor itself is often the primary cause of cognitive difficulties. One large prospective trial with baseline evaluations (i.e., before whole-brain radiotherapy [WBRT]) found that more than 90% of patients with brain metastases had significant cognitive impairment in one or more cognitive tests, and another trial of patients with brain metastases found mean and median baseline cognitive scores well below population norms, ranging from mild to severe impairment.3,4 Other studies have similarly found tumor to be the dominant cause of cognitive impairment in patients with brain metastases,5 low-grade gliomas,6 and high-grade gliomas.7 However, the pattern of cognitive impairment with tumor is often different than that of other disease processes in the brain. For example, impairments are often more subtle and diffuse in patients with tumors than are those observed in patients with sudden-onset neurologic conditions such as a stroke. Differences in the pathophysiology of these lesions are believed to underlie these observations; whereas a cerebrovascular accident may rapidly result in tissue destruction, tumors diffusely and often more slowly infiltrate the brain. There is also mounting evidence that cognitive decline in brain tumor patients after therapy may frequently reflect subclinical tumor progression rather than neurotoxicity resulting from treatment. In a North Central Cancer Treatment Group study of 1,244 patients with high-grade gliomas prospectively treated with radiation and nitrosourea-based chemotherapy, cognitive deterioration was noted at evaluations prior to radiographic failure; in contrast, patients without tumor progression had stable cognitive function.8 In an MD Anderson Cancer Center study of 56 patients with recurrent high-grade gliomas treated on phase I and II trials, cognitive deterioration occurred 6 weeks before radiographic failure, highlighting the sensitivity and predictive val

Prospective studies have established the safety of modern, focal treatments, but risks remain, especially with less focused treatments such as WBRT. When analyzing potential cognitive effects of focal radiotherapy, low-grade brain tumors are a useful population to study because their relatively long progression-free survival makes it easier to separate treatment and tumor effects. In addition, patients with low-grade brain tumors are often young and do not have underlying medical comorbidities that may confound the cognitive analyses. A number of studies have prospectively performed extensive neuropsychological testing on adult patients with low-grade neoplasms before (baseline) and after radiotherapy (up to 6 years after radiotherapy) (Table 136.1). In general, these studies have not found significant cognitive deterioration when compared to either baseline16–19 or control groups with low-grade brain neoplasms not treated with radiotherapy.6,20 For example, a subpopulation of 20 of the 203 adult patients with low-grade gliomas enrolled on an intergroup prospective phase III trial that randomized patients to 50.4 or 64.8 Gy underwent cognitive testing before and up to 5 years after localized radiation therapy.18 No significant losses in general intellectual function, new learning function, or memory function were seen. The group’s mean test scores were higher at follow-up evaluations than their initial performances on all psychometric measures, although the improvement was not statistically significant. However, 4 patients, all in the 64.8 Gy arm, had a mild decline in one or more of the domains assessed. Protons are charged particles that are able to deposit most of the dose into the target and markedly reduce excess dose to surrounding normal tissues. Because of the favorable physical properties of proton radiotherapy, there is a growing interest in using protons to treat brain tumors to decrease the risk of adverse cognitive effects of treatment. A prospective trial of 20 patients with low-grade glioma treated with protons (54 Gy in 30 fractions) found no decline in cognitive functioning or quality of life over time (median follow-up, 5.1 years).22 An extreme form of focal radiotherapy used to treat many benign and neoplastic cranial conditions is stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS). Radiosurgery uses multiple radiation beams and is able to encompass treatment volumes in the high-dose region with small margins because of the stereotactic imaging and immobilization. This results in rapid dose falloff, allowing greater sparing of normal brain tissues, and therefore minimizes risk to the surrounding structures. The cognitive impact of radiosurgery was evaluated in a prospective trial assessing 95 patients with cerebral arteriovenous malformations with extensive neuropsychometric testing before and after radiosurgery (median dose, 20 Gy in one fraction). All measures of cognitive function were stable or improved 3 years after radiosurgery.23 A prospective study of 97 patients with brain metastases treated with radiosurgery (18 to 21 Gy in a single fraction or, for larger metastases, 24 Gy in three fractions) found cognitive function to be stable 6 months after radiosurgery.24 In another prospective trial, hypothalamic hamartomas associated with epilepsy were treated with radiosurgery (median marginal dose, 17 Gy). Complete neuropsychological evaluation was available in 39 patients; evaluation of cognitive function greater than 3 years after radiosurgery found no significant decline, and clear improvement was seen in 13% of patients.25 In sharp contrast to focal cranial radiation, WBRT is associated with high rates of cognitive decline. In a phase III trial comparing radiosurgery alone to radiosurgery and WBRT in 58 patients with up to three brain metastases, 49% of patients in the WBRT group experienced declines in learning and memory at 4 months compared to only 23% of patients in the radiosurgery group.26 An intergroup trial, N0574, randomized 213 patients with
